“I didn’t make it a topic. It was not a topic for me. I’m just thinking about Spain and the team and meetings. The players have more time than me. So I can imagine they talk about it. It’s good they do. I don’t think it was a distraction for them.”

Kane added: “There was a discussion, but when we’re with England, we kind of put club football to one side and it was no different this week.”

Tuchel also refused to point the finger of blame at Guéhi, O’Reilly or Kane, who missed a penalty, for England’s defeat despite admitting his team got off to the worst possible start by conceding a goal after two minutes.

“We will focus on the positives, but also highlight the stuff we can do better,” Tuchel said. “Not even speaking about individual mistakes because this is normal. It just happens. It should not happen, and for sure not in this amount. But there is no sense in showing the individual mistakes or telling them ‘please don’t make mistakes’. That is normal, but we can do things better. We can defend the third goal better. But we will focus on the positives. There is a lot to take away from the game.

“We wanted to be the team desperately to beat them [Spain] and we think we had them. We still think we had them at half-time. That was the way the team showed up after half-time. So we will focus on that, but the reality is we lost and the reality is we need to prove it again.”

News.title: Red Roses triumph over New Zealand in chaotic late scenes – how it unfolded
News.content:
Just when it looked like the Red Roses’ lustre was beginning to fade, up stepped Zoe Harrison.

In one of the most dramatic finishes to an England match in recent memory, the fly-half gobbled up Amy Du Plessis’s pass to glide over the whitewash and secure a pulsating win over New Zealand.

Ever the epitome of calmness, Harrison was undeterred by the fact she had just missed what would have been a match-winning penalty from 42 metres out with the score locked at 19-19.

But after their arm-wrestle with Canada last weekend in Exeter, which finished 26-26, there was simply no way the Red Roses were going to settle for a draw for a second week running.

A year to the day since they were crowned world champions in their own back yard, England’s status as the most dominant side in the women’s game was all but confirmed by this never-say-die victory over the Black Ferns.

News.title: Russell holds his nerve to see off Verstappen and win Azerbaijan GP
News.content:
The Azerbaijan Grand Prix weekend went the way many believed the 2026 season would play out. George Russell strolled to victory from pole, though with a little late jeopardy, whilst Kimi Antonelli’s crash in qualifying meant he had to fight his way through the field to finish fifth. That, after all, was the order of things last season.

Yet the past few days in Baku are an inversion of the season’s storyline. It is Antonelli who has been the faster driver, heading for a maiden world title at the second time of asking. Russell has been the troubled one. This was only the Briton’s third victory of the season and his first since Austria in late June. Antonelli has racked up eight wins and, before this weekend in Baku, a well-deserved 81-point lead over Russell.

Russell’s dominant and impressive run from pole to the chequered flag on Saturday is both a reminder of what he is capable of and also what might have been, had he been able to find this type of form earlier and more often. The reality, though, is that he needs to replicate this for the rest of the season to even be in with a sniff, barring a catastrophic meltdown from Antonelli. Still, Russell looked elated to have ended his barren run.

The finish was a little more tense than Russell deserved, having established a healthy lead in the first half of the race. Two late safety cars eradicated his advantage and helped put Max Verstappen’s Red Bull on his gearbox. In the end, he triumphed by just under 0.2sec and, as Antonelli finished fifth – with some help from two safety-car inducing crashes – he made up 15 points on his Mercedes team-mate. Isack Hadjar completed the podium for Red Bull after missing the past three races with a wrist injury.

News.title: Scotland’s Pocognoli era starts with encouraging signs but familiar issues in front of goal
News.content:
Scotland’s ramped-up second-half performance offered some cause for optimism as Sébastien Pocognoli’s tenure as head coach began with a goalless draw with Slovenia in Ljubljana.

The 39-year-old Belgian head coach, appointed in August as Steve Clarke’s successor, refreshed the side for the Nations League Group B1 opener in the Stozice Stadium, but they were fortunate on a couple of occasions at least not to fall behind before rallying before the break.

Scotland had been insipid and uninspiring for most of the first half but after the interval they played with pace and purpose as Slovenia captain and goalkeeper Jan Oblak became a key figure, making saves from Oli McBurnie and Kieron Bowie.

News.title: Carreras’ try-of-season contender helps Bath eclipse Harlequins
News.content:
And they kept playing, it was not until Richards scored in the 72nd minute that the game was decided. Still for Bath, a five-try victory away from home, felt like a decent return.

If they were to stand any chance of finding a way back into the game, Quins had to score first after the restart. They were rewarded for their attacking intent after running from a scrum deep in their half, with Murley cutting a brilliant line before Pedro Delgado drove over for his side’s third try.

Quins had the opportunity to further cut the deficit when first Sam Riley carried down the left wing and Cameron Anderson drove into the Bath 22. But as Quins looked to pick and go, Beno Obano and Guy Pepper combined to hold the ball up over the line.

It felt like a significant moment and when Riley was shown a yellow card for a high tackle on Obano moments later, the odds against a Quins comeback lengthened again. Yet there was something sticky about their resilience.

“I am really happy with the grit and the fight that they showed, particularly in the second half,” said Gilmore. “We had some massive defensive sets on our goal-line which we withstood. I reckon they were the moments last year that Bath would probably run in three tries really quickly and kick the score out, which is good.”

Bath emptied their bench, including the introduction of England flanker Pepper, but they could not pull away as expected in the final quarter, despite some impressive contributions by Tom de Glanville.

It was left to their line-out maul to score their first points of the second half, with Richards touching down to seal Harlequins’ fate. Still, there were enough promising glimpses to give Harlequins supporters hope that more encouraging days lie ahead.

The alter-ego of one Marvel superhero, the Incredible Hulk, used to famously say: “You won’t like me when I am angry,” and this is the case with Bellingham.

Although he has yet to turn green, he only seems to be at his best when he is raging, as was the case at Wembley.

Bellingham ended up rowing with Bernabeu team-mate Marc Cucurella yet that inner fury helped him drag England from a potentially disastrous first-half performance to a surprising 2-1 lead.

Bellingham also came agonisingly close to scoring an injury-time leveller but was denied by a save from Unai Simon.

Asked about how he thrives after getting annoyed with opponents, Tuchel smiled broadly. He said: “He likes that. He gets better if that happens. It’s better if he plays with a bit of rage. It’s what he does. I think sometimes he is looking for these moments to get his fire going.”

Sports.title: Whopping 38 Premier League teams could get compensation worth £500MILLION in prize money payback from Man City
Sports.content:

MANCHESTER CITY could theoretically owe over £500MILLION to 38 different clubs after being found guilty of breaching the Premier League’s financial rules.

City were declared guilty on all but one of the 115 charges they have been facing since 2023 following a four-year investigation by an independent commission.



However, sanctions have yet to be finalised as Man City continue to maintain their innocence and plan to appeal.

Breaches of Uefa’s Financial Fair Play regulations and the Prem’s own Profitability and Sustainability Rules were also among the charges.



City are facing severe consequences, such as points deductions, fines and even EXPULSION from the English top flight.

And according to data specialists OLBG, the Citizens could owe domestic rivals more than £527million in lost Premier League prize money if officials decided to make them cough up for it.

The theoretical figures are based from the 2011/12 campaign up until last season.

They are calculated by working out the extra cash each team would have got if City were taken out of the table.

In most cases it would mean teams moving up a spot every season and therefore getting a larger share of the prize money clubs get, which increases the higher a team finishes.

Last term’s figures are estimates as the Premier League has not yet published official payments for the 2025/26 campaign.



And the numbers suggest Man City could owe a total of £527,935,464 after the guilty verdict, if such a punishment was enforced.

Everton would be highest recipients as they could be due a staggering £28,944,186.

CASINO SPECIAL – BEST CASINO BONUSES FROM £10 DEPOSITS

And City’s biggest rivals Manchester United could get the second largest sum worth a whopping £28,118,305.



Arsenal, Chelsea and Liverpool may be owed over £20m EACH from their Premier League foe.

Man City chairman Khaldoon Al-Mubarak maintains the club’s innocence and insists they will be cleared of all charges on appeal.

And some within the legal industry believe that even if their appeal fails they could take matters to the High Court.

If this happens then this unprecedented case could rumble on until 2028.

Doherty clearly saw the funny side of his surprise involvement, sharing a clip of Barzel making the claim alongside a laughing emoji.

Israel boss Ran Ben-Shimon also commented on the matter.

Ben-Shimon said: “He didn’t know about it, this is his way to celebrate every goal he scores. He’s a young player, I’m sure this lesson will stay with him a long time, he made a mistake.”



Farchi appeared to poke fun at the controversy by posting a reel of the celebration on Instagram with a pool ball emoji.

This incident is part of a wider row during a week of controversy which sees Israel facing Ireland tonight.

Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson, whose side lost to Kosovo on Thursday, said: “We’re not playing with genocide, we’re playing against genocide. We’re playing against Israel, we’re not playing with Israel.”

Israel’s FA hit back, saying: “We have contributed to the world and humanity in countless fields, earning an impressive number of Nobel Prizes along the way.

“Unfortunately, we have not yet found a cure for stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy displayed by @IrelandFootball team coach. We’re not playing with ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity, we’re playing against the coach who embodies them.”



Bolton and Ireland goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu then decided to boycott the match over the ongoing conflict in Gaza – meaning Hallgrimsson was forced to name a defender as an emergency keeper for tonight’s match.

Sports.title: Roy Keane reveals stance on managerial return seven days on from surprise Celtic Park appearance
Sports.content:
Next

ROY KEANE has revealed where he stands on making a managerial return, a week after his surprise Celtic Park appearance got tongues wagging.

The ex-Hoops player and Man Utd legend watched on from the stands at Parkhead as the Celts were beaten 1-0 by Rangers.



That result – a second successive Old Firm defeat in the space of a week – saw the pressure from the Celtic fans ramp up.

Those derby defeats came either side of a 3-1 home defeat to Ferencvaros in the Europa League and a month from from the bruising Champions League qualifying exit at the hands of LASK in Austria.



All of that has led to plenty of speculation surrounding Martin O’Neill‘s future as Celtic manager.

Having twice been in interim charge last season, the 74-year old Hoops legend was handed the reins permanently after clinching a league and cup double last season.



Amid those doubts about O’Neill’s future after the second defeat to the Gers, Celtic chief executive Michael Nicholson publicly backed the manager in a statement within the club’s annual accounts last week.

And as it stands, O’Neill remains Celtic boss.

Watching on at Celtic Park last week was Roy Keane.

And his appearance had some putting two and two together and wondering if he was waiting in the wings as a potential next manager?



OUR BEST FREE BETS & SIGN-UP OFFERS

Well, Keane himself has recently insisted he would NEVER attend a game where a manager was feeling the heat.

On an Overlap podcast, he said: “I wouldn’t go and watch a manager under pressure. I know plenty who do that.”

Of course, it’s nothing unusual to see former players attend their old club’s matches.

Keane, 55, was a boyhood Celtic fan and had a spell as a Hoops player from 2005 until 2006.

He retired from playing after that brief Hoops stint and quickly landed the Sunderland manager’s job.



Keane was in charge at the Stadium of Light from 2006 until 2008, securing promotion to the Premier League in the process.

He was then boss of Ipswich from 2009 until 2011 – and that remains his last managerial role to date.

So, 15 years on, would Keane still consider a dugout return?

Well, that’s what he was asked by fellow Sky Sports pundit Micah Richards.

Keane admitted that ‘the pilot light is still on’ regarding a managerial comeback – but did conceded that it’s ‘unlikely’ to happen.



He told Sky Sports: “At weekends when I’m watching games, there are teams I watch and I think ‘I could go in there and do a job.’

“But it’s mostly at weekends, it’s not Monday morning when I’m having my scrambled egg at the local cafe!

“All these managers driving up on the motorway now and stresses.

“But yeah, I do think there’s always something there.

“The pilot light is still on for something.



“If someone gave me a phone call – who knows?

“It’s going to be unlikely.”

Keane added: “I’ve had opportunities over the last few years but then there’s contracts and staff issues and you go: ‘really?’



“Sometimes you go ‘stick to what you’re doing.'”

Keane has, of course, become one of the leading pundits in the country since retiring.

Sports.title: Man Utd dealt second injury blow as star limps off after Bruno Fernandes issue
Sports.content:
Man Utd dealt second injury blow as star limps off after Bruno Fernandes issue

Manchester United have been hit with further injury concerns just days after Bruno Fernandes suffered a 'complicated problem' against Wales in the Nations League

View 2 Images Patrick Dorgu limped off the pitch against Wales

Patrick Dorgu was forced off the pitch during Denmark's Nations League clash with Wales on Sunday afternoon, sparking further injury worries for Manchester United. It comes after Bruno Fernandes found himself injured against the same nation while representing Portugal.

‌



While Dorgu was selected to start on the left wing by Danish head coach, Brian Riemer, the 21-year-old lasted just 30 minutes of the encounter with the Red Dragons. The Red Devils talent was spotted falling to the turf in frustration before holding his leg, with Mohamed Daramy called upon to take his place.

‌



Dorgu was also spotted limping as he made his way off the pitch, in what could be a cause for concern regarding not only Denmark - who have another two matches to play this international break - but also United. He is the second United player who has taken a knock during the current Premier League break.

‌



Club captain, Fernandes, has joined Portugal on international duty, with his nation facing Wales earlier this week - running out 1-0 winners thanks to an early strike from Joao Felix. However, having picked up an injury during that encounter, he is now expected to miss Portugal's game with Norway on Sunday evening.

Bruno Fernandes cut from Portugal squad due to UEFA rules and 'complicated' issue READ MORE :

Premier League clubs consider legal action as Man Utd react to Man City guilty verdict READ MORE :

Head coach, Jorge Jesus, described the injury as a "complicated problem" when addressing the media in the aftermath of Portugal's Nations League opener. He said: "In the game against Wales, we went in with all the available players but Bruno Fernandes came off with a complicated problem."

He added: "He played with an injury he brought from Manchester United. He really wanted to play against Wales. He wasn’t at his usual level, we’ll see if he’s ready."

‌



Jesus continued: "He said he’s been dealing with that pain for about three games, and that was one of the factors that prevented him from being at his usual level against Wales.

"He was my player, I know him perfectly. I’ve already spoken to him. I prefer not to risk him in this game and have him clean and in good physical condition for the Denmark game."

View 2 Images Bruno Fernandes is also carrying an injury (Image: Getty Images)

‌

Sports.title: Liverpool suffer another injury blow as Cody Gakpo hurt on international duty
Sports.content:
Liverpool suffer another injury blow as Cody Gakpo hurt on international duty

Cody Gakpo was forced off with an injury just 17 minutes into the Netherlands' clash with Serbia in the Nations League, providing Liverpool with another scare during the international break

View 2 Images Cody Gakpo has picked up an injury (Image: ANP via Getty Images)

Liverpool have been dealt a second injury blow in a matter of hours after Cody Gakpo had to be substituted for the Netherlands. Gakpo, 27, signalled to come off in the 17th minute of Sunday's game away to Serbia after being on the end of two strong challenges in quick succesion.

‌



The forward had scored for his country last time out to earn a 1-1 draw with Germany on Thursday, continuing a hot streak of form. But Gakpo's productive start to the season could be halted by the injury, having limped off the pitch during the Nations League fixture.

‌



Netherlands boss Xavi Hernandez is expected to provide an update at full-time. Earlier on Sunday, Liverpool discovered that Alexander Isak had picked up a thigh injury while playing for Sweden.

‌



The striker has now left Sweden's camp and will miss their three remaining matches. Although Liverpool don't return to action until October 11 against Manchester City, Reds boss Andoni Iraola will likely be sweating over his team selection already.

Sports.title: Referee calls half-time two minutes early before U-turn after furious player backlash
Sports.content:
Referee calls half-time two minutes early before U-turn after furious player backlash

Players from both teams surrounded the referee after being short changed two first-half minutes and their furious backlash eventually led to a U-turn being made

View 2 Images Several players surrounded Isaac Searle after the first half's early end (Image: Sky Sports)

English Football League (EFL) referee Isaac Searle blew his whistle for half-time two minutes early during the League Two match between Oldham Athletic and Salford City. Only two of the four minutes of additional time had been played at Boundary Park when Mathew Hudson launched a long goal kick up-field.

‌



Searle then called time after the ball crossed in Salford's half just seconds into the 48th minute. Players from both sides, particularly from Oldham, who were 2-1 behind at the time, immediately complained.

‌



After a minute of deliberation, play eventually resumed. Searle had to beckon players who had left the pitch back on.

‌



Commentating on the match for Sky Sports, Joe Shennan: "That is, perhaps a little earlier than expected, the end of the first half. And Oldham are furious here with Isaac Searle."

Ireland forced into unusual decision after squad split over controversial Israel match READ MORE :

Oldham's Jamie Robson bounded over to the referee before shouting an arm's length away from his face. Keenan Appiah-Forson was already on the scene holding up four fingers, a gesture that Mike Fondop made after getting in between Robson and Searle.

Salford pair Brendan Wiredu and Will Aimison were also in the vicinity before eventually departing. The hosts' goalkeeper coach, Scott Davies, also came on the field to remonstrate.

‌



Shennan continued: "Two and a half minutes through four added at the end of the first half, and it appears as though we have reached the break. Oldham cannot contain their fury; they are behind.

"And what is the referee going to say here? Is he gonna call both sets of players back out, perhaps?

View 2 Images It took around a minute before Isaac Searle waved players back onto the pitch (Image: Sky Sports)

‌



JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

"Well, this is something that you don't often see anywhere in the EFL. They were ready for the half-time entertainment, but there is confusion in the stands and on the touchline." Television footage showed Oldham staff carrying two sets of goals back off the pitch.

One of Searle's assistant referees came across to consult with his colleague. So, too, did fourth official Sebastian Stockbridge.

Article continues below

After speaking to the latter, players were waved back onto the pitch, with the majority having walked off. Play restarted from the goal-kick, and they played out the remaining 90 seconds without further incident.

Co-commentator Sue Smith said: "Well, I've never seen anything like it, Joe. Certainly, a misunderstanding wasn't there? "I think some of the players have gone and had their drinks, and they were all ready to have a little half-time break, but I thought, 'it's way too early'.

Sports.title: Thomas Tuchel has failed his main England task and Spain defeat felt inevitable
Sports.content:
Thomas Tuchel’s England have played three matches at Wembley in 2026 and have not recorded a victory. They have been beaten by Japan and Spain and have drawn against Uruguay.

It continues to be a small wonder that Wembley is packed for every international. It will probably be close to full for the visit of the Czech Republic on Tuesday week.

To be fair, the 84,525 who showed up for the UEFA Nations League game against Spain were treated to a highly entertaining contest and an extended look at the wonder of Lamine Yamal.

But they heard familiar reflections from Tuchel. England could have won the game had certain moments gone their way.

‌



If my aunt had … etc, etc. You get the drift.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

The England manager suggested his side would have gone on to win had Harry Kane extended their one-goal lead from the penalty spot early in the second half, and, quite obviously, he has a point.

‌



But the Kane miss averts scrutiny of the gap in class between the two squads.

The statistics showed that Spain were marginally the more threatening side in a game that could have ended up with double its five-goal tally. The eyes showed that Spain were comfortably the more accomplished side.

England managed to win a knockabout bronze medal match against France at the World Cup but are generally found wanting against high-class opposition.

View 2 Images Tuchel's England fell short against world champions Spain

‌



Tuchel was brought in to change that. He hasn’t. Spain could have been out of sight before Anthony Gordon and Harry Kane led England’s impressive resurgence.

And it was impressive. Gordon was a constant threat and Jude Bellingham was at his belligerent best.

But there was a feeling of inevitability about the defeat. It is why punters were heading for the tube station some time before the final whistle.

It is why England’s lap of appreciation went pretty much unnoticed. There was an indifference to Tuchel on Saturday night and that will be the case all the way to the Euro finals.

‌



A victory over the world champions might - just might - have changed that, but the cold truth is that Tuchel failed in his original brief yet is still the manager entrusted to take England forward.

The fantastic attendances at Wembley are all the Football Association needs to be convinced their decision to keep the England team in Tuchel’s hands is the right one. And a slightly cavalier and error-prone display against the Spanish certainly made the latest game value for money.

But even if you did not agree with the move to have a third foreign manager in charge of the England national team, Tuchel’s initial short-term, win-or-bust mission had a frisson of excitement about it.

‌



There was in-game excitement against Spain, that is for sure. But there was also a familiarity about being second best against quality opposition - and an acceptance that Tuchel is unlikely to change that.

Sports.title: Spanish media react exactly as expected to Antony Gordon display as England team-mate ridiculed
Sports.content:
Spanish media react exactly as expected to Antony Gordon display as England team-mate ridiculed

Anthony Gordon's performance against Spain earned plenty of attention in the Spanish media as the Barcelona star impressed at Wembley - but one team-mate in particular wasn't so lucky

View 2 Images Anthony Gordon left his mark on the Spanish media despite England's UEFA Nations League loss at Wembley (Image: Justin Setterfield/Getty Images)

England's 3-2 defeat by Spain in their UEFA Nations League opener saw Anthony Gordon come away with his reputation intact. The Barcelona winger's incisive finish pulled the Three Lions level at Wembley, only to fall victim to a second-half collapse.

‌



Thomas Tuchel's side started on the back foot after conceding almost immediately to a predatory Lamine Yamal finish. Gordon's Barca team-mate pilfered Marc Guehi deep in his own half before finishing smartly past James Trafford.

‌



It was a night of mixed messages for England, who showed fight to lead at half-time thanks to Harry Kane's go-ahead goal. And Gordon received the glut of positive plaudits in the Spanish media despite a tough night for the Wembley hosts.

‌



Assessing the performance of Spain right-back Marc Pubill, AS said: "At times, it was clear he's more accustomed to playing center-back than full-back, and he was outplayed by Barcelona's Gordon, the star of the night at Wembley."

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

The same newspaper counted Gordon as one of five England players to receive a two-out-of-three rating. Jude Bellingham, Myles Lewis-Skelly, Elliot Anderson and Bukayo Saka were the only others to match that mark.

‌



England come out on wrong side of Spain thriller but Thomas Tuchel gets fans back onside READ MORE :

Thomas Tuchel brutally shuts down England question live on ITV with blunt answer READ MORE :

Marca saw it almost identically, except Harry Kane was also counted as a sixth player to receive that commendation. The same couldn't be said for Guehi, who was lambasted following his role in Yamal's breakthrough.

"The paranormal events include Spain's first goal after a joke by Guehi," read its assessment of the opening goal. The same match review described the Manchester City defender's 'howler' before giving him the lowest grade possible.

View 2 Images Marc Guehi's early mistake allowed Lamine Yamal in to score after less than two minutes (Image: Grzegorz Wajda/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)

‌



Marca ranks players on a one-to-three-star basis, with scorers Alex Baena and Mikel Oyarazabal the only players to receive the highest grades. Guehi, on the other hand, was the only player on the field to receive a zero-star grade following his early slip in front of goal.

AS also piled in on Guehi's misery by deriding his contribution leading up to Yamal's 104-second opener. The Barcelona ace capitalised on the England defender's sluggish start and 'pickpocketed' his opposite man in cunning fashion.

"He pulled out the football book he used to teach in the parks of Mataró and, like the street smarts he always was, anticipated Guehi's next move, snatched his wallet, and positioned himself in front of the centre-back to show him that either he let him finish the play, or he'd be sent off," read its review.

Sports.title: Thompson strike seals Chelsea win to end Arsenal's unbeaten run
Sports.content:
Alyssa Thompson scored the only goal as Chelsea secured a 1-0 win against Arsenal to end their unbeaten streak in the Women's Super League.

Arsenal failed to make their early dominance count after striking the post twice through Kim Little and Mariona Caldentey before Thompson broke the deadlock at Stamford Bridge.

Keira Walsh's strike from distance was initially well kept out by Anneke Borbe, but the goalkeeper was left helpless when Thompson pounced in the box to fire home the rebound in emphatic style.

The Gunners - who had drawn their last two WSL matches - improved in the second half, with Chloe Kelly's angled drive blocked and Alessia Russo's shot charged down, but the hosts saw out the closing stages for a third WSL win.

Their unbeaten streak in the WSL, stretching back to October 2025, came to an end with it. The Gunners had not tasted defeat in their last 20 games before their trip to west London.

Victory takes Chelsea to within two points of league leaders Manchester City at the top of the table, while Arsenal are already seven points adrift ahead of their meeting with the champions on October 4.

Sports.title: Imperious Banton century propels England to Sri Lanka series victory
Sports.content:
Tom Banton posted an imperious 126 off just 105 balls to guide England to a dominant 223-run win in the third ODI against Sri Lanka to secure a 2-1 series victory at the Oval.

Banton top scored with his career-best but was aided by sizeable contributions by skipper Harry Brook (77 off 66) and the in-form Jordan Cox (76 off 52) as the batting side set the tourists a mammoth target of 356 after their 50 overs, with Dilhara Fernando (3-52) the pick of the bowlers - albeit with two of his wickets coming with the final two balls of the innings.

That target loomed even larger over Sri Lanka's innings when Sonny Baker nicked off Pathum Nissanka (1) for his maiden ODI wicket with just the eighth ball of their innings.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch every boundary from Tom Banton's maiden ODI century

From there the wickets started to tumble for Sri Lanka who - despite the best efforts of captain Kusal Mendis (35 off 26) - went from 36-1 to 82-6 in just 10 overs, including the confusing run-out dismissal of Pavan Rathnayake (18), which was still given as out despite Jordan Cox taking the bails off before Archer's direct-hit throw dismantled the stumps.

The impressive bowling of Liam Dawson (3-17) and Gus Atkinson (2-26) then ensured Sri Lanka's tail went out with a 50-run whimper, handing England the series victory and marking a successful end of the home summer for Brendon McCullum's side after 12 wins in 14 white-ball games.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Pavan Rathnayake was run out by Jofra Archer after confusion reigned as Jordan Cox broke the stumps early

Banton brilliance headlines complete England performance

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Ben Duckett went early for England as Sri Lanka's Dilshan Madushanka smashed the stumps

Despite England's eventual victory, it took just eight balls for Sri Lanka to take their first wicket as Ben Duckett (0) was clean bowled by Dilshan Madushanka (1-49), before Joe Root was dismissed by Janith Liyanage in an uncharacteristically stiff cameo that saw him notch just 18 off 37 balls.

It was then the partnership of Brook and player-of-the-match Banton that made the difference for England, putting on 150 runs in a lucrative partnership that was eventually ended when the former was caught on the boundary by Dunith Wellalage.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Joe Root fell leg before as Sri Lanka claimed their second wicket against England in their third ODI

Banton's majestic innings - featuring 21 boundaries and including five sixes - came to a conclusion when his effort to hit a sixth maximum was caught by Malinga at long-on.

But England were not done there - alongside Will Jacks (25 off 21), Cox spearheaded a late flurry of runs, notching his half-century off 42 balls before Fernando took his and Dawson's wickets with the final two balls of the 49th over, leaving England in the ascendancy after posting a formidable score of 355-7.

Sri Lanka were immediately left reeling after Baker's early wicket and found it difficult to recover, with no batter scoring above 20 bar their captain Mendis, with their woes being immediately compounded by the controversial run out of Pavan Rathnayake.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sonny Baker got an early wicket within his first two balls for England against Sri Lanka in their 3rd ODI clash

Cox appeared to have made a mishap after taking the bails off the stumps before he was in control of the ball, but - after a near five-minute period of discussion involving both umpires and players - Archer's direct-hit throw uprooting the stump was ruled legitimate.

His dismissal was followed by that of Charith Asalanka and Wellalage within the next eight balls, leaving Sri Lanka on the brink of defeat at 82-6 with no recognised batters left, before the excellent work of Dawson - taking three of the last four Sri Lanka wickets - ensured England's dominant victory was confirmed with 21.5 overs to spare.

Brook: That was a near-perfect performance

Image: Baker took his maiden ODI wicket

England captain Harry Brook, speaking to Sky Sports:

"I thought that was a near-perfect performance there - I thought everyone chipped in and it was an exceptional win.

"There was some tough periods, but I thought the patience we showed, it was exceptional.

"We want to be able to adapt to conditions every game. Every surface has been slightly different. That is the side we want to be - we want to win when they are not in our favour and when they are, we want to nail sides.

"We are building towards a squad where someone can come into roles and fill it exceptionally well. We are building to a strong squad and I have full trust in anyone who comes in."

Mendis: We made too many mistakes

Image: Mendis top scored for Sri Lanka for the second successive game

Sri Lanka captain Kusal Mendis:

"We struggled with the batting and then we made some mistakes in the field, including me.

"I think we played good cricket in the second ODI and when go to Pakistan after this, we need to be better.

"We made too many mistakes."

Sports.title: Hearn: Fury vs AJ press conference not 'confirmed'
Sports.content:
With so much uncertainty around the Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua fight, even their first press conference has been thrown into doubt.

Fury and Joshua have a rivalry that's been more than a decade in the making. This week the fight was finally set for December 11 at the Principality Stadium in Cardiff, but within 48 hours of it being announced a promotional dispute erupted leading to mounting speculation that the mega-fight could be called off.

Fury and Joshua's first head-to-head press conference was due to take place on Wednesday. But that may not go ahead now.

Joshua's promoter Eddie Hearn told Sky Sports: "At the moment nothing confirmed for next week press conference wise."

As to whether Fury could hold one without Joshua and Hearn, the Matchroom promoter said: "With regards to are we expecting to be there, there wouldn't be one without us."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Dillian Whyte believes that rumours the fight between Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua could fall through is nothing more than mind games - and gives his prediction for the fight

The announcement for the long-awaited Fury-AJ fight stated that Saudi financier Turki Alalshikh's The Ring and Dana White were staging the bout, although Hearn has publicly claimed the American promoter cannot be involved.

Speaking after Johnny Fisher's victory over Michael Pirotton on Saturday night, White revealed he was uncertain whether the Fury-AJ fight itself would still go ahead. As to whether Wednesday's press conference would happen, White said: "I have no idea."

He also didn't confirm whether he'd be in attendance himself. "I guess I'll leave that as a surprise," White said.

Sports.title: Zverev seals Laver Cup success for Team Europe at London's O2
Sports.content:
Team Europe regained the Laver Cup as newly-crowned US Open champion Alexander Zverev sealed victory against Learner Tien to complete a 13-5 success at The O2 in London on Sunday.

Zverev, who won the French Open and US Open titles this year, lived up to his 'best player in the world' tag to secure Laver Cup success give rival Carlos Alcaraz the day off.

The German clinched the trophy for Team Europe after defeating Tien in the second match of Sunday's finale 7-6 (7-3) 6-3.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Team Europe won the Laver Cup after Zverev defeated Tien

Laver Cup: Tournament editions 2017 Team Europe 15-9 2018 Team Europe 13-8 2019 Team Europe 13-11 2020 No competition due to the COVID-19 pandemic 2021 Team Europe 14-1 2022 Team World 13-8 2023 Team World 13-2 2024 Team Europe 13-11 2025 Team World 15-9 2026 Team Europe 13-5

"I haven't won a match here in two years, so I'm happy that I did it today," said Zverev, who recorded his first Laver Cup singles victory since 2024.

"Massive credit to the entire Team World. They pushed us all the way again. They were champions last year. This year, we had a great team chemistry and I'm very happy that we won."

Zverev had been talked up by Alcaraz after recent Grand Slam wins before this Ryder Cup-style event at The O2, but he lost in the doubles on Friday and let slip multiple match points against Alex De Minaur on Saturday.

Alcaraz wrestled back the initiative at the end of day two before Zverev teamed up with Casper Ruud to triumph in the doubles and leave Team Europe only two victories from glory ahead of Sunday's session.

After initially falling a break behind, Cobolli and Mensik settled into their rhythm and took control, racing past Team World's De Minaur and Taylor Fritz 7-5 6-3 to stretch Europe's lead to 10-5.

Flavio Cobolli and Jakub Mensik moved the boys in blue a step closer by beating Fritz and De Minaur in the doubles, which opened the door for Zverev to bring a run of three defeats in four editions for Team Europe to an end.

Sports.title: Man Utd earn first WSL win of season as Arsenal's 11-month unbeaten run ends
Sports.content:
Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the WSL match between Manchester United and West Ham United

Man Utd beat West Ham 2-1 at Leigh Sports Village to collect their first WSL win of the season.

Eva Olid's side - who picked up just one point from their first three league games of 2026/27 - took the lead inside 10 minutes, when Elisabeth Terland headed in Anna Sandberg's header unchallenged.

They might have been 2-0 up had it not been for Hammers goalkeeper Constance Picaud, who brilliantly tipped Hanna Lundkvist's header over the bar in the last action of the first half.

United came out with the bit between their teeth and had three chances in three minutes: Andrea Medina hit the bar, Jess Park shot wide and Terland forced another fingertip save from Picaud.

It took an hour for West Ham's first shot on target, which came when Estelle Cascarino ran through the middle untracked and hit a dipping drive, which Phallon Tullis-Joyce had to be alert to tip over.

With 18 minutes of the 90 to play, the excellent Medina did make it 2-0 when she collected a peach of a pass from Park and found the postage stamp after her initial shot was blocked.

But Viviane Asseyi prevented United from keeping a clean sheet when she rolled a penalty into the bottom left corner after she was tripped by Sandberg.

Dan Long

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the WSL match between Chelsea and Arsenal at Stamford Bridge

Chelsea extended their unbeaten run in the WSL to 12 games and moved up to third in the table with a 1-0 London derby win over Arsenal at Stamford Bridge.

The streak - comprising 10 wins and two draws - stretches back to February 8 and ended the Gunners' own unbeaten record, which spanned 23 games and just under 12 months.

Arsenal were the dominant force for much of the first half and Kim Little, then Mariona Caldentey, were both denied by the woodwork, but they ended the half without a single shot on target.

And they fell behind when Keira Walsh's shot from 20 yards was saved by Anneke Borbe, with the rebound fired high into the net by Alyssa Thompson.

Renee Slegers brought on Chloe Kelly, Caitlin Foord and Stina Blackstenius to freshen things up going forward for the visitors, but to no avail.

As a result, her side have failed to win for the third league game in succession, meaning they trail leaders Man City by seven points.

Dan Long

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the WSL match between Liverpool and Everton

Liverpool secured a 2-0 win against Everton to hand the club their first WSL Merseyside derby victory at Anfield.

Liverpool had previously lost eight of their nine WSL games played at Anfield, with five of those losses coming against Everton.

However, a looping header from Beata Olsson gave Gareth Taylor's side the perfect start in just the fourth minute.

The Reds threatened throughout but were denied a second on two occasions due to the stoic defensive performance of Ruby Mace in midfield, blocking Natalia Ramos' goal-bound shot and clearing Cornelia Kapocs' effort off the line.

Kapocs would not be denied on the second time of asking, however, as she swept home the second to seal the win with just under five minutes to go.

Patrick Rowe

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the WSL match between Tottenham Hotspur and Aston Villa

Tottenham surged to a 4-0 win against Aston Villa following a dominant second-half performance to keep within touching distance of Manchester City at the top of the table.

The victory moves Spurs within two points of the league leaders with 10 points from their opening four games.

Villa, who sit in 13th, kept their opponents at bay before the break but the floodgates would open following Victoria Pelova's opener in the 54th minute.

The 27-year-old doubled the lead with a curling effort soon after before Caitlin Dijkstra's back post header and Cathinka Tandberg on the rebound put the game out of reach.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the WSL match between Birmingham City and Crystal Palace

Newly-promoted Birmingham are still searching for their first WSL win after rescuing a point in a six-goal thriller against Crystal Palace at St Andrew's.

Suzu Amano came off the bench for the Blues to hit a deflected 87th-minute equaliser to salvage a point in a 3-3 draw.

Birmingham had looked on course for a first win of the season as they led 2-1 at half-time thanks to Oceane Hurtre's double.

The forward hit an opener after just 40 seconds, but Palace equalised in the 30th minute after a goalkeeper howler allowed Shanade Hopcroft's free-kick to go in.

But just three minutes later, Hurtre restored Birmingham's lead with a powerful strike from a tight angle.

Palace, however, mounted a second-half comeback as Bethany England rebounded in a 70th-minute equaliser before Lexi Lloyd-Smith completed the turnaround with a fine one-on-one finish.

But the home side battled back in a topsy-turvy encounter as Amano struck to pick up Birmingham's second point of the campaign and deny Palace their second win of the league season.

Sports.title: Why Tuchel's critics have been forced to stay quiet despite Spain loss
Sports.content:
The narrative before this first post-World Cup international was clear: if England lose, the pressure on Thomas Tuchel could become unbearable.

The big name on the big bucks, brought in to win the big games, could not afford to lose to Spain after the tactical disaster of the World Cup semi-final defeat to Argentina. The court of public opinion, and the bile of the English media, would combine to make life very difficult for the England boss.

Well, here we are, in the aftermath of a 3-2 loss to the newly-crowned world champions, where England were outclassed on numerous occasions, where the scoreline should have been much one-sided, where for long periods Spain looked far superior to the Three Lions, where after half an hour the visitors should have been four-nil up. That's surely it, then? Auf Wiedersehen, Thomas?

Nope. Strangely, despite all of that, Tuchel's critics have been forced to bite their tongues and bide their time. Why? Because England were true to their DNA, they gave it a real good go; there were a lot of positive signs, and ultimately everyone saw again just how incredibly good Spain are.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Rob Dorsett gives his verdict on England's 3-2 defeat to world champions Spain at Wembley in the Nations League

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' Rob Dorsett and Peter Smith rate the England players' performances in their Nations League loss against Spain

It's hard to criticise Tuchel or his players when they were narrowly beaten by a team who have repeatedly proven they are the best by a mile at what they do.

The game was decided by two collector's items at either end of the pitch - one a Marc Guehi calamity on the edge of his own box that gifted Spain the lead in the second minute. The other was a Harry Kane missed penalty because of a slippery pitch. And if England's captain had scored from 12 yards, giving his side a two-goal cushion, who knows what might have been.

The match statistics make for comforting reading for Tuchel too. Up against the tika-taka maestros, England had a very respectable 48 per cent possession, made more successful passes in the final third than Spain, had two fewer shots, had over double the amount of touches in the opponent's box and five times as many crosses.

Those stats may not pass the sniff test. They might seem at odds with what most spectators saw with their eyes, but the numbers that perhaps help us understand better show that Spain created twice as many big chances.

How do we digest all of that? In basic terms, Spain may have had the ball less than England in dangerous areas, but when they did, Luis de la Fuente's team had more quality and were more clinical. And the team that has not lost a match in two-and-a-half years didn't make costly individual errors with the ball, because that's not in their DNA.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player England's Anthony Gordon reflects on defeat to Spain

If it is possible, the defeat has improved the national mood. Notably, there were no boos within the 88,000 Wembley crowd at full time, because for half an hour either side of half-time, England dominated the world champions and they played in a very "English" way.

All verve, pace and passion, full of attacking intent. They scored two goals in that period against a side that has only conceded goals to two teams in the last 12 months, and the home side could have scored more in that golden 30 minutes. If only they could sustain that for a full 90 minutes, eh?

Captain Harry Kane told me after the match that this is the mission, having not managed to put in a complete 90-minute performance at the World Cup, and he felt the same was true at Wembley on Saturday night.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Harry Kane reacts to England's loss against Spain and his penalty miss

What really matters now is how England follow up on this Spain defeat. They have three games in eight days. Three games they ought to win, with Czech Republic home and away sandwiching Croatia away. If they do win all three, it will have been a positive international break, one that very much keeps alive their hopes of making it to the Nations League quarter-finals in the spring. Remember, the top two qualify from each group in League A, and so practically it does not matter if England finish below Spain, so long as they finish above the other two nations.

But once again it is the next game that feels critical for Tuchel. You can imagine the England boss saying to his squad in the post-match debrief: "After the Spanish Inquisition, my friends, comes the test from the Czechs, mates".

Sports.title: Fitzpatrick completes big win in France to continue amazing season
Sports.content:
Matt Fitzpatrick closed out a fourth worldwide win of the season with an impressive three-shot victory at the FedEx Open de France at Le Golf National.

The world No 4 took a five-shot advantage into the final day and never relinquished control, mixing two birdies and one bogey in a final-round 70 that saw him register an 11th DP World Tour title.

Fitzpatrick ended the week on 20 under and comfortably ahead of closest challenger Angel Hidalgo, who birdied three of his last five holes to card a final-round 67, while Eugenio Chacarra was among the group five back in a share of third.

The Englishman's sizeable overnight lead was quickly reduced when Chacarra, playing in the group ahead, followed three birdies in his first four holes by adding another from 12 feet at the par-four sixth.

Chacarra cancelled out a three-putt bogey from long range at the eighth by taking advantage of the par-five next, lifting him back within two of Fitzpatrick after the former US Open champion made par on every hole on his front nine.

Chacarra's title challenge was derailed when he was forced to take a drop after an errant tee shot at the 13th, then found water with his third shot, leaving the Spaniard having to get up and down from the drop zone to scramble a double bogey.

Fitzpatrick then regained full control of the tournament when he fired his approach at the 13th to kick-in range and rolled in from 20 feet at the 15th, with those birdies lifting him to 21 under and five clear.

Stress-free pars over the next two holes kept Fitzpatrick in control heading to the par-four last, where he failed to get up and down from just off the green but tapped in to close out victory with a bogey.

"Golf is a game of multiple skills and I used them all in the end this week. Just coming down the stretch there, to get the shots I did and make the putts I did was special."

Sports.title: Israel v Republic of Ireland, Norway v Portugal, Germany v Greece: Nations League – live
Sports.content:
The Israel v Ireland game comes after a day of intrigue over whether the game would be played at all.

Gavin Bazunu will not take part.

double quotation mark Bazunu, writing on Instagram, said: “Representing my country means everything to me. I have the utmost respect for every single one of my teammates, the manager, his staff, and the Irish people.

“However, I have reached a decision that I have not taken lightly. I am a man of strong faith, and try my best to be a person of character and principle, therefore I feel it would be wrong to participate in the upcoming fixtures against Israel.

“My decision is based purely on my personal belief that the killing of innocent people is wrong. It is important to note that my stance is not in opposition of the Israeli people or the Jewish community, but against the atrocities in the region.

“There are a few times where you get a chance in life to stand up for something bigger, and I strongly believe that this is one of them.”

Sports.title: Liverpool sink Everton and end derby drought after Olsson and Kapocs strike
Sports.content:
At last, their wait is over. ­Liverpool’s players could gather in front of the Kop for a celebratory team photograph after the final whistle and rejoice in a new feeling, after beating their local rivals Everton at Anfield in a Women’s Super League fixture for the first time and finally ending their long run of derby pain.

After six wins from six visits to Anfield for Everton in the WSL era and even quips from their former manager Brian Sørensen in ­previous campaigns about making Anfield their “training pitch” during their persistent run of victories in this showpiece fixture, Beata Olsson’s early header and Cornelia Kapocs’s late finish were enough to give them a deserved 2-0 victory.

“It’s nice to break that duck, definitely,” the Liverpool head coach, Gareth Taylor, said. “We just downplayed the game, if that makes sense, because it becomes something that’s so big that players start to worry. We want players to go out and feel ­natural, like they’re playing like they were when they were growing up.

“It is nice because it’s a stat that can just grow and grow. I felt we were hard done by [at Anfield] last season – if you look at their xG in that game, they scored four goals but they were absolute worldies, whereas today we’ve scored two [but] we probably could have had six.”

Taylor was not wrong; the hosts were undeniably the better side and should have scored more goals. Indeed, they would have done had it not been for the heroics of the Everton midfielder Ruby Mace.

When Olsson got in front of her marker, Hannah Blundell, to meet Natalia Ramos’s right-sided ­corner and angle her header perfectly, dia­gonally across goal and into the far corner inside the first four minutes, she had scored with such simplicity that you could have been forgiven for thinking Liverpool were set for an easy afternoon. Instead, what followed was something of a slog at times with Liverpool trying to break down an Everton backline that initially proved difficult to open up.

After the break, another set piece almost did the job for Liverpool but Vivien Endemann’s volley smacked against the crossbar. By now the pressure was almost relentless and, with just over 20 minutes remaining, Ramos looked certain to score, with time to shoot fewer than 10 yards out. But the effort was blocked by Mace, who threw her body in front of the ball to keep her side in the contest.

Five minutes later, Mace again came to Everton’s rescue and hooked clear Kapocs’s effort off the line. The Liverpool forward’s attempted header had come off the top of her shoulder and bounced goalwards, but Mace intervened just in time.

View image in fullscreen Cornelia Kapocs secures victory for Liverpool with her team’s second goal against Everton. Photograph: Nick Potts/PA

Eventually, Kapocs found room inside the area to turn and fire home in the closing stages, much to the relief of Liverpool’s ­supporters. The result continued the side’s ­encouraging start to the campaign as they moved on to seven points from their opening four games, with their only defeat having come away against the defending champions, Manchester City.

It took Taylor’s side until 25 January to accumulate seven points last season but they look significantly improved and have built on the progress they made during the second half of 2025-26.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The visitors had spurned a couple of decent chances on the counterattack before the break, ­including ­Hannah Cain scuffing over from a promising position. Overall, ­however, Everton, whose only two league goals this season have been own goals, will be concerned about their comparative lack of ­creativity.

Asked about that wait for one of his own players to score a league goal, the Everton head coach, Scott Phelan, spoke calmly, saying: “We know we need to be more decisive in those actions, 100%. We have won two games as well and three on the bounce, so we don’t forget that. [But] yes, we want to start contributing more in the final third and that’ll be a challenge for all of us.

“We’ve played four games, so it’s definitely not panic stations. We’ve got good players in those areas of the pitch, we’re convinced they will contribute more – we’ve just got to wait for that moment to appear and hopefully it’s sooner rather than later.”

Phelan’s team still sit comfortably in the middle of the early-season table with two wins from four games. Perhaps the most disappointing for Everton fans will be that they can no longer rely on their annual collection of three points from Anfield.

Sports.title: Tony Pulis says he and Stoke were ‘cheated’ in 2011 FA Cup final after Manchester City verdict
Sports.content:
Tony Pulis has said his Stoke City team was “cheated” out of the 2011 FA Cup after Manchester City were found guilty on virtually all counts of breaching Premier League financial rules.

Pulis’ Stoke lost the 2011 Cup final 1-0 after Yaya Touré’s strike. Yet following Friday’s news that City are guilty on all but one of the more than 100 charges laid by the Premier League in February 2023, Pulis feels serious discontent. City are expected to appeal and they deny any wrongdoing.

“When do we get our FA Cup?” the 68-year-old wrote in his BBC Sport column. “That is what all Stoke fans have been asking me since the news broke on Friday. I thought exactly the same. I don’t expect Manchester City to offer back the 2011 FA Cup and the winners’ medals their players received. I don’t seriously believe any other trophies and titles will be handed back over either. A points deduction and a massive fine feels far more likely.

“But I still feel cheated. We won’t ever get that day back and the chance to celebrate around Stoke-on-Trent with the cup and medals we so honestly fought for. After breaking the rules, Manchester City got to do that instead. While the process is far from over because City are expected to appeal, I have to say this verdict and the whole situation has left a very sour taste in my mouth.”

Pulis pointed to City’s outlay on Touré, who was signed from Barcelona for £24m and earned around £180,000-a-week. He said: “Yaya Touré, who scored the winning goal, was reportedly earning 10 times what we were paying any of our players and, on his own, had cost more than our entire starting 11 when they had signed him from Barcelona in 2010.”

View image in fullscreen Manchester City’s Yaya Touré (left) scores during the 2011 FA Cup final. Photograph: Andrew Yates/AFP/Getty Images

Pulis underlined how his emotion has been changed by the verdict. “My disappointment was buried in the fact we had played a team full of superstars, and faced an elite coach in Roberto Mancini, and had just fallen short. Today, I feel very differently, as I am sure people connected with the other clubs affected by City’s successes in the same period, between 2009 and 2018 [will feel].

“We lost, but to a team that have been found guilty of breaking the financial rules set out by the Premier League. In doing so, they did not just beat Stoke in an FA Cup final, they collected a stack of titles and went on to completely dominate English football for more than a decade. So, with those rules having been broken, what will the punishment be?”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Tony Pulis of Stoke City reacts in defeat. Photograph: Laurence Griffiths/The FA/Getty Images

Pulis believes action may be widespread. “I know all Stoke supporters will be demanding that City pass the trophy over and every club that has been affected by their actions will be considering their legal options,” he said.

On Saturday, Khaldoon al-Mubarak, reiterated the club’s position. “There is so much noise swirling around us, nothing has changed. We have faced challenges together before and have prevailed. There remain many who want to undermine the momentum of our club. We will not give them that opportunity,” said City’s chair.

On Friday a City spokesperson had said: “The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality. As such Manchester City FC’s position remains consistent with the club’s statement of February 2023. The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence.”

Sports.title: Messi’s exit leaves Argentina with impossible task of replacing their superhero | Jonathan Wilson
Sports.content:
It isn’t quite over yet. Lionel Messi will return a week on Wednesday for his formal farewell in a friendly against Benin, but, before that, Argentina face two games when they will begin to experience a future without the most potent get-out-of-jail-free card football has known.

Messi’s international career falls into two distinct halves. There was the first decade when there was a sense that he didn’t quite fit, was somehow insufficiently Argentinian, didn’t care for his country. That was always absurd and can be recognised now as a manifestation of the Argentinian public’s frustration at their trophy drought despite the presence in their forward line of one of the best three to play the game.

Then Messi retired, distraught after a missing a penalty in the shootout against Chile in the Copa América final in 2016. Suddenly, Argentina, rather than just lashing out at their biggest star, was forced to confront what it would mean to live without him. The prospect was so appalling it provoked a mass campaign to encourage Messi to reverse his decision.

Since then he has been loved and, despite a shambolic World Cup in 2018, has delivered with two Copas América, a World Cup and another World Cup final. His career was dogged by the accusation that he never matched Diego Maradona’s achievements in a national shirt; he ended up having won more.

This retirement will not be overturned. Messi is 39. Those who persuaded him to change his mind in 2016 were perhaps imagining – hoping for – six more years: they got 10. There will be no second thoughts this time. The rupture is real. No longer when things are going awry will Argentina be able to turn to the superhero in their midst and ask him to fix it.

The best example came almost at the end, when Argentina trailed Egypt 2-0 with 11 minutes of their World Cup last-16 tie remaining. Barcelona youth team coaches used to speak of the teenage Messi “getting the face on”, at which point he would be unstoppable. It happened in Atlanta: it was as though Messi simply decided that wasn’t going to be his last World Cup game. Argentina won without needing extra time.

Optimists will draw solace from the fact that Argentina’s best performance under Lionel Scaloni probably came in their 4-1 victory against Brazil in a World Cup qualifier in March 2025, when Messi did not play. Even allowing for the odd tactical choices of the opposing coach, Dorival Júnior, Argentina were exceptional. Leandro Paredes anchored a midfield as Alexis Mac Allister and Enzo Fernández linked exhilaratingly with Rodrigo De Paul and Thiago Almada on the flanks and Julián Alvarez at centre-forward.

But football is not just about when things are going well. Even in the bleak times, the years of doubt under Edgardo Bauza and Jorge Sampaoli, when games were spiralling out of control, there was always the possibility Messi would put things right. But Argentina now have to deal with a future without that get-out potential.

The post-Messi future begins next week with games against Bolivia and Burkina Faso. Scaloni, has hinted he will sign a contract extension that would take him through to the 2028 Copa América with an option to the 2030 World Cup. That, at least, would provide a measure of stability, but there is little disguising the fact that a new cycle is beginning, just as Scaloni instituted a new era after the 2018 World Cup.

View image in fullscreen Lionel Messi cries at the end of the World Cup final after Argentina’s loss to Spain. Photograph: Stephanie Scarbrough/AP

Other than Messi and Nicolás Otamendi, who are retiring after the Benin valediction, Scaloni named a 35-man squad. Of those, 20 were at the World Cup; given Paredes and Nahuel Molina are serving lengthy bans, that represents a remarkable degree of continuity, although Nicolás Tagliafico, at 34, is also understood to be considering his future. But 12 of the squad had played three internationals or fewer and De Paul and Giovani Lo Celso, who are in their thirties, will play only against Benin, giving the new cohort space to impress in the first two friendlies.

The biggest opportunities, at least in the short term, look to be at the back. Cristian Romero and Lisandro Martínez, both 28, look likely to be the first-choice central defensive pair, but Valentín Gómez of Real Betis and Tomás Palacios, on loan at Estudiantes from Inter, are competing to be back-up.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

With Molina suspended, Tagliafico ageing and Gonzalo Montiel injured, the real interest, though, is at full-back, where a pair of 22 year olds could stake a claim to be the future: Agustín Giay of Palmeiras and Román Vega of Zenit.

In Messi’s absence, there remains a question of formation. Although that Brazil game demonstrates what is possible through inter-movement even without a huge amount of overt creativity, it maybe that Scaloni opts for more traditional wingers. Again there are young options: Leonel Flores of Boca Juniors and Roma’s Matias Soulé are likely to make their debuts over the next few days.

And replacing Messi? That’s just not possible, either at a tactical level or, perhaps more significantly, in terms of what he meant for the spirit of the team. It’s not that Argentina need Messi to play well. Indeed, a purist could even argue that Argentina played better in that game that they ever could have played with Messi (or at least the pedestrian Messi of late), because of his lack of movement and the way the game had to be built around him.

That is always the danger with individualists, but Messi was so spectacularly consistent that the percentage option was to rely on his extraordinary genius, the true extraordinariness of which was how reliable it was.

No matter how well-organised an opposition defence, there was also the possibility – the probability even – that he would find an opening, no matter how badly things were going, there was always the chance he would get the face on and sort everything out single-handed.

Plenty of sides have found a new fluency, a more team-based dynamic, after a major star has moved on. Argentina’s ceiling could conceivably rise, but Messi offered a reassurance, a possibility of salvation, that will be sorely missed.

Sports.title: Gateshead’s fruitless trip south offers hint of Manchester City’s doomsday future
Sports.content:
Among many doomsday scenarios facing Manchester City is plunging down the football pyramid. Would that be so bad? Instead of yawning at the prospect of yet another meeting with Real Madrid or repeated Aviva train-hampered journeys to Wembley, how about the exoticism of away travel to Wealdstone? In the National League, City’s ownership may wish to know, there are no formal financial fair play or strict salary cap regulations.

Wrexham, Notts County and Chesterfield have taken advantage of such lax constraints to regenerate. For City fans, Ruislip’s buzzy high street, full of nail bars, estate agents and a couple of homely pubs, would represent a welcome world away from Milan’s Via Monte Napoleone, as would the suburbia of Grosvenor Vale, Wealdstone’s home in the middle of a housing estate, which may jog memories of late-90s visits to Macclesfield and Lincoln. Simpler, happier times, perhaps.

On the fringes of west London, with rich, non-league history, last season’s FA Trophy finalists, managed by the 1980s QPR hero Gary Waddock, Wealdstone is the club from where Stuart Pearce, Vinny Jones and Jermaine Beckford began their journey.

In the digital age, the club became famous for the meme pioneer Gordon Parmar Hill, AKA the Wealdstone Raider, whose “you’ve got no fans” war cry went viral on a pandemic scale in 2014, the same year his assault on the UK Christmas No 1 with, naturally, “Got No Fans”, reached No 5. The Raider even made himself available for hire on stag weekends, though despite a recent social media comeback that revenue stream has been shuttered, a quieter life now observed.

Kicking off fifth from bottom in the National League, if this season’s outlook could be brighter for the Stones, then Saturday confirmed there is always someone worse off. Gateshead hosted a Football League club on the southern bank of the Tyne from 1930 to 1960, the last team the legendary Hughie Gallacher turned out for, though extinction came in 1973. The re-founded Gateshead that has been knocking around the non-league pyramid since 1977 has little hope of reaching the Football League anytime soon.

Before kick-off, the Vale club bar outside the stadium was doing brisk business. At a fifth-tier club, drinking in view of the pitch is verboten. A revocation of the 1985 alcohol statute the prime minister this week floated would prove a significant revenue driver for clubs of Wealdstone’s size; clubs in the divisions below make considerable cash from in-game hospitality.

In the Gateshead dugout, the familiar face of Lee Cattermole. For the time being, at least – his first senior management role is not going at all well. The former hard-tackling Middlesbrough, Wigan and Sunderland midfielder, collector of 88 yellow cards and seven reds in 271 Premier League games, has approached management in a characteristically uncompromising fashion. His team bottom of the National League, one win from 10 matches, Cattermole has employed the “bomb squad” approach favoured by Enzo Maresca at Chelsea and Ruben Amorim at Manchester United.

Eight players are reported to be training at alternative times to the first team, having also been removed from WhatsApp group chats. Neither Maresca nor Amorim’s shunning of players was particularly successful at an elite level, and being six goals down by half-time at home to Southend the previous week hardly heralded the success of Cattermole’s tough-love strategy either.

Alfie McCalmont, a Northern Ireland international lately of Central Coast Mariners in Australia, joined the Heed in midweek. Anchoring midfield, after what were bright beginnings for the team that had travelled 278 miles, about 100 away fans willing them on, the new arrival soon found himself dragged into the torpor of his new teammates.

Gateshead’s manager visibly sagged once Olufela Olomola scored the first of two unanswered goals before half-time. Not half as bad as Southend, but bad enough. “Make them work,” bellowed Cattermole while his team were still level, among other, more colourful, language.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Once Wealdstone’s second goal came, Luke Norris converting a softly conceded penalty, Cattermole sat himself down, distractedly fiddling with notebook and pen before a half-time team talk delayed by his slow return to the away dressing room.

Whatever was said, a third Wealdstone goal came within two minutes of the resumption, and a fourth just before the end. Waddock, who as a player was not dissimilar to Cattermole – combative, lover of a tackle – could keep quiet counsel, relaxedly leaning on a handy gatepost. Such serenity in a difficult season for Wealdstone came by contrast to the portentous chants of “sacked in the morning” from the away end, followed by “time to go”.

It was Ben Clark, Cattermole’s assistant, sent out to deliver a post-match verdict. “We conceded a soft goal, and struggled from there on in,” he said. “The lads are struggling a bit with their confidence.”

The possibility of Cattermole being bombed out had heightened, such news likely to be accompanied by a corner-flag image on the club website. Should City drop down the divisions to alight on suburban outposts such as Wealdstone, it is already unlikely Cattermole would get the chance to face them, let alone manage them.

Sports.title: Pocognoli’s reign as Scotland coach begins with stalemate in Slovenia
Sports.content:
Sébastien Pocognoli grimaced on Friday when recalling his debut as an international player for Belgium. Alessandro del Piero and Italy discovered favourable opposition when preparing for the 2006 World Cup. Pocognoli will also look back, in time, at his first game as the manager of Scotland.

Blue skies, a dainty stadium in Ljubljana and a second-half display that provided glimpses of optimism in respect of Scotland’s world, post-Steve Clarke. The best-forgotten first 45 minutes can be explained away by a squad operating under a new regime. By full time, Slovenia were grateful for their point. Scotland’s players took deserved applause.

Scotland’s failing here was a familiar one. A lack of goals haunted Clarke. Nonetheless, this version of Scotland did at least create a series of openings. Scott McTominay, a key attacking threat, was missing. Instilling ruthlessness in a team is no easy task; it is one, however, Pocognoli has the coaching credentials to meet. Slovenia, on this evidence, have the more significant challenges.

“The feeling in the dressing room is positive because of the second half,” said Pocognoli. “We should have scored but I am very happy with the general performance of the strikers. It was only the last details we missed.” His demeanour was upbeat.

Ninety-four days had passed since Scotland’s loss to Brazil all but confirmed World Cup elimination. When that meek exit was certain, Clarke announced his resignation. Players and supporters alike seem caught between being highly grateful to Clarke for materially altering Scotland’s fortunes and heralding regime change.

In Slovenia, Pocognoli sampled international management for the first time at the age of 39. Slovenia failed to reach the World Cup, with the rows of empty seats telling the story of a country that is not at all convinced by its footballing outlook. The absence of Benjamin Sesko did nothing to help a shot-shy side.

Scotland could hardly bemoan poor preparation. Pocognoli had whipped his squad and mini-army of backroom staff to La Manga in the buildup to this Nations League game. With a sense of revolution in the air, the head coach unleashed a hitherto unseen front two: Robbie Ure was making his international debut while Oli McBurnie returned after years in the wilderness. The opening half only proved there is little point deploying multiple strikers if there is no adequate means of supplying them.

Scotland were awful in that first period. The football was passive and directionless. Players looked well-enough drilled off the ball, but descended into a state of panic when in possession. Slovenia, who were little better than ordinary, should have seized upon these shortcomings. To his credit, whatever message Pocognoli forcefully pressed home during the break had an effect.

View image in fullscreen Sébastien Pocognoli barks instructions during his first game in charge of Scotland. Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PA

Andraz Sporar had the ball in the net for the hosts in the eighth minute only for an offside flag to go up. Sporar subsequently missed a golden opportunity from six yards after fine work from Danijel Sturm. As Aljosa Matko shanked wide of Angus Gunn’s goal, the Tartan Army’s groans were audible.

Save a Ure shot from 20 yards that clipped the outside of a post, Scotland were nonexistent as an attacking force. An overhit Billy Gilmour pass that flew out of play when intended for the marauding Andy Robertson rather summed things up.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

McBurnie should have marked his Scotland return with a goal within five minutes of the restart. He opted to try to jink around Jan Oblak rather than slam a shot past the goalkeeper. Oblak morphed into Inspector Gadget, stretching out his arms while grounded to pinch the ball from McBurnie’s feet.

This triggered Scottish improvement; Gilmour forced a save after a one-two with McBurnie. Aaron Hickey could not quite divert a John McGinn corner on target. Oblak had to be sharp to deny the Scotland substitute Kieron Bowie before doing likewise to McBurnie from the resultant corner.

Second-half Scotland involved a huge upturn. McBurnie said he would not be able to sleep due to his profligacy. Seventeen Scotland caps are yet to yield a goal.

Bowie’s miss, 12 minutes from time, was in the category of howler. Gilmour, increasingly influential as Scotland dominated, had fed his teammate. Pocognoli was emboldened, sending on Ben Gannon-Doak to replace Hickey. In old money, that represented a winger for a full-back.

Scotland huffed, puffed, pushed and wheezed. Slovenia stood firm. Pocognoli nodded with approval as the whistle blew. Next up, a Hampden Park bow against Switzerland on Tuesday.

Sports.title: Footgolf and the Jabulani: a second life for ‘the worst ball I’ve seen in my life’
Sports.content:
About once a month, Ben Clarke, the world’s leading footgolfer, carefully pumps up his collection of coveted Adidas Jabulani footballs.

Like most elite players, Clarke possesses an extensive array of balls, all of which require regular inflation to prevent degradation, even those sitting pristine in their original boxes, unsullied by a single boot. Footballs are prime currency in a niche sport that tasks players with kicking one around a course, and into 18 oversized holes, in as few strokes as possible. Precision is everything.

It seems absurd, then, that pride of place among Clarke’s hoard is the infamous Jabulani, once described by Fabio Capello as “the worst ball that I have seen in my life”. The former England manager was far from alone in his scathing assessment. England goalkeeper David James called it “dreadful”, his Brazilian counterpart Júlio César said it was “like one of those you buy in the supermarket”, while Brazil forward Robinho suggested “the guy who designed this ball never played football”.
