World.title: Speaking Out Is Citizenship, Not Rebellion, Matambo Tells Zambians
World.content:
Opposition Tonse Alliance figure Brian “Coach” Matambo has said Zambia’s post-election crisis is the result of five years of public silence. In a video address released on Sunday, he said citizens repeatedly allowed the boundaries of political freedom to shift because those under attack were opposition politicians.

The 31-minute address, titled “The Cost of Silence: How Zambia Reached the Crisis of 2026”, accompanies the documentary “Silence Brought Us Here”. In it, Mr Matambo traces what he describes as a steady erosion of democratic space from 2021 to the treason arrests that followed the August polls. “We did not just land here. We did not just wake up after the 2026 election and suddenly discover that something had gone terribly wrong with our democracy,” he said. “This has been coming.”

Watch the full video and read the complete column here.

Mr Matambo began with the 2021 transfer of power, when former President Edgar Lungu conceded defeat and handed over peacefully. That moment strengthened Zambia, he said, but what followed began to weaken it. He cited the loss of parliamentary seats by Bowman Lusambo and Joseph Malanji, and what he called concocted criminal cases against Ronald Chitotela. Many Zambians, he said, dismissed these as the PF paying the price for losing power.

“Democracy is not tested by how government treats its friends. Democracy is tested by how government treats its opponents,” Mr Matambo said. “The rights of your political opponent are also your own rights.”

He listed a series of developments he said the public had accepted in turn: police blocking opposition rallies, cyber laws passed despite warnings from lawyers, civil society and journalists, and Bill 7. He noted that the Constitutional Court had itself found the Bill 7 process inconsistent with the spirit of the Constitution and requiring wider consultation. Parliament passed it anyway, and “again, Zambia moved on,” he said.

Mr Matambo reserved some of his sharpest criticism for the appointment of Mwangala Zaloumis as chairperson of the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ). He said she had previously acted as President Hakainde Hichilema‘s lawyer, and that opposition MPs had raised concerns at the time. He compared it to a World Cup qualifier refereed by someone who once worked for the opposing coach. “You cannot have a referee who supports one of the teams,” he said.

Turning to the former head of State, Mr Matambo said Zambians had watched Edgar Lungu humiliated after leaving office, from police involvement in his jogging to disputes over his travel and medical care abroad. He also cited the arrest of former First Lady Esther Lungu, and the Government’s legal battle with the family in South Africa over Mr Lungu’s remains, which he said lasted more than a year. “You don’t defend somebody’s rights because you like them. You defend their rights because they are rights. Otherwise, they are not rights. They are favours,” he said.

Mr Matambo named opposition figures who he said had spoken out and ended up behind bars. They include Brian Mundubile, Makebi Zulu, Munir Zulu, Celestine Mukandila, Jay Jay Banda and Raphael Nakacinda. He said they were among hundreds held “for merely speaking out”.

On the August election, he said he personally witnessed blocked roads, police surveillance and disrupted rallies. He described a suspension of counting for more than two hours, the military taking over polling stations, raids on Mr Mundubile’s home and on Tonse offices in Ibex Hill, and the arrest of Bishop Trevor Mwamba among others.

He called 14 August “the night democracy died”. Mr Matambo said former minister Mutotwe Kafwaya was shot dead by soldiers who found him unarmed in a wardrobe during a security operation at Mr Mundubile’s home. He said a militia story was then used to charge Mr Mundubile and his running mate, Mr Zulu, with treason. He described the events as “a coup against the democratic process itself”, adding: “I choose my words very, very carefully.”

“August 2026 was not the beginning. August 2026 was the consequence,” he said. “We walked here.”

The address closes with an appeal for peaceful civic speech. Mr Matambo said speaking out did not mean insulting, lying or threatening anyone. “It means telling those in power: I disagree. That is not rebellion. That is citizenship,” he said.

He urged fellow opposition leaders to set aside party interests until democratic institutions are secured. “I want a Zambia where my candidate can lose and I can believe that he genuinely lost,” he said. “I want a Zambia where UPND can lose and peacefully hand over power.”

Mr Matambo ended by calling on Zambians to act now rather than wait. “Zambia must speak before the boundaries move again,” he said.

World.title: The cost of silence: how Zambia walked into the crisis of 2026
World.content:
The cost of silence: how Zambia walked into the crisis of 2026

Democratic decline rarely arrives in a single dramatic moment. It comes gradually, when actions that once seemed exceptional become normal, and when citizens begin treating the rights of political opponents as somebody else’s problem. Democracy is not protected only when our own side is under attack. Its real test comes when we are prepared to defend the rights of people with whom we disagree.

Zambians, we need to talk. There is something very important we are missing about the crisis our country finds itself in today. We did not just land here. We did not wake up after the 2026 election and suddenly discover that something had gone terribly wrong with our democracy.

No. This has been coming. It has been building slowly, one incident after another, one institution after another, one boundary after another. And every time the boundary moved, Zambia adjusted.

We complained for a few days. We fought it out on Facebook and discussed it on the radio. Then we moved on, and the Government learned something from our silence: that Zambia would always move on. That is how we got here.

Go back to 2021. Edgar Lungu lost an election, conceded and handed over power peacefully. Whatever you thought of him, that moment strengthened Zambia. Power changed hands with no soldiers, no refusal to leave State House and no constitutional crisis. One president handed over to another, and that was the Zambia we inherited in 2021.

But look at what happened afterwards. Bowman Lusambo and Joseph Malanji had their parliamentary seats taken from them through the institutions of Parliament and the judiciary. Remember Ronald Chitotela? Concocted criminal cases, one after another. Because these were PF politicians, many Zambians convinced themselves that this was simply the PF suffering the consequences of losing power.

So we stayed quiet. Some even celebrated. But we missed the bigger questions. What was happening to our institutions? What precedents were being set?

Democracy is not tested by how a government treats its friends. It is tested by how a government treats its opponents. The rights of your political opponent are also your own rights. The institution you allow to be abused today against somebody you dislike may be the very institution you will need tomorrow, when the Government comes for somebody you love.

We did not see it that way. We said: that is Bowman, that is Malanji, that is Chitotela, that is PF. And we moved on.

Then opposition rallies became almost impossible to hold. Police stopped meetings, roads were blocked and political gatherings were cancelled. In a multi-party democracy, an opposition party increasingly had to negotiate with the police simply to speak to the people it wished to govern. Again, Zambia adjusted. We normalised it.

Then came the cyber laws, and we were warned. Lawyers warned us. Civil society warned us. Journalists warned us. They said these laws were dangerous, that the powers they created could and would be abused, and that they could become an instrument for controlling speech.

Many Zambians simply replied: if you have done nothing wrong, what are you afraid of? Again, we missed the point. The question was never whether President Hakainde Hichilema would personally sit somewhere reading your WhatsApp messages and decide that you were guilty.

The question was how much power we were comfortable giving the State over the speech of its citizens. How much power? Governments change and presidents change, but the powers handed to the State remain.

Then came Bill 7, and it was the Constitutional Court itself that raised the alarm. Not the PF, not Mundubile, not Makebi, not some opposition blogger: the Constitutional Court. It found that the process undertaken was inconsistent with the spirit of the Constitution and required wider consultation.

That should have been a major constitutional moment for this country. When the Constitutional Court speaks about the Constitution, the Government is supposed to listen. But we all know what happened. Somehow the political process found its way around the obstacle. Bill 7 was retained, the vote happened in Parliament, Bill 7 became law, and again Zambia moved on.

Somewhere along this road, something else happened that I believe Zambia will one day look back on and ask: why did we allow this? Mwangala Zaloumis was appointed chairperson of the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ).

Concerns were raised immediately. This was somebody who had previously acted as Hakainde Hichilema‘s lawyer, so there was a relationship there. Opposition MPs raised concerns about links to the UPND. People questioned the political associations surrounding appointments to the very institution that would eventually referee an election involving Hakainde Hichilema. And again, Zambia moved on.

But think about this. Forget the UPND. Forget the opposition. Forget Hakainde Hichilema. Forget Mwangala Zaloumis. Let us just use common sense: you cannot have a referee who supports one of the teams.

It does not matter how qualified the referee is. It does not matter how professional he promises to be. The moment a referee walks onto the field carrying the history and associations of one of the competitors, confidence in the match is already damaged.

Imagine Zambia playing a World Cup qualifier where the referee previously worked for the opposing coach. Would we wait until the 89th minute, when he awards a penalty, before raising the question? Of course not. We would say: we know this man, he worked for that coach, he cannot referee this game. We would demand a change of referee before kick-off.

We would not do it because we had proved he was going to cheat. We would do it because the integrity of the competition requires a referee whose independence cannot reasonably be questioned. That is how serious institutions protect themselves, and the ECZ should have been protected from even the appearance of political allegiance.

We failed to do that with the ECZ and Mwangala Zaloumis. Four years later, that same institution was refereeing the most consequential election in our country’s history. We were warned. Again, we moved on.

Then there was Edgar Lungu, and this is another place where our politics blinded us. He had lost an election and handed over power. He was no longer president, but he was still a former Head of State. And we watched the State humiliate him again and again.

There was a time when a former president of this country could not even go jogging without the police becoming involved. Imagine that. A man who had commanded the armed forces of this Republic, who had occupied State House and who had handed over power peacefully, could not go for a jog. He could not step out of his house.

We found ourselves watching a dispute over whether Edgar Lungu could go jogging, and some Zambians laughed because they did not like him. Then came the disputes over his movements and his travel. Even his attempt to get medical care outside the country became another point of confrontation. How petty. How petty.

And again, people said: that is Lungu, that is the PF, that is their problem.

Then his wife was arrested. Former First Lady Esther Lungu, a woman who had occupied State House as First Lady of this country, found herself locked up. It arose from what was presented as a family property dispute, one in which she maintains she was herself the aggrieved party. Somehow the State, the UPND, whoever was in charge, found it necessary to make her the victim.

Again, many Zambians stayed quiet because it was Esther Lungu, because it was the Lungu family, because it was PF. That is where we fail to understand something fundamental.

You do not defend somebody’s rights because you like them. You defend their rights because they are rights. Otherwise they are not rights; they are favours, and favours disappear when the wrong person comes to power. The Bill of Rights is not a list of favours. It is a list of rights.

When Edgar Lungu died, you would think death would finally end this political war. It did not. The man died in South Africa, leaving a widow, children and a grieving family.

Instead of allowing that family to bury their husband, father, brother and relative, the full might of the Zambian State sued the widow in the courts of a foreign country. Imagine that for a moment. The Government fought the family over the remains of Edgar Lungu for more than a year. And even when it lost the case, it refused to pay the costs.

Forget the politics for a moment. A woman loses her husband and then spends more than a year fighting the government of her own country, in a foreign court, over his body. If you think that is normal, if you can find a way to justify it, you need to be checked. Where was our humanity? Where was Zambia? Where were our voices?

Some people celebrated because the dead man was Edgar Lungu. Others simply looked away. And again, the boundaries moved.

This is the pattern I want you to see: every time the boundary moves, the people warning us are dismissed. Brian Mundubile spoke. Makebi Zulu spoke. Munir Zulu spoke. Celestine Mukandila spoke. Jay Jay Banda spoke. Raphael Nakacinda spoke. Others spoke.

And what happened? One after another, they became enemies of the State: troublemakers, threats to the UPND, people who needed to be arrested and silenced. Today they sit in prison alongside hundreds of others, merely for speaking out and exercising their rights. So perhaps Zambia needs to ask herself whether these people were really the problem, or whether some of them were warning us about the problem.

Then came the 2026 election, and suddenly all the things we had treated as separate incidents began to come together. I hope that one day we go to our colleagues in prison and say: you warned us.

The referee we had questioned was now refereeing the match. The opposition had been restricted by the police and the system for years, struggling even to hold rallies, and now it had to campaign for national power. The cyber security machinery we had warned against was now in place, and the constitutional boundaries we had watched being pushed had already moved.

The political opponents arrested over the years had already taught Zambia what would happen to dissenters. They were made an example: you speak, we lock you up.

When the August 2026 election came, we saw opposition campaigns blocked. We experienced it ourselves; I was there. Roads were blocked, police followed us, rallies were stopped, meetings were disrupted and people were arrested. Ruling party violence reached even the police, with an officer hacked on the head by a ruling party cadre. And Zambia kept moving.

Then came election day. Counting was suspended for more than two hours, and then the military took over polling stations. Next came the raids on Brian Mundubile‘s home and on our offices; some of you may have seen that they raided our offices in Ibex Hill. Then innocent people were arrested, among them Bishop Trevor Mwamba and Dr Emmanuel Nkoma.

Then came Honourable Mutotwe Kafwaya. For me, 14 August 2026 is the night democracy died, because when Mutotwe Kafwaya was killed, something fundamental changed.

This was no longer Bowman Lusambo‘s parliamentary seat. It was no longer Edgar Lungu‘s jogging, an opposition rally being cancelled, or somebody being arrested for something they had said. This was much deeper. A man was dead. A former government minister was killed in cold blood, murdered during what was called a security operation at the home of Brian Mundubile, the principal opposition presidential candidate, in the middle of an election dispute.

Armed soldiers descended on Mr Mundubile‘s home and faced no armed resistance at all. They subdued everyone in the yard and went up the stairs to the master bedroom. There they found Mutotwe Kafwaya taking cover in the wardrobe, unarmed. They shot him in the chest, and he was pronounced dead.

Then came the cover story: militias, an insurrection, threats to national security, all the flamboyant security language they could find. On the strength of that militia story, which UN Special Rapporteur Gina Romero has described as concocted, Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu were arrested and charged with treason.

For me, what happened that night was a coup d’état against our democracy, and I choose my words very carefully. I am not talking about the old-fashioned African coup, where soldiers appear on television and announce that they have taken over the government. These ones were clever. I am talking about a coup against the democratic process itself.

What is democracy? It is elections, institutions and courts. It is the right to change, the right to organise, the right to disagree and the right to seek legal remedy when you believe something has gone wrong.

So what happens when the electoral process fails, and the judicial process meant to correct it also becomes inaccessible? What happens when the courts are surrounded at the very moment citizens need them? What happens when the opposition candidate who should be challenging the result ends up in prison, accused of treason?

And what happens when his running mate ends up in prison with him, even though he was not at the scene of the alleged militia and nothing connects him to it? What do Zambians do?

We stop examining each incident separately and finally look at the complete picture. Let us try that. Let us stop looking at these events one by one. That is my case: August 2026 was not the beginning. August 2026 was the consequence. It did not suddenly arrive. We walked here.

The funeral. Celestine Mukandila. The campaign restrictions. The military. Treason. One incident after another, all painting a single picture that is painful to reflect on. And every time something happened, Zambians found a reason to remain silent.

That is the opposition. That is Lungu. That is politics. Maybe he said something wrong. Let the courts decide. The Government knows what it is doing. Until eventually we arrived here. That is how we got here.

So the question today is no longer simply how we got here. I think we know. We got here through silence, by being quiet, by not speaking when we should have spoken. The question now is what more will be done on the back of our silence.

That is what frightens me. If this much became possible while Zambia was quiet, what becomes possible if Zambia stays quiet? What is the next boundary? The next institution? Who is the next person? What will we normalise next? That is the big question.

This is where I want to speak directly to Zambians. Speaking does not mean insulting anybody. It does not mean lying, threatening anybody or turning to violence. Speaking simply means airing genuinely held views. It means telling those in power: I disagree. I am concerned. Explain this. Show us the evidence.

Speaking means telling them to respect the Constitution, the courts and our rights. It means telling them to release the people they are holding unlawfully and to give people due process. Let political parties organise. Let journalists work. Let citizens question power. That is not rebellion. That is not resistance. That is citizenship.

I think we have reached the point where Zambians must stop defending democracy according to political colours. If somebody’s rights are violated, do not first ask which party they belong to or what tribe they are. If an opposition rally is stopped, do not first ask whether you support that party. If somebody is arrested for expressing an opinion, do not first ask whether you agree with it.

That is the lesson in democracy this country needs. What we must ask is whether what is happening is right. Today it may be Brian Mundubile; tomorrow it may be somebody you support. Today it may be Makebi Zulu; tomorrow it may be you.

That is why I am saying something even to my own colleagues in the opposition. For now, put the parties aside. There will be time for party politics, but first we have a country to defend and a democracy to defend. What is the point of fighting over who gets to live in a house whose foundation is broken? The foundation comes first.

There is a verse I like in the Bible that asks: when the foundations are destroyed, what can the righteous do? Zambia’s foundations are cracked right now, and that foundation is our democracy.

We must first defend the electoral process, the judiciary, freedom of expression, political competition and the right to disagree. We must defend the principle that no president, no government and no political party is bigger than Zambia. When that foundation is secure, then let us fight politically. That is democracy.

I do not want a Zambia where my candidate can never lose. I want a Zambia where my candidate can lose and I can believe he genuinely lost. I want a Zambia where the UPND can lose and peacefully hand over power, and where the opposition can lose and remain free to organise. That is the Zambia we must strive for.

I want a Zambia where an opposition leader can criticise the President today and still sleep in his own bed tonight. I want a Zambia where a journalist can ask a difficult question without wondering whether somebody will knock on the door. I want a Zambia where a citizen can say, “Mr President, I think you are wrong,” and wake up free the next morning, and where a civil servant can support whoever they want without anyone coming after them.

That is not asking for too much. That is the Zambia we are supposed to be: tolerant and united. And we will not recover that Zambia through silence.

So I challenge you: speak. Peacefully, responsibly and truthfully, but speak. Speak because you understand what is at stake. Speak because democracy cannot defend itself, and institutions cannot defend themselves when the citizens who own them have surrendered their voices.

Do not wait until it reaches your house. That is the mistake we have been making: because it was not your son who died, you felt comfortable. When it was Bowman, we waited. When it was Edgar Lungu, we waited. When it was Munir Zulu, we waited. When rallies were being stopped, we waited in silence.

When people warned about the ECZ, we waited. When people warned about the cyber laws, we waited in submissive silence. When people warned about Bill 7, we rested on our laurels and waited like little men and women.

And now Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu are in prison facing treason charges, and Mutotwe Kafwaya is dead and buried, six feet under. So tell me, what exactly are we waiting for now? That, my fellow Zambians, is the question.

No foreign country is coming to build our democracy for us. No international organisation can substitute for the voice of the Zambian people, and no politician can carry this responsibility alone. Zambia belongs to Zambians. If we believe something has gone terribly wrong in our democracy, then Zambians must say so: not violently, not recklessly, but clearly and together.

This is bigger than any of us. Presidents will come and go. Political parties will rise and fall. Those of us holding political positions today will one day be gone. But Zambia will remain, and what kind of Zambia remains will depend partly on what this generation is prepared to defend today.

Our parents gave us a multi-party democracy. We cannot be the generation that hands our children something less. This is the moment to find our voices again. We can refuse to be silent.

The question is no longer whether Zambia should have spoken yesterday. Yesterday is gone, and there is no use crying over spilt milk. The question is whether Zambia will speak today. My answer is that Zambia must speak, before the boundaries move again.

By Brian “Coach” Matambo, Tonse Alliance

Source: “The Cost of Silence: How Zambia Reached the Crisis of 2026”, video address accompanying the documentary “Silence Brought Us Here”

World.title: Maamba Solar Injects 100MW Into National Grid As El Niño Threatens Hydropower
World.content:
Maamba Solar Energy Limited (MSEL) has injected 100 megawatts of electricity into the national grid, bringing one of Zambia’s largest solar plants online just as the country braces for an El Niño season expected to squeeze hydropower generation. First power from the Maamba Solar PV Project entered the grid on 24 September, marking the start of the plant’s commissioning phase.

The project is a joint venture in which ZCCM Investments Holdings (ZCCM-IH) holds a 35 per cent stake, with the remaining 65 per cent held by Nava Global PTE Limited, the international arm of India-listed Nava Limited. Total investment in the project stands at about US$90 million.

ZCCM-IH Chief Executive Officer Kakenenwa Muyangwa said the timing could not have been better. In a statement issued on Friday evening through corporate affairs manager Loisa Mbatha, he said that with Zambia bracing for El Niño and the pressure it would place on hydropower, 100 megawatts of solar capacity was a direct and timely response to the country’s energy security needs.

Mr Muyangwa said the project strengthened the diversification of Zambia’s energy mix, reducing reliance on a single source and building resilience into the national grid. “As a sovereign-anchored investor, ZCCM-IH is proud to play its part in Zambia’s energy transformation,” he said.

He said the investment reflected ZCCM-IH’s commitment to deploying capital into strategic energy projects that would underpin economic growth, support the Grow Zambia agenda and contribute to the national ambition of 10,000 megawatts of generation capacity. The company, he said, would keep working with its partners to bring more reliable and clean power to the grid, create lasting value for shareholders and support industry.

The plant sits in Maamba, Sinazongwe District, in Southern Province, alongside the existing Maamba thermal power operations. It is a 100 MWac utility-scale photovoltaic facility using bifacial panels mounted on single-axis trackers, which follow the sun through the day to maximise output.

A dedicated 330 kV substation connects the plant to the grid. Its output is contracted to ZESCO Limited under a 20-year Power Purchase Agreement, giving the project long-term, predictable revenue.

Commissioning will now move through testing and verification of the generation system, trackers, inverters, medium-voltage collection network, substation, protection and control, metering, SCADA and communication systems. The plant will then go through synchronisation, reliability and performance checks, including confirmation of its response to grid requirements, before full commercial operation, and ZCCM-IH said it would update shareholders and the market on further milestones.

The new capacity arrives while the country’s main hydropower reservoir is declining but holding. The Zambezi River Authority (ZRA) put Lake Kariba at 481.15 metres on 21 September, with 26.21 billion cubic metres of usable storage, or 40.44 per cent of the water available for power generation. That is above the 477.87 metres recorded in 2025 but below the 485.67 metres of 2018.

Energy expert Engineer Bornface Zulu said electricity supply remained stable despite the falling lake, but warned that the situation showed why Zambia must keep diversifying away from hydropower. National demand stands at about 2,400MW, peaking at around 2,800MW, against current generation of about 3,500MW, with Kafue Gorge Upper producing about 990MW and Kafue Gorge Lower about 750MW.

Solar is already carrying more of that load. More than 841MW of solar power has been added to national generation capacity, and a further 159MW is expected from Chipata West and Senga by December 2026.

Maamba now moves through synchronisation and performance testing towards full commercial operation, adding its 100 megawatts to the grid before the rains.

World.title: Africa: Africa's Mineral Strength Is Wasted If Countries Don't Work Together - New Report
World.content:
The OCP Group in Morocco, which holds vast reserves of phosphate - a key ingredient in fertilisers, is responsible for the country's extraction, processing, manufacturing, and export of phosphate products.

analysis

Green technologies are mineral-intensive: electric vehicles, batteries, solar panels, wind turbines and grids need cobalt, lithium, copper, manganese, graphite and rare earths. The International Energy Agency estimates that electric cars require six times more minerals than a petrol or diesel car. A wind power plant requires about nine times more minerals than a gas-fired plant.

As the global green transition speeds up, the growing demand for green technologies and minerals creates an opening for Africa, which has deposits of several of the minerals needed.





Yet just having these minerals in the ground does not automatically create industries or shared prosperity. In fact, developing countries endowed with minerals often struggle to benefit economically from mining.

We are scholars of how countries build industries and reshape their economies. Our latest study, commissioned by the World Bank, explored how far African countries have moved beyond mining the minerals needed for the energy transition. We examined whether they are processing and refining these minerals or making components for green technologies that use them.

Our analysis followed four steps. First, we identified the transition minerals found in each African country. Second, we examined trade data to see which countries export these minerals and where they are sold.



Third, we looked at where African countries participate in the value chain of green technology. We wanted to find out whether they only mine the mineral and then export it raw, or whether they process it before selling it or produce a final product for sale, such as solar panels. Fourth, we reviewed national and regional mineral and industrial policies.

We found that African countries have deposits of 41 minerals that are used across bioenergy, electricity networks and infrastructure, batteries, energy storage and electric vehicles, and carbon capture and storage. These minerals are also sought after for fuel cells and hydrogen, geothermal energy, heat pumps, hydropower, nuclear power, solar power and wind power.

However, most African countries still export transition minerals in raw or lightly processed form rather than turning them into higher-value materials, components and finished products.



African countries therefore have only a very small presence in the green-technology industries that depend on these minerals. As a result, Africa's mineral wealth has not yet led to high levels of industrial activity, well-paid jobs, higher incomes or wide improvements in living standards.

We found that national and regional institutions are taking steps to change this, but most initiatives are still at an early stage.

Collective mineral strength, shallow value capture

Our research found deposits, reserves, or production of at least one transition mineral in 48 African countries. South Africa had 24 of the 41 minerals; Nigeria and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) each had 14.

Collectively, Africa holds about 96% of global platinum group metal reserves, 77% of phosphate reserves, and 55% of cobalt reserves. Phosphate and cobalt are used in electric vehicle batteries, while platinum is used in technologies that produce and use green hydrogen.

Yet most countries individually accounted for only small global shares. This matters because small national volumes can make it harder for a country acting alone to influence buyers, attract large processing plants, build complete supply chains or compete with established producers elsewhere.



Trade data reinforces these findings. Notably, apart from South Africa, Nigeria and the DRC, most African countries exported less than 1% of each mineral globally. For several minerals, such as nickel, rare earths, silver and lithium, Africa's five largest exporters together supplied less than 10% of world exports.

African countries could strengthen their position in mineral markets by coordinating their trade policies rather than acting separately. Private companies hold mining licences, but permission to extract minerals does not always include an unrestricted right to export them. Governments may therefore have some scope to coordinate trade rules. How this would work alongside companies' existing rights, and whether it would require their agreement, needs to be further studied.



A deeper weakness identified in our study is limited local processing of minerals. This mainly happens in a few countries such as South Africa, Democratic Republic of Congo, Zambia and Zimbabwe. The processing these countries do often involves crushing and concentrating ore, rather than making products from the mineral.

African countries lose out because of this. For example, Congolese cobalt can sell for US$5.80 per kilogram at the point of extraction. But after local refining, the price increases to US$16.20 per kilogram, nearly tripling its value.

A green economy built on old dependencies

Asia (China in particular) is the leading importer of 16 minerals from Africa. It imported over 30% of those exports on average, and was the second biggest buyer of six other green transition minerals.

Our research found that China absorbed over 40% of Africa's annual mineral ore exports. This shows that Africa is repeating a familiar pattern: mining raw materials while other countries turn them into more valuable products.



The history of Africa, plus low industrialisation levels, means that African countries are also almost invisible in green technology value chains. Between 2017 and 2023, Africa's global patent share across the technologies studied remained below 0.4%, while its export share was below 1% in every category. African countries currently participate in the green economy more as consumers, rather than producers.

African governments are asserting agency

We also found that African governments are changing mining laws, restricting exports, taking ownership stakes and forming partnerships to gain more from their minerals. They want more processing, investment, jobs and income to stay at home. Most are acting individually, although some are working together across borders.

Acting alone has limits. Many countries supply too little to influence large international buyers. If one country demands higher prices or local processing, buyers can shop elsewhere.

Many also lack reliable electricity, affordable loans, transport and skilled workers to process minerals and make components.

Close 

What needs to happen next

Africa is very strong in minerals as a continent. However, deeper regional cooperation would help African countries build industries, not simply trade more easily with one another, a central thesis of a related study, Integrating Africa: From Threads to Hubs. Pooling mineral supplies, markets, infrastructure and skills could lower costs and give them more power when negotiating with global companies. A shared processing centre serving countries across Africa would also help the continent.



To make this happen, African finance and mineral institutions and national governments must agree on common priorities and similar rules about how minerals are processed, and how environmental damage is managed.

Development finance has a role to play. Regional development banks and other African financiers could help fund shared electricity, transport and mineral-processing infrastructure, while universities and businesses develop the technical skills these industries need.

Partnerships with foreign governments and companies should also go beyond extracting and exporting minerals. They should include commitments to process more minerals in Africa, share technology and know-how, train workers, and help local firms become suppliers to emerging green industries.

Gideon Ndubuisi, Assistant Professor of Economics, Delft University of Technology

Elvis Korku Avenyo, Associate professor, University of Johannesburg

Solomon Owusu, Assistant Professor of Global Economic Policy, Boston University

Woubet Kassa, Economist, American University

World.title: Sudan: RSF Drones Strike El Gezira Fuel Depot As Both Sides Report Shootdowns
World.content:
Wad Madani — Paramilitary Rapid Support Forces drones struck the Umm Alila fuel depot east of Wad Madani in El Gezira early on Sunday, triggering fires as Sudan's warring sides reported further drone activity across the country.

Residents said they heard several explosions shortly after dawn prayers in Abu Haraz, about 20 kilometres northeast of Wad Madani. Videos circulating online showed flames across parts of the depot as Civil Defence teams worked to contain the blaze.

The facility stores and distributes petrol and diesel across El Gezira. Civil Defence said it contained the fire and prevented it from reaching other tanks, with damage limited to the petrol and diesel tanks.

'Drones shot down'

The Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) said on Thursday that its air defences shot down an FH-95 drone northeast of El Kokiti in North Kordofan, the second drone of the same type it said it had downed this week.

North Kordofan has seen an escalation in fighting in recent weeks.

The RSF, meanwhile, said it shot down a Turkish-made Bayraktar drone over the Blue Nile region on Thursday. It accused the army of systematic attacks on populated areas and called on the international community and regional organisations to condemn them.

World.title: Ethiopia: UN Voices Grave Concern As Fighting Spreads Across Northern Ethiopia
World.content:
An ambulance damaged during the conflict in the Tigray region, stands idle outside a health centre in Gijet in July 2021.

The UN said on Friday it remains gravely concerned by the continued deterioration of the security situation across northern Ethiopia, as fighting spreads across multiple fronts and increasingly disrupts humanitarian operations.

Briefing reporters in New York, UN Spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric said the UN was "particularly troubled by reports of the use of drones as well as incidents of harm to civilians," and again urged all parties to "exercise maximum restraint and address their differences through dialogue."

He said Secretary-General António Guterres was following developments closely and continues to engage on the issue with leaders in New York in a bid to de-escalate the growing crisis - which threatens to return the country to the state of full-scale war in the north which erupted in Tigray in 2020.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Internet outages

According to news reports, internet and call services have been largely cut across the Tigray region. Many rely on banking and mobile transactions due to lack of access to cash and bank ATMs.

The 2020-2022 Tigray war began after political tensions between Ethiopia's federal government and the region's former ruling party, the TPLF, erupted into fighting between Government troops and Tigrayan militia in November 2020.

Eritrean forces joined on the Government's side, and the conflict spread into neighbouring regions, with the UN documenting widespread atrocities and warning of famine-like conditions before it ended two years later.

The UN welcomed the peace deal of November 2022 under African Union mediation, though it continued to flag slow progress on implementation as a risk to the peace now under threat from this week's escalation.

UN mediation

The Secretary-General's Special Envoy for the Horn of Africa, Guang Cong, is engaging with national and regional interlocutors and coordinating closely with partners, including the AU and regional intergovernmental body IGAD, to support a resumption of dialogue under 2022 accord, Mr. Dujarric said.

On the humanitarian front, the UN aid coordination office (OCHA) said the escalation risks adding to already substantial needs, including among civilians displaced by previous fighting in Tigray, in an area also experiencing below-average rainfall linked to the El Niño weather pattern - which promises to exacerbate already extreme weather conditions worldwide.

The UN and partners are continuing regular humanitarian operations where security allows, in Tigray as well as the northern regions of Amhara and Afar, assessing emergency needs.

Fighting chokes off aid

Close 

But insecurity is already taking its toll: this past Sunday, a drone strike in northwestern Tigray hit a truck carrying food assistance for internally displaced people.

Road closures have paused or displaced planned humanitarian movements, Mr. Dujarric said, while operations in parts of Amhara face significant constraints, including the seizure of humanitarian vehicles by armed groups.

The UN stressed that all parties must ensure safe and unhindered access for humanitarian partners to reach those in need, wherever they are.

UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk, also issued a strong statement on Friday saying he was deeply alarmed by the escalation and urged all parties to de-escalate tensions and avoid a return to full-scale war.

He said reported airstrikes hit five schools in Tigray on 22 September, and a mortar strike two days later killed civilians in Kobo, Amhara.

World.title: Ethiopia: Ethiopia's Foretold War Arrives
World.content:
analysis

No one can claim that a return to war in Tigray and northern Ethiopia is a surprise, but it makes it no less horrifying. In just a handful of days, and after months of spiralling tensions and sporadic fighting, the 'grey conflict' the federal government pursued against Tigray has escalated into ''full-blown war,' in the words of Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) vice president Ammanuel Assefa.

The atrocities of the Tigray war are all too recent in the mind; the estimated deaths of 600,000 people, massacres at Axum and Adigrat, the incessant drone strikes on schools, hospitals, and industry, the rape and sexual assault of over 120,000 girls and women, and the harrowing consequences of the man-made famine. To be facing a return to a broader conflict not even four short years after the Pretoria agreement was signed is catastrophic, and this time, threatens to intersect with the metastasising Sudanese civil war.

On Sunday, a diverse coalition of Ethiopia's ethnic-based opposition movements announced a new alliance, unveiled by Fano commander Zemane Kassie on Tigrai TV. Among them are the TPLF, the Amhara Fano National Movement (AFNM), the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA), the Ogaden National Liberation Front (ONLF), and three smaller ethno-nationalist movements from Afar and the Benishangul-Gumuz regions. Operating under the title of the Ethiopian Peoples' Forces Alliance for Survival, these groups are united by their stated intention to oust the federal government led by PM Abiy Ahmed, and little else. The alliance has been a year in the making, emerging out of the Eritrea-TPLF rapprochement known as 'Tsimdo,' with its core appearing to be the TPLF and Fano; the OLA's commitment seems more circumspect. Still, by mid-week, fighting had renewed on a large scale on several fronts in Amhara and Afar, with over two dozen federal airstrikes reported in several locations, whilst the TPLF seized control of three key airports in Tigray.



The fog of war is immense, and with the situation on the ground so fluid, much remains unknown. Both sides are seeking to paint the other as the aggressor, and how this escalates in the volatile theatre of northern Ethiopia-partially bordering Eritrea and Sudan-is of huge concern. So far, though, fighting has reportedly been concentrated along the Tigray-Afar and Tigray-Amhara borders, as well as the Kobo-Tumuga road in North Wollo, with Tigrayan and Fano purportedly fighting side by side for the first time. Including Abala and Erebti in Afar, Tigrayan units have seized several towns, setting up a potential push across the edge of the Danakil's salt and potash belt towards the Djibouti Corridor, through which most of Ethiopia's trade flows. Armed movement toward the ancient town of Lalibela has also been reported, with Ethiopian Airlines cancelling flights there, as well as to Mekelle, Aksum, and Shire.

Significantly, reports of fresh fighting along the Tekeze River near the Eritrean border emerged yesterday as well, accompanying government drone strikes and Eritrean troop advances into Western Tigray, suggesting that Asmara may be throwing its weight behind its Amhara nationalist and TPLF allies. Eritrea's potential role in the coming days and weeks- beyond shaping the Tigrayan, Fano, and Sudanese army ties and facilitating weapons-- will no doubt prove hugely significant. Ironically, Asmara's transformation from pariah state in the Horn to king-maker lies at the door of Abiy and the Gulf states who ushered in the transactional 'peace deal' in 2018 that paved the way for the Tigray war. It is another cruel twist of fate, and Addis's own short-sighted regional strategy, that places Mekelle and Asmara on the same side after Eritrean troops plundered and massacred their way across much of Tigray in the last war. But- as ever- Isaias Afwerki's strategic logic is one of survival, seeking to place any burden of war on Ethiopia and spare his depleted army. Whether Addis has the appetite to strike at the Eritrean supply lines that will furnish this war remains to be seen.

Mekelle and Addis, as well as Asmara, have been on a war footing for months, reshuffling respective units and commanders, sourcing weapons for the looming conflict, and trading barbs on a host of issues, particularly the status of the Pretoria agreement- which ended the fighting but failed to resolve the brutal Tigray war of 2020-2022- and PM Abiy Ahmed's quasi-imperial desire for 'access to the sea.' In February, battle-ready federal forces were redeployed from the raging insurgencies in Oromia and Amhara to the edges of Tigray, then abruptly stood down. Some had hoped that the surging fuel costs from the US-Iran war might have deterred a return to war, with Addis having budgeted for 4.2 million tonnes of fuel this year before the metastasising war across the Middle East sent costs skyrocketing. But the reprieve has lasted just a season.

In August, substantial, multi-day clashes erupted in Western Tigray between federal and Tigrayan forces. Even then, flickers of diplomacy did nothing to avert the impending broader conflict, with global attention still trained on the fallout of American adventurism in the Middle East now spilling over into Yemen. At the same time, government drone strikes ramped up in Tigray, one of Addis's favoured tools, which have been deployed en masse against the Fano and OLA insurgencies in the Amhara and Oromia regions, respectively. As such, the growing conflagration in northern Ethiopia is another indictment of Abiy's militarised, marketplace style of politics. Unable to conquer Tigray in 2020-2022, Addis has wielded the Pretoria agreement to delegitimise Mekelle, disregarding its responsibilities for dialogue to instead stoke division and pressure Tigray. In particular, Western Tigray was never restored to Mekelle's control, nor was the broader region reintegrated into the federal contract, stranding it in a debilitating limbo.

Mekelle has hardly helped itself either. In the past 18 months, the TPLF has steadily asserted increasing political and military control of the region, stifling dissenting voices and introducing forced conscription. In May, it pushed out Tadesse Werede and installed a council headed by Debretsion Gebremichael, who led Tigray through the last war. But the TPLF is not the party it was six years ago, let alone thirty. It is a poor simulacrum of its former self, bitterly divided and inward-looking, unable to muster support from a wearied Tigrayan population. The cohesion that sustained Tigray against the Derg and the 2020-2022 war has dissipated, and tens of thousands of Tigrayans have fled ahead of the renewed conflict in recent months. Reports from Tigray in the past 48 hours further suggest that those suspected of potential disloyalty, including Tadesse Werede, have been detained.

Questions, too, about the broader alliance remain. Though Fano, Eritrea, and Tigray actors have been coordinating for months, the extent of the new alliance is less clear. Kjetil Tronvoll has aptly referred to it as one of "constructive ambiguity", with the parties bound by little more than an antipathy towards the Addis regime. And though the TPLF vice-president Ammanuel Assefa has pledged to "sit at the table later to solve our problems peacefully," the situation today reflects how fractured the Ethiopian body politic is. For instance, whilst the Fano commanders in Gojjam and Wollo may have fewer qualms with this Tigrayan alliance, those closer to the disputed territories in Western Tigray - who actively participated in the ethnic cleansing of the fertile region in late 2020 and 2021 - are likely to baulk. Still, if these arrayed forces can establish a coherent command centre to coordinate operations in several regions, it will no doubt heap further pressure on the federal government.

The international community--or what remains of it--has responded by urging dialogue and cooler heads to prevail. But on Sudan, and now on Ethiopia, the African Union and foreign capitals have repeatedly failed to rein in the belligerents or their foreign backers. Pretoria was a hastily expanded cessation-of-hostilities document, a flawed handful of paragraphs that failed to address the war's root causes. Even so, the African Union abdicated its role as mediator, whilst its observers failed to hold the parties accountable or convene comprehensive talks. This week, a handful of embassies issued condemnatory statements, including the US offering fulsome support for Abiy, but hopes for any serious intervention remain low. Washington- whilst simultaneously seeking to rehabilitate Eritrea on its prime maritime real estate- and Brussels have broadly prioritised renewing their ties with Addis over holding the federal government accountable to Pretoria despite the drumbeat of a widening war.

What is clear is that humanitarian suffering is set to intensify across northern Ethiopia. Last year, Tigrayan scholar Teklehaymanot G. Weldemichel described Tigray as a "death world", a region deliberately kept in awful precarity. Though Tigray today is not encircled as it was in 2020, a drone strike on a truck ferrying 41 tonnes of food aid bound for the displaced in Sheraro on 20 September recalled the logic of the last war, when famine was induced through the deliberate destruction of the means of survival. Cash is already running short, and with the rains failing and the campaigning season beginning, the lean months will fall inside the war. The humanitarian situation in much of the Amhara region - with the countryside dominated by Fano and urban centres by government forces - is equally dire.

2026 is not 2020, and this cascading Ethiopian conflict comes with Sudan, and the Red Sea, aflame. For the past two years, fears of a renewed Tigrayan-Ethiopian-Eritrean conflict have centred on its convergence with broader Horn instability, with Sudan's internationalised civil war and competing Gulf and Middle Eastern powers backing its protagonists, increasingly connecting conflicts once treated as separate. Since late 2025, Ethiopia has moved more squarely into supporting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), with whom it shares an Emirati paymaster, hosting an Emirati-facilitated camp for the paramilitaries at Mengi near the Sudanese border. At the same time, another ally of the Sudanese army, Egypt, has aggressively pursued Ethiopia's encirclement over disputes over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) and the Nile water basin, forging closer ties with Eritrea and, to a lesser extent, Somalia and Djibouti.

Close 

Though this conflict is intimately shaped by distinctly Ethiopian grievances, it may quickly assume the intractable characteristics that have dominated the Sudan war --and the tools of the 21st century. External patrons would further complicate the battlefield, making a negotiated settlement harder to reach and military escalation easier to sustain. With the UAE and Saudi Arabia squaring off across the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, yet another conflict offers space for regional competition to seep further into Ethiopia's war. Still, it is early days, and if and how the Sudan war might intersect with the unfolding situation in Ethiopia remains to be seen, but the prospect of a conflict system stretching from Chad to the Djiboutian border makes one shudder.

If this descends into a broader conflict--and the augurs are bleak--it will not follow the script of 2020. Then, the war was broadly contained within Ethiopia's borders. Today, several wars are already running at once, with a host of patrons, no single mediator able to end them and the margins between Ethiopia's conflict and others wafer-thin. And so, in the face of the horrors of 2020-2022 and neighbouring Sudan, Ethiopia has returned to war.

Matthew de Waal is a freelance analyst on peace and security focused on the Horn of Africa and Red Sea based in Nairobi. Until recently, he was the Deputy Head of Research and Publications at Sahan Research, a think-tank focused on conflict and governance in the region. Matthew has a particular focus on the geopolitics of the Horn and Al-Shabaab.

World.title: AEW’s Steven Borden hospitalized after scary injury during match at All Out
World.content:
Steven Borden made his first appearance at an All Elite Wrestling (AEW) pay-per-view on Saturday night when he teamed with Darby Allin to take on Kevin Knight and Kyle Fletcher at All Out.

Borden, the son of pro wrestling legend Sting, has been working his way up the ladder in the sport as he bears a striking resemblance to his father. He and Allin were looking to become No. 1 contenders for the AEW Tag Team Championship with hopes of lining up some gold in the near future.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE

All four men in the ring were cooking up something special. Borden and Knight were attempting a must-see moment in the ring but things went awry.

Knight was on one side of the ring and Borden was on the other. The two were perched on top of the turnbuckles and were trying to go coast-to-coast at each other. Knight appeared to connect with his move, but Borden came down hard and appeared to hit the back of his head on the mat.

An AEW referee stopped the match and Knight and Fletcher were declared the winners.

AEW broadcaster Tony Schiavone provided an update on Borden during the show, saying the wrestler was conscious and responsive and was taken to the hospital for a further evaluation.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

AEW owner Tony Khan addressed Borden’s injury in the post-event media scrum.

"Thankfully, Steven Borden (is) awake, responsive at the hospital. He had a CT scan and all the tests have come back good," he said. "So far, all good results and we are hopeful Steven is going to fly home tomorrow to his family."

It’s the best update one can get given the circumstances. Nobody ever wants to see a pro wrestler, or any athlete, go down with an injury. In-ring injuries are just as common as those that occur on the football field or basketball court.

For Borden, hopefully, he will be able to get back in the ring soon.

World.title: Pope Leo calls out ‘false compassion’ of medically assisted suicide during French hospital visit
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline at 988 or 800-273-TALK (8255).

Pope Leo XIV called for an end to medically assisted suicide during a visit to medical facilities in Lourdes, France, on Sunday.

The pope gave Mass in Lourdes before addressing a large crowd who cheered as he emphatically affirmed the dignity of all human lives and admonished listeners to reject the "false compassion" of assisted suicide.

POPE LEO XIV BEGINS HISTORIC 4-DAY VISIT TO FRANCE

"It is precisely in the name of this inalienable dignity of the human person that we must reject the temptation to cause death under the guise of false compassion," the pope said, speaking in French.

"It is impossible to regard causing death as something normal. What is legal is not necessarily moral," he continued. "Here in Lourdes, the city of the sick and of hope, I appeal to the entire healthcare community to remember the profound meaning of your vocation, which is to care for a suffering person, not to eliminate that person."

CATHOLIC NUNS SUE NEW YORK, SAY ASSISTED SUICIDE LAW FORCES THEM TO VIOLATE THEIR FAITH

"No one ever has the right based on laboratory algorithms to decide the life of a given embryo or elderly person. Medicine must never become the servant of programmed death," he said.

Assisted suicide is legal in many Western countries, including France.

MICHIGAN DEMOCRATS PROPOSE PACKAGE SEEKING TO LEGALIZE ASSISTED SUICIDE

The practice has come under heavy criticism, particularly in Canada where it has seen widespread use.

Last week, the family of an 83-year-old Canadian woman demanded answers after she died through the country's medical assistance in dying program despite allegedly becoming distraught when told the procedure would end her life.

ASSISTED LIVING CENTER SENT RESIDENT TO DOCTOR'S APPOINTMENT AFTER GIVING HIM 18 SHOTS, 5 AM BEER: OFFICIALS

The Daily Mail reported that 83-year-old Christian grandmother Brigitte Stegemann was killed under Canada’s physician-assisted suicide program, called Medical Assistance in Dying (MAID), on July 10.

Her granddaughter, Brigitte Kranendonk, said that she was her grandmother’s primary caregiver and that her family had decided to place Stegemann at The Pearl care home in Cannifton due to physical and mental decline.

ORGAN HARVESTING BEGAN WHILE PATIENTS STILL SHOWED ‘SIGNS OF LIFE,’ FEDERAL INVESTIGATION FINDS

But according to Kranendonk, her grandmother still had a good appetite even following a stomach cancer diagnosis, and rejected the idea of using MAID when it was presented as an option.

Kranendonk said she was present for Stegemann's second MAID assessment, and said that the doctor used "really loose terms, never using the words death or dying."

NEW YORK NUNS' CHALLENGE TO ASSISTED SUICIDE LAW IS ABOUT PROTECTING FREEDOM, LAWYER SAYS

"She explains MAID to my grandmother by saying: 'We’re going to give you medicine, you’re going to feel at peace. And I just want you to know that you won’t have a bowel movement,'" Kranendonk said.

When Kranendonk interjected and said, "She doesn’t understand what you’re saying," the doctor allegedly looked at Stegemann and said, "We’re going to make sure you won’t have any more pain."

CAN FAITH HELP PATIENTS HEAL? VETERAN DOCTOR REVEALS WHAT HE'S WITNESSED FIRSTHAND

According to a doctor, Stegemann was "deemed fit for MAID, and we're going to proceed," The Daily Mail reported.

Kranendonk said that two days before Stegemann's death, she asked her grandmother directly whether she understood that the scheduled procedure meant she would die.

According to Kranendonk's account to the outlet, Stegemann began crying and said she had "made a mistake."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Stegemann was allegedly told by the doctor her grandmother could "deny" MAID on the day of the procedure, but Stegemann was already unsure if her grandmother had actually consented to it, did not want to cause her more stress, and wanted to enjoy what could be the last few days she had left with her grandmother.

World.content:
The Young Bucks are back on top of the All Elite Wrestling (AEW) tag team division.

Adam Copeland and Christian Cage put the AEW Tag Team Championship on the line against Matt and Nick Jackson and Dax Harwood and Cash Wheeler (known as FTR), who returned to the fray at All In. At All Out, it was a three-way ladder match.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE

For anyone who has watched Copeland and Cage’s careers, seeing them go into the ladder match would be akin to Michael Jordan playing at the United Center. The match was almost as exciting as watching Jordan cook defenses on the court.

It was all about the spots and the bumps.

Harwood and Copeland met each other at the top of a ladder with one ladder set up perpendicular to the ropes. Harwood suplexed Copeland onto the ladder. Cage and Wheeler got to the top turnbuckles and each hit a big splash on Harwood and Copeland respectively.

In another spot, Wheeler was sent flying through a table from the ring onto the floor. Matt Jackson placed Harwood onto a table next and Nick Jackson hit a 450 splash onto the competitor.

The Young Bucks had another big moment minutes later. Each wrestler climbed to the top of a tall ladder with Harwood and Copeland sprawled across tables on the floor. They each hit an elbow drop and a splash. Wheeler was in the ring watching it all unfold. He saw an opportunity to hit a suicide dive through the middle of the ladder and onto Cage.

Bodies were strewn across the floor. The match came down to who wanted it more. The Young Bucks survived a Shatter Machine from FTR.

Matt and Nick Jackson climbed to the top of the ladder and captured the title belts.

It is the fourth reign for the Young Bucks. They have the most tag team titles in AEW history. Their win also ended Copeland and Cage’s reign at 125 days. It is the Young Bucks’ first title reign since April 2024 when they won the titles at Dynasty.

World.title: Texas voters have plenty to say about whether Lone Star State could turn blue
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

DALLAS — Everything is bigger in Texas, including the political stakes this November.

Texas voters head to the polls Nov. 3 in an election that could reshape the state's political landscape, with major battles for governor, U.S. Senate and seats in Congress and the state legislature. Republican Gov. Greg Abbott faces Democrat Gina Hinojosa, while Republican Ken Paxton squares off against Democrat James Talarico for a U.S. Senate seat.

At the State Fair of Texas in Dallas, voters told Fox News Digital that pocketbook pressures are shaping how they view the state's future, with some predicting the reliably red Lone Star State will stay that way while others see an opening for Democrats this fall.

REPUBLICANS JUST GOT A POWERFUL NEW PLAYBOOK FOR THE BATTLE FOR CONGRESS. HERE'S WHAT'S INSIDE

"I think we're going to struggle, but I think it will stay red," Briana of Garland, told Fox News Digital.

Mike and Cynthia, a couple from Houston, were more definitive.

"Red. It's going to stay red," they said.

Chris took that confidence a step further.

"Hell will freeze over before Texas flips blue," Chris told Fox News Digital.

Patrick and Jennifer, of Dallas, shared that confidence.

"Texas will always be a Republican state," Jennifer said, while acknowledging that Republican candidates will not win every race. "But we still think it will stay Republican," Patrick added.

Not everyone at the fair was betting on Texas staying firmly in Republican hands.

WE ASKED AMERICANS TO GRADE THE ECONOMY. THEN WE ASKED IF IT WOULD CHANGE THEIR VOTE.

Mary said she believes the Dallas-Fort Worth area is moving in the opposite direction.

"It's definitely leaning more blue. Texas as a whole, I'm not sure," she said. "I think if there would be an election that swings blue, it would be this one. So we'll see if it happens."

Party politics aside, several voters said the economy remains top of mind.

Cynthia, who moved to Texas from New York, said she is looking for policies that will grow the economy, support businesses and leave families with enough disposable income to enjoy outings like the State Fair.

FOX NEWS POLL: SQUEEZED BY COSTS, FRUSTRATED VOTERS TURN TO THE DEMOCRATS

"If you don't have enough disposable income, then you can't really enjoy something like this," she said. "It's pricey."

Jennifer also pointed to inflation and the prolonged strain of higher prices.

"I think people were expecting some sort of inflation," Jennifer said. "But I don't think we were prepared for it to last this long."

Meanwhile, Roxanne also expressed frustration with the country's current direction, saying dissatisfaction with the current administration is influencing her political outlook.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"I just don't agree with the current administration, so I really want to see somebody else come in and do a better job," she said.

From the midway to the ballot box, Texas voters offered competing views of where the Lone Star State is headed, but agreed the economy will be difficult to ignore as they prepare to cast their ballots Nov. 3.

World.title: DAVID MARCUS: Why JD Vance's reshoring message is a perfect fit for struggling small towns like St. Cloud
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Three weeks ago in Dallas, at the midterm convention, Republicans chose to put Vice President JD Vance in the spotlight, to lead the troops to November. His speech, about the future of the nation, could have been addressed directly to the town of St. Cloud, Minnesota, and its environs.

In those remarks, referring to the future of his own kids, Vance said, "I want, whether they work in tech or manufacturing, American businesses to hire American workers, to rely on American people and to ensure that we build the next generation of great American products with American hands."

You can almost hear those words echoing around the historic downtown of 19th century red brick, and it is a bit of a puzzle, because usually it is fairly obvious whether a city of this size — about 80,000 souls — is ascending or descending. But St. Cloud seems, well, stuck in the middle.

Image 1 of 2 next

Image 2 of 2 prev

THE ONE LINE FROM JD VANCE’S GOP KEYNOTE THAT REVEALS HIS VISION FOR AMERICA

On the positive side of the civic ledger is the fact that the businesses that are open seem to be thriving. It's not in every minor metro downtown that you see packed restaurants for lunch on a Tuesday. There were also volunteers out painting the planters that line the sidewalk, another very positive sign of civic engagement.

On the downside, almost half of the available commercial space is empty — like a handsome hockey player with some missing teeth — and foot traffic, at least for now, is not heavy enough to support many more retailers.

Rob, now in his 40s, went to college at the nearby university in the early 2000s and told Fox News Digital, "Back then downtown was packed every night, you could barely move, I don’t think it's ever getting back to that."

When I asked how he thought the town was doing, he said, "Better these days, better since COVID, but it's kind of plateaued," and he was not the only person I spoke to who used that particular word.

One that can also be applied to much of the broader nation.

Janice, another long-time resident dating back to the 1990s who works in real estate, set the date of the town’s downturn a bit earlier, with the closing of Herberger's department store — which opened in 1927 and shut down for good in 2018.

"It’s a huge hole, right in the heart of downtown," she said, "and there isn’t anything to fill it."

It was around this time that several factories in the area also closed down. To add insult to injury, in 2019, St. Cloud State University dropped its football program, never a great sign for a college town.

But there are seeds of growth as well, and one of the planters, Chad O’Brien, opened a vintage store downtown in March 2025, just after Trump’s inauguration, and now has two on the same block, as businesses bubble up to life.

"I think that the way the downtown works, the way that it draws people in, our business model and structure and the things that we sell seems like a really good fit," O’Brien told Fox News Digital, though he also said that more people living in the area would certainly help.

Ultimately, this is why Vance’s mission to reshore manufacturing and reward firms that stay in America is such a perfect fit for St. Cloud. Honestly, a handful of businesses, with a few thousand jobs, could easily bring some of the hustle and bustle back.

Perhaps one big plant with 1,500 factory jobs that can fill the single-family homes that semicircle the city, and a big tech firm hiring 300 to 500 younger workers to live downtown in walking distance to the bars and eateries. In a city this small, that's all it takes to make a difference.

The biggest concerns you hear in St. Cloud surround the Somali immigrant community, but this issue is actually two distinct problems — both of which are firmly in the Vice President’s portfolio, the first being the massive fraud scandal.

VICE PRESIDENT VANCE SAYS MIGRANT COMMUNITIES SHOW 'CLEAR PATTERN' IN FEDERAL FRAUD AS INVESTIGATIONS WIDEN

Even on the ride back to the airport, Lynn, who also works in the beauty industry, told me of a ride she had given recently where an immigrant woman was bragging to her friend that she had just secured government-subsidized housing — but her boyfriend already had it, so they were going to rent hers out for cash.

I could see Lynn’s knuckles whiten on the steering wheel as she said, "It just makes me so mad, I want to help the poor, but this can’t be the way."

Everyone can agree that the fraud is bad, and hopefully, that the efforts spearheaded by Vance to stop it are good.

But, the second part of the Somali issue is trickier and more intractable. It is the cultural component, another strong theme in Vance’s convention speech, and here opinions vary.

Several people I spoke with expressed deep frustration at the seeming unwillingness of Somalis to assimilate, but not everyone. Trey, in his late 20s, is the sales manager at a local phone store who hired a Somali to help with customers of Somali descent.

"He’s worried that their kids are becoming too Americanized and losing their roots," Trey said, adding, "I do see some of that, a lot of the teenagers don’t even speak their language now."

Another gentleman in his 60s, who I met at a fairly high-end lounge told me, "There is no downside to these immigrants, it is all upside and the only reason to be against it is racism." I gently suggested that there are certainly people who think they have non-bigoted objections, but he doubled down, "It’s only racism."

Downtown, though, is the place where the cultural and economic concerns meet, or, in this case, do not meet, because just as is true with the Haitian community in Springfield, Ohio, the Somalis in St. Cloud are not to be seen downtown — living instead, almost exclusively in their own enclave.

The influx of Somali immigrants has not revitalized downtown because they don’t go there. A few thousand blue and white collared native-born workers absolutely would.

Just northwest of St. Cloud is Sauk Centre, Minnesota, the real-life inspiration for Sinclair Lewis’ seminal novel Main Street, which over a century ago captured the uniqueness of the American small town — something that still charmed so many foreign World Cup travelers this past summer.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

In these towns, like St. Cloud, and there are hundreds, Vance’s message is a perfect fit. His blend of America first and reshoring jobs to small communities truly does resonate, and makes sense.

Just as Vance and his muscular populist message kicked off the midterms for the GOP, in October, it must carry it through. In other words, Mr. Vice President, are you ready for your close-up?

World.title: Texas clinic owner convicted in $26M military health fraud tied to gold-plated Cybertruck
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A Texas mental health clinic owner was convicted by a federal jury after prosecutors said he orchestrated a $26 million scheme to defraud the military's health care program, using some of the proceeds to fund luxury purchases, including a gold-plated Tesla Cybertruck worth more than $100,000.

Kevin D. Curry, 64, of Frisco, was found guilty Thursday in federal court in Fort Worth on three counts of health care fraud, three counts of offering and paying illegal health care kickbacks and three counts of engaging in monetary transactions in criminally derived property, according to the Justice Department.

Federal prosecutors said Curry exploited TRICARE, the health care program serving active-duty servicemembers, retirees and their families, by billing for transcranial magnetic stimulation, or TMS, therapy that was medically unnecessary or, in many cases, never provided.

FBI LAUNCHES 'MOST WANTED FRAUDSTERS' LIST AS DOJ CHARGES OHIO DEFENDANTS IN $30M MEDICAID SCHEME FOR KIDS

According to evidence presented at trial, Curry owned and operated mental health clinics in Plano and Fort Worth, Texas, as well as Fort Walton Beach, Florida. Prosecutors said he paid more than $5.5 million in illegal kickbacks to persuade active-duty servicemembers, veterans and their family members to consent to TMS therapy they did not qualify for and, in many instances, did not receive.

The Justice Department said Curry falsely represented himself as a medical doctor, used licensed doctors' credentials without their knowledge or consent to submit claims to TRICARE, and directed employees to fabricate medical records to justify fraudulent billings.

FRAUD EXPERT EXPOSES HOW HIDDEN NETWORKS DROVE MINNESOTA FRAUD, OTHER MAJOR SCAMS: 'CRIMINAL ENTERPRISE'

Authorities said Curry's clinics submitted more than $26 million in false, fraudulent or kickback-tainted claims to TRICARE, which ultimately paid approximately $17 million.

Prosecutors said Curry laundered some of the proceeds by spending the money on luxury hotel stays, a lavish casino-themed party and a gold-plated Tesla Cybertruck valued at more than $100,000.

TAXPAYER FUNDS MEANT FOR LA HOMELESS ALLEGEDLY SPENT ON TAHITI TRIP, NIGHTCLUB, LUXURY CARS: FEDS

"This defendant exploited a critical health care program serving active-duty servicemembers and their families, diverting taxpayer dollars to bankroll personal luxuries ranging from hotel stays to a casino-themed party and even a gold-plated Tesla Cybertruck," Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald said in a statement.

U.S. Attorney Ryan Raybould said Curry "shamelessly preyed on the trust of servicemembers, veterans, and their families," accusing him of fabricating medical records, stealing doctors' identities and submitting fraudulent claims while profiting from kickback-tainted money.

Many episodes in the "Gilmore Girls" series are set during autumn in New England, and the show lends itself well to the season. Many viewers associate the show with crisp air and coziness, with The New York Times even calling it a "fall tradition."

STARBUCKS BRINGING BACK VIRAL MENU ITEM DESPITE 2017 BARISTA REVOLT: 'MAY GOD SAVE US ALL'

"I won’t really get a pumpkin spice latte, but I’ll go chocolate mint, like a peppermint mocha," she said.

In 2025, Starbucks released its peppermint mocha, a holiday menu item, on Nov. 6.

The pumpkin spice latte, or PSL, has become a popular fall beverage over the years.
