World.title: Choosing a school as a parent in Mexico? We know how it feels
World.content:
There are myriad choices you can never fully prepare for as a parent. Some are sticky, some are slippery and many are a combination of both. Perhaps the most emotionally distressing of them all, though? Figuring out where and when to send your child to school in Mexico for the first time.

Relocating to Veracruz for family and flexibility

My son, who is now 3, was 1 year old when we decided to relocate to Veracruz from California. We knew we would be able to better maximize our presence with him in Mexico than in the San Francisco Bay Area — where most of our waking hours would be spent commuting to work, hustling around the clock and paying exorbitantly for childcare.

When we arrived in Mexico, we chose to prioritize our family unit over our professional careers by spending more time together, exploring the country as a group of road-tripping buddies and having daily access to a larger ecosystem of relatives in Veracruz (including my mom, cousins, aunts, uncles and grandfather, who are all native to the area and live within a few miles or less from our home).

For nearly two years, we’ve been enjoying the flexible work-from-home allowances that we’ve been fortunate to experience. We’ve made the most of our time with our son in that span.

Facing the biggest parenting decision yet

But this fall, we’ve inevitably had to make the biggest decision in our parenting journey thus far: Where will our son attend school and spend the majority of his days, outside of the environment that we’ve so carefully and intentionally invested in? In our case, as the parents of a bilingual toddler, it was a weighty decision that my wife and I had to deeply consider. At what point, after all, did it make sense to send our son away in hopes of further developing his Spanish fluency and social adaptability? And what nonnegotiable benefits did we expect that school to provide that we couldn’t?

Choosing a school isn’t exactly an easy formula, and even the most adept parents are often underinformed about it all.

It’s a complex, time-consuming process. And with the start of the school year, my family just went through it for the first time while living in Mexico. Here’s what it looked like for us.

Surveying the options through friends, family and online research

The largest advantage of being in Veracruz is the sheer amount of extended family we have here. We live in the city where both of my parents were raised, and in which many of their immediate relatives — whom I grew up visiting throughout my life — remain. My dad, who now lives in California but regularly visits, likes to point out the schools he once attended all over the city; my mom has done the same. It’s fun to imagine what those eras must have been like for them as students navigating other dynamics. It helps me imagine my son doing the same, in his own way.

Having that deep connection here was a primary factor in our choice to relocate to this specific region of the Gulf Coast. Here, I can speak with my older cousins who have sent many of my nieces and nephews to schools in the area; it gives me valuable perspective on what others seem to have figured out or recommend.

Leaning on community when family isn’t nearby

If that extended family network isn’t available for you where you live in Mexico, look to your neighbors. In our case, we’ve been lucky to have neighbors with children of different ages living on our street. It has been hugely beneficial. We’ve been able to connect and develop friendships with other parents in our community by attending kids’ parties or simply chatting in passing.

We ask questions about where their children currently attend, or formerly attended, schools in the city, and what those experiences have been like for them. For more than a few families, it seems, sending the child to school where one of the parents worked was a key factor. Having an adult at the child’s school and being able to minimize the scramble of pickup and drop-off, or any back-and-forth, was the most convenient choice and trumped any other needs or desires. In our case, that wasn’t applicable.

Public vs. private schooling in Mexico

We learned that families had to choose an educational route in Mexico: public or private? In talking to family members and friends, we quickly realized that anyone who could afford to send their child to private school almost always preferred it as the most viable option. In many cases, private schools seemed to provide a sense of security and status for families, with a majority of private schools focusing on English as a second language. That part wasn’t necessarily important for us. We simply wanted a nourishing, enriching environment with multimodal learning and students from various backgrounds.

In the United States, going to private school signals a certain class, income and family background. Outside of scholarships, my wife and I never dreamed of such access to private education in California. Nor did we need to — the baseline level for free schooling in California is world-class, offering educational diversity in every form.

Measuring the realities of private education

In Mexico, though, that’s not exactly the case. And, contrary to what one might assume, Mexican private schools don’t necessarily translate to outstanding academic outperformance. In a Mexico Decoded essay titled “The Strange Mediocrity of Mexico’s Private Schools,” data revealed that Mexico’s private school students underperformed their global counterparts and even slightly lagged behind their national public school peers. With roughly 12% of Mexico’s total student body opting for private school, enrollment has actually been declining in the country, with an ongoing trend of fewer students entering private schools over the past five years, as reported by Miguel Ángel Dávila. That’s not exactly encouraging information. But, of course, as a former public school teacher in the United States myself, I know that standardized tests don’t tell the whole story about a child’s social, intellectual and creative progress or potential.

What’s the best fit?

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Escuela Montessori de la Ciudad de México (@montessoricdmx)

To clarify our school selection process, we began to visit a few budget-friendly options within walking distance in our neighborhood. But those environments felt out of sync with what we wanted. From what we saw, the lower-cost programs for preschool toddlers were overfilled, understaffed or enclosed in tighter spaces without any access to outdoor play. It didn’t feel comprehensively nurturing in the way we would hope for our son. And public schools could only offer around three hours of instruction per day, whereas private schools offered upwards of five. The longer hours appealed to us as working parents, so that made our decision even easier.

After being in contact with a handful of other private schools, the three of us visited the most appealing option in our area. Going in person confirmed what we had hoped: After many weeks of searching, we had landed on a school that best fit our circumstances, budget and philosophy of parenting, months before the school year began.

What kind of education matters to you?

Growing up in California taught my wife and me a lot about other cultures, other ways of seeing the world and other social classes. It’s the beauty of being Californian, in my opinion.

In contrast, we knew that in the mountains of Veracruz, we could never replicate that level of elasticity and exposure for our son. Instead, we set out to find the closest version of that global mixture within our new context — a school that offered some level of international presence, but maintained its core Mexican spirit. We also didn’t necessarily want to send our son to a private school with children whose families had exorbitant wealth or were disconnected from the humble lifestyle that we had grown up knowing as the children of immigrants ourselves.

It’s a delicate balance to strike, and one that I personally find difficult to find in Mexico — that is, a middle class, a middle ground, where the gap between everyone in the room is neither too small nor too gaping.

Finding common ground in Montessori philosophy

Through my wife’s research and background as an educator, she had grown interested in Montessori: the belief that a child-centered framework focused on independence, hands-on education and collaborative activity is the key to holistic developmental growth. In our minds, sending our son to a Montessori private school already communicated that the families involved on the campus were generally committed to similar principles and were invested, to whatever degree they could be, in maintaining and supporting that community with care and informed decision-making. Knowing that provided a middle ground for us. That felt reassuring.

Prioritizing nature and green space in Xalapa

Lastly came the surrounding environment of the school. We currently live in the bustling, chaotic center of Veracruz’s capital city, where concrete and smog abound. Naturally, as we spend all of our days in this neighborhood — which, to be clear, has other benefits, such as an abundance of nationally acclaimed cafes, restaurants and other services within a short walking distance — we prioritized a greener, more natural environment for our son. That may not be possible in every city (access to the outdoors isn’t easy if you’re in the middle of Mexico City or Guadalajara), but in Xalapa, there are cloud forests, rivers and mountains within a quick drive from our front door.

After looking around, we found a couple of schools located in such an area, where students are exposed daily to interaction with nature and tend a bountiful garden as part of their weekly curriculum. From there, we narrowed it down to our top choice after visiting and speaking with the school head. (If such an outdoor community isn’t available for you and your family, perhaps seeking out a school where urban gardening is emphasized would be the next alternative.) Having that final fresh-air component in place was essential for us, based on our location and context.

Reaping the rewards of our decision

In all, we’ve been happy with our choice. It isn’t the most affordable option, but then again, putting a price on your child’s education and sense of wonder is impossible (and the yearly tuition at the school is equivalent to what we would pay for a couple of months of childcare in California).

Our son attends a school where butterflies inadvertently greet him at the entrance — a big change from the rumble of vehicles just outside our front door. He attends a school where Spanish is the dominant language, but other bilingual families from other countries attend, and everyone is able to show up as their own unique selves (no uniforms, for instance).

It doesn’t make it any easier to drop him off when he’s in tears — spoiler alert: It’s the hardest thing we’ve ever done as parents — but we trust, intuitively, that he is in the right place and that we have made the best possible decision based on what’s available. His Spanish is already fluent and only improving by the day the more he interacts with native speakers in various contexts at his school and in the world.

And with that, our move to Mexico has already paid off.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: How are things going in Mexico? A perspective from our CEO
World.content:
What seems like such a simple question is actually not so easy to answer. Oftentimes, to provide an answer, we tend to gravitate towards economic indicators to describe how a country is doing. We look at data on GDP growth, inflation rates, productivity growth, investment levels, etc. This type of data is well documented across most countries, is published frequently (monthly or at most quarterly), and as a result has become the default in how we tend to analyze, talk about, and ultimately rank different countries’ performances. But we must also recognize that economic indicators alone are far from a complete answer.

The team at Mexico News Daily is working hard to bring you the news and information you need to be able to answer this important question. To start with, we cover the country’s economic news on a daily basis. But we understand that it can be difficult to connect the dots so earlier this year, we created a series of monthly indexes. These indexes — the MND Sheinbaum Index, the MND Mexico Economic Index, the MND Peso Index — all attempt to go beyond the raw data and provide a deeper understanding of what is really going on in the country. Our hope is that with this data, readers are willing and able to have a more informed opinion on the direction of the general economy.

That being said, from day one of the creation of these indexes, we acknowledged that they were clearly economic-focused and did not sufficiently take into account other aspects of life in Mexico. We needed more time to research, organize and present additional data in these non-economic areas.

It is with that backdrop that we are very excited to bring you a new series of reports called the MND Mexico Well-being Series. In this series of six reports, we will do a deep dive into dozens of non-economic indicators that help provide more comprehensive insight into the overall well-being of the country. We will look at how Mexico is currently doing in different aspects of well-being, how much progress has been made in the past decade, and how Mexico ranks compared to other countries globally. Mexico is now the 11th most populous country, the 12th largest economy and the sixth largest tourism destination. It is a country that is increasingly present and important on the world stage. Our goal is to answer the question of how Mexico is doing in terms of the overall well-being of its people.

As with all of our work, this analysis is prepared with an attempt to avoid any political bias. It is organized and presented as a fact-based analysis attempting to answer the important question: Beyond economic indicators, how is Mexico progressing in non-economic (well-being) indicators? The goal of this series is to educate and inform those who have the curiosity to learn more about the country. Through this increased visibility, we hope to bring more attention, resources and ultimately improvement in these areas. Many of our readers have experience in these areas and can most certainly provide help in many different ways.

Even with the additional insight that will come with this new series, we acknowledge that there is still a very significant and even more difficult-to-measure cultural component that goes far beyond the data to explain the true well-being of people living in Mexico. Our team is working on how we can organize and present the cultural piece in additional articles coming soon.

The first report in this series, “Health and healthcare,” was published earlier this week. You can read it here:

To accompany each of these deep dive reports, we will also be publishing a shorter-format, more visual “Mexico in Numbers” on each of these topics as well. Be on the lookout for the one on health and healthcare next week.

Stay tuned in the coming weeks for additional MND Mexico Well-being reports on education, poverty, happiness and gender equality — as well as a follow up series on the cutural component underlying all of this data.

We hope that this series of reports will inform and educate you. We also suspect that it will surprise and hopefully inspire you.

Please do give us your feedback on what you read and suggestions on what we might have missed or what additional information you would like to see. And please share these reports with colleagues, friends and family that might be interested in the data as well.

Thanks for reading MND.

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

World.content:

Key Facts —Today. Chile is bracing for another round of severe weather: thunderstorms are forecast for the south on Sunday, rain returns to Santiago on Monday, and forecasters already see a second atmospheric river forming for the first days of October.

Rain over Santiago. The capital is set for showers and possible thunderstorms on Monday, while the south remains under storm warnings.

Thunderstorm Warning for Sunday

The Dirección Meteorológica de Chile (DMC) issued aviso A507/2026 on Saturday evening, warning of probable thunderstorms from Sunday afternoon into the night. In La Araucanía the warning covers the valley and precordillera; in Los Ríos it includes the coastal range, valley and precordillera; and in Los Lagos it extends across the valley, precordillera, Chiloé and the interior coast, La Tercera reported on Sunday.

The aviso is linked to persistent atmospheric instability after the passage of last week’s frontal system — a pattern that has barely let up across the centre and south of the country.

What the Category-4 River Did This Week

The system that crossed Chile on Wednesday and Thursday arrived with an atmospheric river rated category 4 — the second-highest level on the five-step scale. Meteored put the probability of an extreme event at over 90% between Los Ríos and La Araucanía, and at 80–90% for Biobío. Corral, on the Los Ríos coast, accumulated 123 mm of rain in just 18 hours.

The DMC maintained alerts for moderate to heavy rainfall from the Maule to Los Lagos, with winds of up to 80 km/h in the precordillera and cordillera, and warned of a high freezing level — the “isoterma cero” — which turns precipitation to rain even high in the mountains and sharply raises the risk of river flooding. A separate thunderstorm warning covered nine regions, including the Santiago cordillera, from Thursday into early Friday. Senapred said the event stretched from O’Higgins to Magallanes, and red alerts with evacuations were declared in parts of the south on Thursday, according to Prensa Latina.

Santiago’s Turn on Monday

The capital, largely spared by last week’s core rainfall, is next in line. Meteored confirms that showers return to Santiago on Monday 28 September, possibly accompanied by thunderstorms and wind gusts of up to 70 km/h. Central Chile more broadly should expect thunderstorms at the start of the week as the instability drifts north.

In the north, a warm coastal atmosphere — boosted by the coastal El Niño warming Pacific waters — will favour intense drizzle and light rain in places such as Tocopilla, Paposo, Caldera and Huasco, an unusual pattern driven by high sea temperatures and a developing coastal trough.

Another Atmospheric River at the Start of October

The European ECMWF model points to a wet week almost everywhere: above-average precipitation is likely across 14 of Chile’s 16 regions, with the heaviest falls concentrated between Biobío and Aysén. That is where the next frontal system is expected to arrive at the start of October, again reinforced by an atmospheric river — this time possibly category 3 — and again with a high freezing level in the south.

The sequence fits an extraordinary year. July brought what specialists called Chile’s most intense storm system in three decades, with more than 16,000 people evacuated at its peak and a tornado that injured one person in Ñuble. September has continued the pattern: preventive alerts ran through the Fiestas Patrias weekend, and two significant frontal systems are now set to bookend the month.

What We Could Not Confirm

Senapred had not published a consolidated national damage and evacuation balance for the 23–24 September system at the time of writing, so we cannot give verified totals beyond the confirmed Corral rainfall figure and Thursday’s red-alert declarations. The strength of the early-October atmospheric river remains a projection — category 3 is the current model estimate and could change. We could also not confirm whether class suspensions will be ordered in any region on Monday.

More: Chile news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the DMC warning for Chile this Sunday?

Aviso A507/2026 warns of probable thunderstorms on Sunday afternoon and evening in La Araucanía, Los Ríos and Los Lagos, including Chiloé. It follows days of heavy rain driven by a category-4 atmospheric river earlier in the week.

Will it rain in Santiago on Monday?

Yes, according to Meteored. Showers return to the capital on Monday 28 September, with possible thunderstorms and wind gusts of up to 70 km/h, as the instability affecting the south moves into central Chile.

Is another atmospheric river coming to Chile?

Forecast models show a new frontal system reinforced by an atmospheric river — possibly category 3 — arriving at the start of October, with the heaviest rain between Biobío and Aysén and a high freezing level that raises flood risk in the southern mountains.

World.title: Healthcare in Venezuela for Expats: Clinics, Insurance and the Private Option
World.content:
GUIDES · VENEZUELA

Key Facts — The country Venezuela, an oil state of about 28.5 million people, has been run since January 2026 by acting president Delcy Rodríguez under close US oversight.

— The public system Free by law but badly run down. The Venezuelan Medical Federation said in September 2026 that 95% of hospitals had their doors “almost closed”.

— The private option Caracas has well-equipped private clinics, such as La Trinidad, El Ávila and Policlínica Metropolitana. They expect payment, usually in dollars, before treatment.

— Why it matters now Earthquakes on 24 June 2026 damaged hospitals across the north, just as airlines began to return.

— Insurance Local dollar policies cover private clinics. Canada’s travel advice urges cover for medical evacuation and hospital stays.

— The catch Governments still warn against travel, so check that your insurer covers Venezuela at all before you rely on it.

Healthcare in Venezuela works for foreigners only through the private tier. That means a good clinic, a dollar reserve, the right insurance and an exit plan.

Healthcare in Venezuela runs on two tracks in 2026. A free public system has decayed for more than a decade. Private clinics in Caracas still offer specialist care for those who can pay. This guide explains how both work for a foreign resident, as of September 2026.

How healthcare in Venezuela is organised

The 1999 constitution makes health a fundamental right and promises a free national public health system. The Ministry of Popular Power for Health runs most public hospitals and clinics. In law, anyone in the country can use them without paying.

In practice, most foreigners and middle-class Venezuelans use private clinics. These are paid out of pocket or through private health insurance, usually priced in US dollars.

Free care does not mean supplied care. Canada’s travel advice says some medicines are no longer available in hospitals at all.

The Hospital Universitario de Caracas, the capital’s main public teaching hospital, on the Central University campus (Photo: Caracas1830, CC BY 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

The public system in 2026

The US State Department describes Venezuela’s healthcare system as “in a state of severe crisis”. Its advisory, reissued on 26 June 2026, cites critical shortages of medicines, broken equipment and staff shortages.

Doctors say the same. Douglas León Natera leads the Venezuelan Medical Federation. On 23 September 2026 he said 95% of hospitals had their doors “almost closed”. He said only four or five were working properly and 302 needed repairs.

Money explains much of the decline. Transparencia Venezuela, an anti-corruption group, found that health received 4.24% of the 2025 public budget, a cut of 28% on 2024.

Then came the earthquakes. Two shocks of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 struck north-central Venezuela on 24 June 2026. By 17 September authorities had reported 6,509 deaths and 226,696 people treated, according to the relief charity Direct Relief.

Direct Relief found 75 of 211 assessed health facilities inoperative in September, though 52 had already been closed before the quakes. The International Rescue Committee reported that Pariata hospital in La Guaira state fell from 108 beds to 35.

For a foreign resident, the lesson is simple. A public hospital may stabilise you in an emergency, but you should not plan to rely on it.

Private clinics in Caracas

Caracas has a cluster of large private clinics, many in the east and south-east of the city. The health ministry listed about a dozen of them, including all named below, among centres receiving earthquake patients in June 2026.

Clinic Area What to know Centro Médico Docente La Trinidad La Trinidad, El Hatillo (south-east) Teaching hospital on Avenida Intercomunal La Trinidad, with specialist clinics and units. Clínica El Ávila Altamira (east) Clinic on Avenida San Juan Bosco, with adult emergency care, imaging and a laboratory. Policlínica Metropolitana Caurimare (south-east) Full-service clinic with intensive care, emergency, obstetrics and cardiology. Hospital de Clínicas Caracas San Bernardino (centre-north) Private hospital on Avenida Panteón, in a district known for clinics and doctors’ offices. Clínica Santa Sofía, Sanatrix, La Floresta East and south-east Caracas Other private clinics on the ministry’s June 2026 list.

Clinics named by the Venezuelan health ministry in June 2026; addresses and services from clinic websites, checked 27 September 2026.

Expect to pay before you are treated. Canada’s travel advice, updated on 24 September 2026, says private facilities are “extremely costly”, low on supplies and require payment in advance.

That usually means a deposit, a card guarantee or an authorisation from your insurer before admission. Ask for a written estimate and for what the deposit covers, because doctors’ fees are often billed separately.

Ambulance services are very limited and slow, Canada warns. Private emergency services exist; one, Venemergencia, was among the providers listed by the ministry in June.

Policlínica Metropolitana in Caurimare, a full-service private clinic in south-eastern Caracas (Photo: Eleonora Mata Mirabal, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

What private care costs

Clinics do not publish price lists, so treat every figure as a planning range. The Rio Times’ July 2026 cost-of-living survey put a private consultation in Caracas at about US$20 to US$50, depending on specialty.

For comparison, a US$50 specialist visit is about what a Venezuelan earning the state’s dollar-indexed income bonus receives in a week. That bonus was US$200 a month in May 2026, according to FEWS NET, a famine early-warning network.

Surgery and hospital stays can run into thousands of dollars. Complex procedures “can reach several hundred or thousands of dollars”, the same survey found, which is why deposits are standard.

Medicines are cheaper than in most of the region. Industry data from the drugmaker Grupo Leti put the average price at US$5.23 per unit in July 2026. That is about 36% below the Latin American average of US$8.18 at the end of 2025.

Health insurance: local and international

Venezuela’s insurance market is dominated by health cover. Hospitalisation, surgery and maternity policies, known locally as HCM, made up 68.21% of premiums in April 2026. That is according to the insurance regulator, Sudeaseg.

Mercantil Seguros held 30.55% of the market that month and Seguros Caracas 18.18%, Sudeaseg data show. Insurers collected US$418.84 million in net premiums from January to April 2026.

Local policies are sold in dollars and give direct access to clinic networks. Their limits can be low for serious illness, so check the sum insured, waiting periods and whether treatment abroad is covered.

Prices vary widely by age and cover. Journalism students at the Central University of Venezuela reported two examples in June 2026. One policy gave US$100,000 of cover for US$932 a year; another gave US$30,000 for US$993.

International expat insurers sell worldwide plans that can include evacuation. Many travel and health policies exclude countries under government warnings or sanctions, so get written confirmation that Venezuela is covered.

Medical evacuation: your exit plan

Evacuation cover pays to fly you to a better hospital abroad when local care is not enough. Canada’s travel advice tells visitors to buy insurance that covers medical evacuation and hospital stays.

Air ambulances are expensive. One US operator put long-distance and international transfers at US$50,000 and upward in June 2026, depending on the mission. That equals more than 20 years of the US$200 monthly income bonus.

Consular help is thin. Canada’s embassy in Caracas has not been open since 2019. The US embassy resumed operations in March 2026 but offers emergency services to US citizens only. Your insurer’s assistance line will organise an evacuation.

Flights help too. Caracas’s Maiquetía airport reopened partially on 1 September 2026 after the earthquakes. Airlines including Iberia, Air Europa and LATAM have resumed routes.

The check-in hall at Simón Bolívar International Airport in Maiquetía, Caracas’s main gateway, which reopened under restrictions on 1 September 2026 (Photo: Wilfredor, CC0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Medicines in 2026: shortage or supply?

The picture is contradictory. Canada warns of a severe shortage of pharmaceutical drugs and says most hospital pharmacies and drugstores no longer stock basic medicines.

Industry figures point the other way for private pharmacies. Grupo Leti data show 248.2 million units distributed from January to July 2026, up 11.31% on a year earlier. Industry groups said in January 2026 that stocks covered about 90 days.

Both can be true. Private chains in Caracas are generally stocked for those who can pay, while public hospitals and smaller towns face gaps.

Bring what you need. Canada advises packing all prescription and over-the-counter medicines, with a spare supply. Carry prescriptions using generic drug names.

Disease risks to plan for

Mosquito-borne diseases are common, the US advisory says, including dengue, chikungunya, Zika, Oropouche and yellow fever. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends malaria prevention for some travel.

Contaminated water is a significant source of stomach infections, according to the same advisory. Drink bottled or treated water, especially where the earthquakes damaged supply.

See a travel clinic before you arrive. Ask about yellow fever vaccination and malaria tablets, depending on where in Venezuela you will live or travel.

What this means for you

Choose your clinic before you choose your flat. Living near La Trinidad, El Ávila or Policlínica Metropolitana shortens the most important journey you may ever make in Caracas.

Hold a dollar reserve for deposits, even with insurance, because authorisations take time. Combine a local dollar policy for clinic access with international cover that names Venezuela and includes evacuation.

Healthcare in Venezuela can serve a foreign resident well in the private tier. It cannot yet be trusted for serious illness without a plan to leave, so treat evacuation cover as essential rather than optional.

Sources: Health-system facts come from the US State Department, the Government of Canada, the Venezuelan Medical Federation, Direct Relief and the International Rescue Committee, with market data from Sudeaseg and Grupo Leti as reported in Venezuelan media.

What Is Not Known

No independent national survey of hospital conditions for 2026 was found. The Venezuelan Medical Federation’s figures are statements by its president, not a published audit. The government has not released comparable data.

How far the earthquake damage has been repaired is not established. Direct Relief and the IRC counted inoperative and damaged facilities in September 2026. No official timetable for rebuilding the affected hospitals has been published.

Private clinic prices are not published. The consultation range in this guide comes from a Rio Times survey, not from clinic tariffs. Deposits and daily room rates vary by clinic, doctor and diagnosis.

Which international insurers currently cover residence in Venezuela is not documented in one place. Policies differ by issuing company and country, and exclusions tied to travel warnings or sanctions change. Only written confirmation from an insurer settles the question.

How reliable medicine supply is outside Caracas is unclear. Industry data measure units sold nationally, while Canada describes severe shortages. No independent 2026 survey of pharmacy stock by region was found.

More: Venezuela news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is healthcare in Venezuela free for foreigners?

Public care is free by law under the 1999 constitution, and foreigners can use it. In practice public hospitals are short of medicines, staff and equipment, and patients often have to bring supplies. Most foreigners use private clinics and pay in dollars or through insurance.

What are the best private clinics in Caracas?

Large private clinics used by foreigners include Centro Médico Docente La Trinidad, Clínica El Ávila in Altamira, Policlínica Metropolitana in Caurimare and Hospital de Clínicas Caracas in San Bernardino. All were listed by the health ministry among centres receiving patients after the June 2026 earthquakes. Expect to pay a deposit or show insurance before treatment.

How much does a doctor’s visit cost in Caracas?

A private consultation costs roughly US$20 to US$50, depending on specialty, according to a Rio Times survey from July 2026. Surgery and hospital stays can reach thousands of dollars. Clinics usually ask for payment or an insurer’s guarantee in advance.

Do I need medical evacuation insurance for Venezuela?

Yes. Canada’s travel advice tells visitors to buy insurance that covers medical evacuation and hospital stays. International air-ambulance transfers can cost US$50,000 or more, and Canada’s embassy in Caracas has not been open since 2019.

Are medicines still scarce in Venezuela in 2026?

The picture is mixed. Canada warns of a severe shortage, especially in hospital pharmacies. Industry data show 248.2 million units distributed from January to July 2026, up 11.31%, so private pharmacies in Caracas are generally stocked. Bring your own supply of any regular medication.

Does travel insurance cover Venezuela?

Not always. Many policies exclude countries under government travel warnings or sanctions. The United States rates Venezuela Level 3, reconsider travel, and Canada advises against all travel, so get written confirmation that your policy covers Venezuela and evacuation.

World.title: What Is Petrobras? Brazil’s Oil Giant Explained: the Business, the Politics and What to Watch
World.content:
GUIDES · BRAZIL

Key Facts — What it is Petróleo Brasileiro S.A., Brazil’s state-controlled oil and gas company, founded in 1953 and headquartered in Rio de Janeiro.

— Production 3.34 million barrels of oil equivalent a day of its own output in the second quarter of 2026. About 83 percent came from the deep-water pre-salt fields.

— Latest results Net income of US$10.4 billion in the second quarter of 2026, more than double a year earlier. Sales revenue was US$33.6 billion.

— Who controls it The federal government holds 50.26 percent of the voting shares but only 29.02 percent of the total capital, as of August 2026.

— Chief executive Magda Chambriard, in office since 24 May 2024 and still in post as of September 2026.

— Shares Preferred shares closed at R$47.99 (about US$9.25) in São Paulo on 25 September 2026. The New York receipts, ticker PBR, closed at US$20.37. The real traded at R$5.19 to the US dollar, according to market data.

What is Petrobras, how does it make its money, who really controls it, and why do fuel prices keep turning into politics? A plain guide for foreign readers and investors.

What is Petrobras? It is Brazil’s oil company, owned partly by the state and partly by private investors around the world. It pumps most of its oil from beneath a thick layer of salt far off the coast. And because the government controls it, every change in fuel prices is also a political decision.

What is Petrobras and what does it do?

Petrobras was created by law in October 1953 under President Getúlio Vargas. For more than four decades it held a legal monopoly on Brazilian oil. The sector was opened to competitors in the late 1990s, but Petrobras remains by far the country’s biggest producer.

Its core business is exploration and production: finding oil and gas and pumping it out. Oil companies usually measure operating profit as EBITDA: earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation. In the second quarter of 2026, this division produced US$15.9 billion of Petrobras’s adjusted EBITDA.

Most of that oil comes from the pre-salt. These reservoirs lie under a salt layer up to two kilometres thick. They sit deep beneath the Atlantic off Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo. The oil is costly to reach but cheap to lift once wells are running.

How cheap? In the second quarter of 2026, lifting a barrel from the pre-salt cost Petrobras US$4.45, before taxes and leasing. Brent crude, the international benchmark, averaged US$104.52 a barrel over the same three months.

Petrobras also refines. Its refineries ran at 101.2 percent of nominal capacity in the second quarter, a company record. They produced about 1.9 million barrels a day of diesel, petrol, jet fuel and other products. It sells gas and generates some electricity too.

What Petrobras does not do is run the green-and-yellow petrol stations that carry its name. Those belong to Vibra Energia, the former BR Distribuidora, which Petrobras sold off. Vibra uses the Petrobras brand under licence.

A Petrobras-branded fuel station; the stations are run by Vibra Energia, the former BR Distribuidora (Photo: Moacir Ximenes, CC BY 3.0 BR via Wikimedia Commons)

The numbers: what the latest results show

The latest reported results cover the second quarter of 2026, the three months to 30 June. Petrobras published them on 6 August 2026. It reports in reais and in US dollars; the dollar figures are used here.

Sales revenue was US$33.6 billion, up 60 percent on a year earlier. Net income was US$10.4 billion, up 120 percent.

Stripping out one-off items, such as currency gains and the new export tax, net income was US$11.1 billion. Adjusted EBITDA on the same basis was US$20.0 billion. The company called it one of its highest quarterly results on record.

Two things drove it. Oil was expensive, with Brent averaging US$104.52 a barrel against US$67.82 a year earlier. And output was at a record: own production rose 14.1 percent on the year, as new production ships reached full flow.

The cash side matters most to shareholders. Operating cash flow was US$12.3 billion and free cash flow, what is left after investment, US$7.7 billion. Capital spending in the quarter was US$5.3 billion.

Debt is under control by the company’s own yardstick. Gross debt was US$70.8 billion at the end of June, below the US$75 billion ceiling in its 2026–2030 business plan. Net debt was 1.14 times a year’s adjusted EBITDA.

Petrobras is also one of the state’s biggest cash sources. It says it paid R$88.6 billion (about US$17.1 billion) in taxes to federal, state and municipal governments in the quarter. That is roughly R$1 billion (about US$190 million) a day.

Petróleo Brasileiro S.A. – Petrobras explores, produces, and sells oil and gas in Brazil, China, the United States, the Americas, Asia, Europe, Singapore, and internationally. It operates through three segments: Exploration and Production; Refining, Transportation & Marketing; and Gas & Low Carbon Energies. The Exploration and Production segment explores, develops, and produces…

Owners and management: who controls Petrobras

Petrobras is a mixed-capital company. It is listed on the São Paulo exchange, B3, and in New York. By law, however, the federal government must keep voting control. That control is the single most important fact about the company.

As of August 2026, the federal government held 50.26 percent of the common, or voting, shares. It held no preferred shares, which carry dividend priority but no vote. So its stake in the whole company was only 29.02 percent.

The state development bank, BNDES, and its investment arm hold another 6.43 percent of the capital. Together the state bloc owns about 35.45 percent. Non-Brazilian investors held 48.29 percent, more than the state.

Voting control means the government chooses the majority of the board and, through it, the chief executive. The board is chaired by Guilherme Santos Mello, appointed by the controlling shareholder.

Magda Chambriard, an engineer who spent more than two decades at Petrobras and later headed the national oil regulator, the ANP, became chief executive on 24 May 2024. She replaced Jean Paul Prates, whom President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva removed. She was still in post as of September 2026.

Turnover at the top is a known risk. Chambriard is the sixth chief executive since January 2019. Several of her predecessors left after clashing with the government of the day over fuel prices.

Magda Chambriard at her swearing-in ceremony as Petrobras chief executive in Rio de Janeiro, June 2024 (Photo: Ricardo Stuckert/PR, CC BY-SA 2.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Its role in the market

Petrobras is not just a company in Brazil’s economy; it shapes it. Its refineries supply much of the country’s diesel and petrol, so its wholesale prices set the tone for what drivers pay. It commissions the giant floating production ships that shipyards and suppliers depend on. Its platform contracts run to billions of dollars each.

It is also a large exporter. Crude exports approached one million barrels a day in the second quarter, while imports of crude fell to 89,000 barrels a day. The pre-salt has made Brazil Latin America’s largest oil producer, well ahead of Guyana and Venezuela, its neighbours to the north.

The business plan approved in November 2025 foresees US$109 billion of investment from 2026 to 2030. About US$69 billion goes to exploration and production, most of it in the pre-salt. Production is planned to peak at around 3.4 million barrels of oil equivalent a day in 2028 and 2029.

The plan was drawn up in late 2025, when oil was much cheaper. Prices in 2026 have been far higher, largely because of the Middle East war. The gap explains the record profits, and why the government wants a share of them.

Petrobras also holds 47.03 percent of the voting shares in Braskem. Braskem is the largest producer of thermoplastic resins in the Americas. Braskem is trying to restructure about US$11 billion of debt, and Petrobras has said it will not inject capital alone.

Risks and controversies: fuel prices, politics and the Amazon

Fuel prices are the permanent flashpoint. Until May 2023 Petrobras priced fuel at “import parity”, tracking what it would cost to import. It then switched to a commercial strategy that also weighs the domestic market. That lets it smooth out swings in world prices rather than pass them straight on.

2026 has tested it. When the Middle East war pushed oil prices up, the government acted on 12 March. It created a 12 percent export tax on crude and a 50 percent export tax on diesel. It also paid a subsidy of R$0.32 a litre (about US$0.06) on road diesel.

Petrol followed the same pattern. On 28 May Petrobras raised its petrol price to distributors by R$0.48 a litre (about US$0.09). A federal discount of R$0.44 (about US$0.08) absorbed most of it. On 9 September the discount ended and Petrobras added R$0.19 (about US$0.04), lifting the cost to distributors by R$0.63 a litre (about US$0.12).

That left the average wholesale price at R$3.24 a litre (about US$0.62). A temporary cut in federal fuel taxes of the same size was meant to keep pump prices unchanged. In an election year, the effect has been to keep higher oil costs away from drivers.

The crude export tax is contested. Producers say it is unconstitutional. A court suspended it in late August, and an appeals court reinstated it on 31 August. The original emergency measure had lapsed in July; since then the government has kept the crude levy alive through resolutions of its foreign-trade committee, Gecex. It had raised R$7.98 billion (about US$1.54 billion) by July and cost Petrobras US$965 million in the second quarter alone.

The Margem Equatorial is the environmental fight. This is a stretch of Brazil’s northern coast, near the mouth of the Amazon, which geologists compare with the fields off Guyana. After refusing a first request in 2023, the environment agency IBAMA licensed Petrobras to drill there in October 2025.

On 14 August 2026 Petrobras reported signs of hydrocarbons in its Morpho well. The well is in block FZA-M-59, about 175 kilometres off the state of Amapá. It has not said whether the find is commercial. Environmental groups and federal prosecutors still question the licensing.

The past also weighs. The Lava Jato, or Car Wash, investigations from 2014 exposed a bribery and cartel scheme around Petrobras contracts. In 2018 the company agreed to pay US$2.95 billion to settle a US class action and US$853 million to US authorities.

The mouth of the Amazon seen from the International Space Station; Petrobras’s Margem Equatorial well lies offshore to the north, off Amapá (Photo: NASA, public domain via Wikimedia Commons)

What to watch

The election. Brazil votes on 4 October 2026, with a possible runoff on 25 October. Whoever takes office in January 2027 will shape Petrobras’s board, its pricing and its dividends. Our election briefing sets out the race.

The export tax. The 12 percent levy runs until November, and the court case over it is not settled. Whether it is renewed or dropped will move Petrobras’s export earnings.

The Amazon well. Drilling at Morpho was expected to end in October 2026. IBAMA authorised three more wells nearby on 4 September 2026, and Petrobras plans to start drilling them in January 2027. The results will decide whether the Margem Equatorial becomes a new pre-salt or a costly dry run.

The next business plan. Petrobras usually approves its five-year plan in late November. The key numbers are investment, the debt ceiling and the oil price it assumes.

Braskem. A buyout auction is set for 16 October, with the debt deadline in November. Any call on Petrobras’s cash would be a test of its investment discipline.

What this means for foreigners and investors

Foreign investors can buy Petrobras in New York. Each PBR receipt represents two common shares, and each PBR.A receipt two preferred shares. In São Paulo the tickers are PETR3 for common and PETR4 for preferred shares.

At the closing prices of 25 September 2026, the whole company was worth about R$656 billion (about US$126.5 billion). The PETR3 common shares closed at R$53.04 (about US$10.23).

Dividends are the main attraction, and they follow a formula. When gross debt is at or below the plan’s ceiling, Petrobras must pay out 45 percent of free cash flow. For the second quarter of 2026 it approved R$17.4 billion (about US$3.35 billion) in dividends and interest on capital.

A few things this does not mean. Majority voting control does not mean the state owns most of the company; directly it owns less than a third. And Petrobras does not set pump prices. It sets wholesale prices; taxes, ethanol blending and retail margins do the rest.

It also does not mean the dividend is fixed. The formula depends on free cash flow, which depends on oil prices, taxes and investment. A new government can change the policy through the board. Our Brazil explainer covers the wider political system.

Sources: Results and production from Petrobras’ second-quarter 2026 filings with the US Securities and Exchange Commission and its news agency, ownership from its investor-relations site, and share prices and exchange rates from market data at the close on 25 September 2026.

What Is Not Known

Whether the Amazon find is worth developing. Petrobras has reported signs of hydrocarbons, not a commercial discovery. It has given no estimate of volumes, and appraisal wells start only in 2027.

What the next government will do. Petrobras policy on prices, dividends and investment has changed with almost every administration. The winner of the October election is not known, and neither is their choice of chief executive.

How long the export tax lasts. It has been extended by resolutions of the government’s foreign-trade committee, suspended by one court and restored by another. The final ruling on whether it is constitutional has not been made.

Where oil prices settle. The 2026 results rest on prices well above the company’s own planning assumptions. How long the Middle East war keeps them there cannot be forecast.

What Braskem will cost. The restructuring talks are unresolved. Petrobras has not said how far it would go if the other owners do not match its terms.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Petrobras?

Petrobras, or Petróleo Brasileiro S.A., is Brazil’s state-controlled oil and gas company, founded in 1953 and based in Rio de Janeiro. It produced 3.34 million barrels of oil equivalent a day in the second quarter of 2026, mostly from deep-water pre-salt fields.

Who owns Petrobras?

The federal government holds 50.26 percent of the voting shares, which gives it control, but only 29.02 percent of the total capital. With the development bank BNDES, the state owns about 35 percent. Non-Brazilian investors held about 48 percent as of August 2026.

Who is the CEO of Petrobras in 2026?

Magda Chambriard, an engineer who spent more than two decades at Petrobras and later headed the national oil regulator, the ANP. She took office on 24 May 2024 and was still chief executive as of September 2026.

Does Petrobras pay dividends?

Yes. Its policy requires it to pay out 45 percent of free cash flow while gross debt stays at or below the ceiling in its business plan, currently US$75 billion. For the second quarter of 2026 it approved R$17.4 billion, about US$3.35 billion.

Does Petrobras set petrol prices in Brazil?

It sets the wholesale price it charges distributors, not the pump price. Pump prices also include federal and state taxes, the ethanol blend and distributor and retailer margins. In 2026 the government used tax cuts and discounts to offset Petrobras price rises.

Can foreigners buy Petrobras shares?

Yes. Petrobras receipts trade on the New York Stock Exchange as PBR, each representing two common shares, and PBR.A for preferred shares. In São Paulo the shares trade as PETR3 and PETR4.

World.title: What Is Nubank? Brazil’s Fintech Giant Explained: the Business, the Numbers and What to Watch
World.content:
GUIDES · BRAZIL

Key Facts — What it is A digital bank with no branches, run through a phone app. The listed parent, Nu Holdings Ltd., is registered in the Cayman Islands and headquartered in São Paulo.

— Customers 138.9 million at the end of June 2026. Almost 118 million are in Brazil, 15.8 million in Mexico and over 5 million in Colombia.

— Latest results Net income of US$1.06 billion in the second quarter of 2026, its first quarter above US$1 billion. Revenue was US$5.88 billion.

— Shares Traded on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker NU. They closed at US$13.59 on 25 September 2026, valuing the company at roughly US$66 billion.

— Founders David Vélez, who is Colombian, Cristina Junqueira, who is Brazilian, and Edward Wible, who is American. They started the company in São Paulo in May 2013.

— Currency Nu reports in US dollars but earns most of its income in Brazilian reais. The real traded at R$5.19 to the US dollar on 25 September 2026, according to market data.

What is Nubank, how does it make money, who controls it, and what could change its story over the next year? A plain guide for foreign readers and investors.

What is Nubank? In short, a bank that lives in a phone. It began in 2013 with a no-fee credit card in São Paulo and now serves 139 million people in three countries. In the second quarter of 2026 it earned more than US$1 billion for the first time, and it has started serving customers in the United States.

What is Nubank and what does it do?

Nubank is a digital bank. It has no branches. Customers open accounts, borrow, pay and invest through a mobile app. That keeps costs low, and low costs sit at the heart of the model.

It started with one product: a purple credit card with no annual fee, managed entirely in the app. That was its pitch in a market used to branch queues and bank charges. The card is still its biggest business.

Today Nubank offers current accounts, credit cards, personal loans, secured loans, insurance and investments. It also serves small firms, and says it serves more small businesses than any other financial institution in Brazil. It is now pushing upmarket with dedicated offers for higher-income customers, called Ultravioleta and Croma.

The money comes from three streams. In the second quarter of 2026, lending produced 41 percent of gross profit, fees 25 percent and “float” 34 percent. Float is the income Nu earns by investing the deposits customers leave with it.

The app also connects to Pix, Brazil’s instant-payment system run by the central bank. Pix transfers are free for individuals, so they earn Nu little directly. What they do is bring customers into the app every day, which makes it easier to sell them credit.

What Nubank is not, at least not yet, is a licensed bank in every market. In Brazil it has operated as a regulated financial and payment institution, and it is buying a banking licence. In the United States it works through a partner bank. Both points matter and are explained below.

The Pix area of the Nubank app, where customers send and receive instant payments free of charge (Image: Nubank, public domain via Wikimedia Commons)

The numbers: what the latest results show

The latest reported results cover the second quarter of 2026, the three months to 30 June. Nu Holdings published them on 13 August 2026. All figures are in US dollars, and growth rates are at constant exchange rates.

Revenue was US$5.88 billion, up 39 percent on a year earlier. Net income was US$1.06 billion, up 49 percent. It was the first quarter in the company’s history in which profit passed US$1 billion. Our report on the quarter has the detail.

For scale, that single quarter’s profit is more than a third of what Nu earned in the whole of 2025. Its annual report puts 2025 net income at US$2.9 billion, on revenue of US$15.8 billion.

Return on equity, which measures profit against the money shareholders have in the business, was 33 percent. A year earlier it was 28 percent. It means Nu earned 33 cents a year for every dollar of shareholders’ equity.

The loan book reached US$39.4 billion. Of that, US$26 billion was credit cards, US$10.3 billion unsecured personal loans and US$3.1 billion secured loans. Deposits were US$45.3 billion, of which US$36.4 billion sat in Brazil. Nu holds more in deposits than it lends out.

Bad loans are the number to watch. Loans more than 90 days overdue were 6.9 percent of the book, up from 6.5 percent a year earlier. Loans 15 to 90 days late, an early-warning signal, were 4.8 percent.

Costs are where Nu stands apart. The average active customer brought in US$17.1 of revenue a month and cost about US$1 a month to serve. Its efficiency ratio, which compares operating costs with income, was 19.5 percent. Lower is better.

Nu says AI agents now handle more than 60 percent of customer-support conversations in Brazil. That is one reason the cost to serve stays so low as the customer base grows.

What Nu Holdings does. Nu Holdings Ltd. provides digital banking platform in Brazil, Mexico, Colombia, the Cayman Islands, and the United States. The company provides spending solutions comprising Nu credit and prepaid card, a digitally enabled card that acts as a credit and a prepaid card; Nubank+ Tier, an evolution of the Nu experience; Ultraviolet credit…

Owners and management

The listed company is Nu Holdings Ltd., registered in the Cayman Islands. That structure is common for Latin American companies listed in New York. It does not mean the bank operates from the Caribbean. Its headquarters are in São Paulo.

Nu listed on the New York Stock Exchange in December 2021 at US$9 a share. Its Class A shares trade under the ticker NU. Investors in Brazil can buy them on the São Paulo exchange as depositary receipts, under the code ROXO34.

David Vélez, the Colombian co-founder, is chief executive. He holds super-voting Class B shares. The company’s 2025 annual report says these give him 74.3 percent of the votes. In practice, outside shareholders cannot overrule him.

Cristina Junqueira, the Brazilian co-founder, is chief growth officer and chief executive of the US business, which is run from Miami. Lívia Chanes has run Brazil since January 2024 and the whole of Latin America since 15 July 2026.

Robert Livingston became chief financial officer in July 2026. Roberto Campos Neto, who governed Brazil’s central bank until the end of 2024, joined in July 2025. He is executive vice-chairman and global head of public policy.

Roberto Campos Neto in 2019, when he governed Brazil’s central bank; he joined Nubank in 2025 (Photo: Marcos Oliveira/Agência Senado, CC BY 2.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Its role in the market

Nubank describes itself as the largest digital bank in Latin America. On customer numbers the claim is hard to dispute. In Brazil, almost 118 million customers in a country of more than 210 million people makes it a household name.

Customers are not the same as money, though. Brazil’s big incumbent banks, such as Itaú Unibanco, Banco do Brasil, Bradesco and Caixa, are older and lend far more to companies. On stock-market value, Itaú was still ahead of Nu in September 2026, The Rio Times reported. The digital rivals include Banco Inter, C6 Bank, PicPay and Mercado Pago; our guide to Brazil’s fintechs and digital banks compares them.

Mexico is the second market. Nu launched its bank there in August 2026. By its own count, that made it the country’s largest digital bank, with 16 million customers in July. It reaches 16.5 percent of Mexican adults, which the company compares with Brazil in 2020.

Colombia is the third, with more than 5 million customers. The unit plans to invest about 5 trillion pesos (about US$1.5 billion, at 3,357 pesos to the dollar) by 2030. Vélez has called Colombia’s legal interest-rate ceiling, known as the usury cap, the biggest obstacle to financial inclusion. In September 2026 Colombia’s president named him an unpaid adviser on artificial intelligence.

The United States is the newest. Nu began serving US customers on 10 September 2026 through a partner, Lead Bank, which carries deposit insurance. The offer includes a savings account paying 3.50 percent and a cashback credit card.

Its own national bank charter has only conditional approval. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the federal bank regulator, granted it at the end of January 2026. Approvals from the Federal Reserve and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation were still outstanding as of September 2026. We explain why Nubank entered without its own licence.

Cristina Junqueira, Nubank co-founder and chief executive of its US business (Photo: Lucasgilbatista, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Risks and controversies

Credit risk comes first. Most of Nu’s gross profit comes from lending, much of it unsecured credit to ordinary households. When Brazilian families come under strain, late payments rise quickly. The 90-day bad-loan ratio rose to 6.9 percent in mid-2026.

Interest rates come second. Brazil’s policy rate, the Selic, stood at 13.75 percent after a cut on 16 September 2026. High rates lift what Nu earns on float. They also squeeze its borrowers.

Card interest is politically sensitive. A Brazilian law in force since January 2024 caps interest and charges on unpaid card balances. The total cannot exceed 100 percent of the original debt. Nu, as a card-led lender, operates under that ceiling.

Regulation comes third. A joint rule of Brazil’s monetary council and central bank restricts the word “bank” to institutions with a banking licence. On 20 July 2026 Nu agreed to buy a small lender, Banco Porto Real de Investimentos, to obtain one. The deal still needs central bank approval.

Control is the fourth. Vélez’s voting power means minority shareholders have little influence. Because the parent is a Cayman company, shareholder rights follow Cayman law rather than Brazilian or American company law.

Currency is the fifth. Nu reports in dollars but earns mostly in reais and Mexican and Colombian pesos. A weaker real shrinks reported dollar results even when the business grows at home. That is why the company quotes growth at constant exchange rates.

Not every analyst is convinced. Itaú BBA is the investment-banking arm of Itaú Unibanco. On 16 September 2026 it cut Nu to market perform, citing slower profit growth in 2027.

What to watch

The Monzo report. In late September 2026 Sky News reported early-stage talks for Nu to buy Monzo, the British digital bank. The report valued Monzo at £8 billion to £10 billion (about US$10.6 billion to US$13.2 billion, at US$1.32 to the pound). Both companies declined to comment. It is a report, not a deal. We covered what was reported.

Investor Day on 8 December 2026 in New York. It will be Nu’s first, and management says it will set out long-term strategy and growth plans. Any new targets will reset how the market values the shares.

The licences. The Brazilian central bank must approve the Porto Real purchase. In the United States, the conditional charter requires Nu to be fully capitalised within twelve months and open within eighteen.

Bad loans. The third-quarter results cover July to September 2026. They will show whether the rise in 90-day arrears was seasonal, as the company says, or more lasting.

Brazil’s election. The first round is on 4 October 2026, with a possible runoff on 25 October. The result may move the real and the interest-rate outlook, and with them Nu’s share price.

What this means for foreigners and investors

For foreigners living in Brazil, Nubank is one of several digital banks that accept the CRNM migration card. Applicants also need a CPF tax number. It applies a residency filter, and applicants without residence status are routinely declined. Our guide to opening a bank account in Brazil sets out the order of steps.

For investors, NU shares are a bet on Brazilian consumer credit, priced in dollars. At US$13.59 on 25 September 2026, the stock stood about 51 percent above its US$9 listing price of December 2021.

A few things this does not mean. A US account opened with Nu is not yet an account at a chartered Nu bank; the deposits sit with Lead Bank. Owning NU shares is not a deposit and carries no deposit insurance. And the Monzo report does not mean a deal will follow.

For anyone weighing Brazil more broadly, our Brazil explainer covers the politics and economy that drive Nu’s home market.

Sources: Results from Nu Holdings’ second-quarter 2026 release furnished to the US Securities and Exchange Commission, management roles from the company’s investor-relations site, and market prices and exchange rates from market data at the close on 25 September 2026.

What Is Not Known

Whether a Monzo deal happens. The talks rest on one media report, both banks declined to comment, and no terms or filings exist. Monzo was also reported to be weighing a new funding round instead.

When Nu becomes a chartered US bank. The Federal Reserve and the deposit insurer have not yet ruled, and no date has been published. Until then, the US business depends on Lead Bank.

When Brazil’s central bank approves the Porto Real purchase. The company has given no timetable, and the approval process is not public.

Whether credit quality holds. The rise in 90-day arrears in mid-2026 may be seasonal, as Nu says. Brazilian household debt, the election and the path of interest rates will decide that, and none can be forecast with confidence.

Whether Colombia loosens its usury cap. Vélez wants it scrapped or overhauled, but no bill to do so had been published as of September 2026.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Nubank?

Nubank is a Brazilian digital bank with no branches, run through a phone app. Its parent, Nu Holdings, is listed in New York and served 138.9 million customers in Brazil, Mexico and Colombia at the end of June 2026. It began in 2013 with a no-fee credit card.

Is Nubank a real bank?

It is regulated, but not a licensed bank everywhere. In Brazil it has operated as a regulated financial and payment institution and agreed in July 2026 to buy a small bank to obtain a full licence, pending central bank approval. In Mexico it launched as a bank in August 2026. In the United States it works through a partner, Lead Bank.

Who owns Nubank?

Nu Holdings Ltd. is a public company registered in the Cayman Islands, with shares traded on the New York Stock Exchange as NU. Co-founder and chief executive David Vélez holds super-voting shares that give him 74.3 percent of the votes, according to the company’s 2025 annual report.

Can a foreigner open a Nubank account in Brazil?

Residents usually can, with a CPF tax number and the CRNM migration card. Nubank applies a residency filter, and applicants without residence status are routinely declined. Approval is always at the bank’s discretion.

Is Nubank buying Monzo?

Not as of 27 September 2026. Sky News reported early-stage talks valuing Monzo at £8 billion to £10 billion, about US$10.6 billion to US$13.2 billion. Both companies declined to comment, and no deal has been announced.

How does Nubank make money?

Mostly from lending. In the second quarter of 2026, credit produced 41 percent of gross profit, income earned on customer deposits 34 percent and fees 25 percent. Very low running costs, about US$1 a month per active customer, keep margins high.

World.title: Moving to Trinidad and Tobago: Visas, Costs, Work Permits and Daily Life
World.content:
GUIDES · TRINIDAD AND TOBAGO

Key Facts — What it is A standing guide to visas, work permits, living costs and daily life for foreigners moving to Trinidad and Tobago.

— Who it’s for Energy and finance professionals, Caribbean nationals, spouses of citizens and long-stay remote workers.

— The rules Most Western visitors enter visa-free, but paid work needs a permit that your employer applies for.

— What it costs A central one-bedroom flat in Port of Spain averages about TT$6,880 a month (about US$1,017), per Numbeo.

— Why it matters A 199-day state of emergency ended on 17 September 2026, and a new special-operations law passed Parliament days later.

— The catch US dollars are rationed at bank counters, so moving money out can be slower than moving in.

Moving to Trinidad and Tobago is easy to start and slow to finish. Entry is simple, but work, residence and money run through permits and queues.

Free daily brief — no card needed Get every Analysis story in one morning email We build you a personalized brief around the topics you follow — free for 7 days. Love it? Your first month after that is US$1. Start my free brief Yes, email me my free daily brief — I can unsubscribe any time.

Moving to Trinidad and Tobago means joining a small, English-speaking energy economy of about 1.37 million people, seven miles off Venezuela. This guide sets out entry, permits, costs, safety and daily life as of September 2026.

Trinidad and Tobago is two islands. Trinidad holds the capital, Port of Spain, the gas industry and most people; Tobago is smaller and lives mainly from tourism.

All US$ figures use the Central Bank of Trinidad and Tobago selling rate of TT$6.7661 per US dollar on 25 September 2026. The central bank manages the Trinidad and Tobago dollar (TT$) closely, so the rate moves little.

Entering Trinidad and Tobago: visas and the online arrival card

Most Western visitors need no visa. The UK government says British visitors can stay up to 90 days, with an onward ticket and proof of funds.

The US State Department says American citizens need no visa for stays of 90 days or less. Citizens of most Caribbean Community (CARICOM) states, the regional bloc, also enter visa-free.

Other nationalities may need a visa. The consulate in New York charges US$143 for a multiple-entry visa, including a US$20 service charge.

That consular fee chart took effect on 22 January 2026. Fees at other missions and online may differ.

Since 17 March 2026, every traveller entering or leaving must file an online arrival or departure card at travel.gov.tt. It is free and can be filed up to 72 hours before travel.

Once submitted, the card produces a receipt with two QR codes for immigration and customs officers. It replaced the old paper forms.

Visitors must declare cash worth more than TT$20,000 (about US$2,956) on arrival or departure. A visa-free stamp is not a work or residence right; it only covers a visit.

Piarco International Airport, the main gateway for new arrivals in Trinidad (Photo: Ssm132, Public domain via Wikimedia Commons)
