Open the full Ask Rio Times → RT Ask Rio TimesCost of living, safety, visas across Latin America › RT Ask Rio Times 17 years of Latin America reporting, on demand. × Best for expats Cost of living Safest places Easy visas Tap a question, or type your own — the answer appears right here. Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

Work permits: your employer applies, not you

Paid work needs a work permit under the Immigration Regulations. The one exception is a single stint of up to 30 days in any twelve months.

Permits are handled by the Ministry of Homeland Security, the renamed national security ministry. Applications go online through TTBizLink, the government’s trade and business portal.

The employer applies, or an attorney does so for a self-employed person. The ministry asks for applications at least six weeks before the start date.

Work permit item Cost or rule (as of September 2026) Processing fee TT$1,200 (about US$177), non-refundable Duration fee TT$900 a month (about US$133), minimum TT$2,700 (about US$399) Job advert At least seven days in daily newspapers, before applying Police certificate No older than six months Extension File at least two months before the permit expires

The monthly fee follows Legal Notice No. 493 of 29 December 2025. The full sum for the approved period must be paid before the permit is issued.

The newspaper advert exists to show that no local candidate was found. Owners and directors of a company do not have to advertise, the ministry’s guidelines say.

After approval, the worker must take the permit to the Immigration Division for an endorsement in the passport. A permit ties you to one employer; it is not a general right to work.

Staying for good: residence, CSME certificates and family routes

Permanent residence has four main routes, the ministry’s residence page says. They are five years of continuous residence, a CSME-based permit, family sponsorship, or marriage to a citizen or resident.

Marriage makes you eligible; it does not make approval automatic. Each application still goes through checks and ministerial discretion, and no official processing time is published.

Caribbean nationals have a faster path. The CSME, or CARICOM Single Market and Economy, lets twelve skill groups work across member states with a Skills Certificate.

Those groups include university graduates, nurses, teachers, artisans, musicians, domestic workers and private security officers. The foreign ministry puts minimum processing at five to six weeks.

The Skills Certificate is not residence and not citizenship. Holders from outside CARICOM do not qualify, so a European or North American still needs a work permit.

For the full rules, see Trinidad and Tobago Visa Rules: Easy Entry, Long Wait to Settle.

Westmoorings and Glencoe, west of Port of Spain, seen from Fort George (Photo: Grueslayer, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

What moving to Trinidad and Tobago costs each month

Rent is the biggest bill, and the gap between the centre and the suburbs is wide. Crowd-sourced Numbeo data for Port of Spain, last updated 6 September 2026, give these averages.

Item (Port of Spain) Monthly average In US$ One-bedroom flat, city centre TT$6,883 about US$1,017 One-bedroom flat, outside centre TT$3,524 about US$521 Three-bedroom flat, city centre TT$14,820 about US$2,190 Three-bedroom flat, outside centre TT$8,120 about US$1,200 Electricity, water, cooling (85 m² flat) TT$617 about US$91 Broadband, 60 Mbps or faster TT$383 about US$57 Single person, costs excluding rent TT$7,047 about US$1,042

For scale, Numbeo puts the average local net salary near TT$5,180 a month (about US$766). A central one-bedroom flat therefore costs more than a typical local wage.

The legal minimum wage is TT$20.50 an hour (about US$3.03), in force since 1 January 2024, the Ministry of Labour says. That shows how far expat budgets sit above local pay.

Petrol is cheap by Western standards, at about TT$7.75 a litre (about US$1.15) in Numbeo’s data. International primary school fees average about TT$73,545 a year (about US$10,870).

These are averages from user reports, not official statistics. Gated compounds in western suburbs such as Westmoorings often cost far more; older guides are in Cost of Living in Trinidad 2026.

Money: a managed currency and scarce US dollars

The TT dollar is stable, but US dollars are scarce. Banks ration foreign currency at the counter, and card limits for spending abroad have been cut.

Republic Bank capped US dollar card spending at US$2,500 per billing cycle from 21 August 2025. The central bank linked that cut to an imbalance between dollar demand and supply.

First Citizens, a majority state-owned bank, cut its standard Mastercard limit from US$6,000 to US$2,000 a month from 10 March 2026. Other cards and banks set their own limits.

For a newcomer, the rule is simple. Keep an account abroad, bring money in as needed, and do not count on converting large TT$ sums back quickly.

Inflation is low: the central bank reported headline inflation of 0.3 percent for June 2026. Low inflation does not mean low prices, because many goods are imported.

Maracas Bay on Trinidad’s north coast (Photo: Kalamazadkhan, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Safety after the state of emergency

Crime is the main worry for most people moving to Trinidad and Tobago. The police recorded 369 murders in 2025, down from a record of more than 620 in 2024.

That is roughly one killing a day, or about 27 per 100,000 people. Most violence is gang-related and concentrated in specific districts.

A state of emergency, proclaimed on 2 March 2026, ended on 17 September 2026 after 199 days. It let police arrest and search without warrants, and it suspended bail for some offences.

Media tallies put murders at 252 by 10 September 2026, slightly below the same point of 2025. Prime Minister Kamla Persad-Bissessar has said she would not hesitate to declare another emergency.

A new Special Operations Bill passed the Senate on 24 September 2026 by 16 votes to 15. The Senate President’s casting vote broke the tie.

The bill lets the President declare “closed areas”, where entry permits, cordons and curfews can apply.

The US State Department rates the country Level 3, “reconsider travel”, in an advisory issued 13 April 2026. The UK Foreign Office names Laventille, Morvant, Beetham, Sea Lots and parts of downtown Port of Spain as places for extra caution.

Neither warning bans travel or residence. They do mean armed robbery is common, so gated housing, locked car doors and avoiding isolated places after dark are normal habits.

Healthcare, taxes and property in brief

Public hospitals are run by five Regional Health Authorities. The UK Foreign Office says private clinics handle most ordinary problems, but serious cases may need evacuation abroad.

Good private insurance with evacuation cover is therefore the practical minimum. See Healthcare in Trinidad and Tobago for Expats.

Tax follows residence, not passport: spending more than half the year (roughly 183 days) there makes you tax-resident. Income above a TT$90,000 allowance (about US$13,300) is taxed at 25 percent, and above TT$1 million (about US$147,800) at 30 percent.

Details are in Trinidad and Tobago Taxes for Foreign Residents. Foreigners may buy a home on up to one acre in Trinidad without a licence, while Tobago purchases need one; see Buying Property in Trinidad and Tobago as a Foreigner.

Daily life: traffic, water, weather and driving

Traffic is the daily tax on life in north Trinidad. Commutes into Port of Spain from the east and south can take far longer than the distance suggests.

Public transport means state buses and “maxi taxis”, privately run minibuses on fixed routes. Many foreigners drive, and traffic keeps to the left.

A UK licence is valid for up to 90 days, the UK Foreign Office says, after which an international permit is needed. It also warns that highway crashes, often high-speed, are frequently fatal.

Water supply can be interrupted, as WASA, the state water authority, warned for central and south Trinidad in September 2026. Ask landlords about storage tanks and pumps. The rainy season, roughly June to December, brings flash flooding in low areas.

The islands sit south of the main hurricane track. The UK Foreign Office says they are rarely hit by hurricanes but can have severe storms, and earthquakes are a risk.

English is the official language, and Carnival, steelpan and cricket shape the calendar. Tobago runs its own assembly and has a slower, more rural pace than Trinidad.

What this means for you

If you have a job offer, the path is clear but paper-heavy. Push your employer to file six weeks early and budget for permit fees on each renewal.

If you are a Caribbean national with a degree or listed skill, the CSME certificate is usually the faster route. If you marry a citizen, residence is possible but not instant.

Choose housing for security and commute first, price second. Keep savings offshore, and check the Special Operations law before signing a lease near a declared closed area.

Sources: Rules and fees come from the homeland security, foreign and labour ministries and the Central Bank of Trinidad and Tobago. Safety data come from the US State Department, the UK Foreign Office and Trinidad press; prices from Numbeo.

What Is Not Known

When the Special Operations law will be brought into force is not known. It takes effect only on proclamation, no closed area had been declared as of 27 September 2026, and none can be until the law is in force.

Whether murders keep falling without emergency powers is not established. The 2026 count was running only slightly below 2025 before the emergency ended.

How long a permanent residence application takes is not published. No official processing time exists, and each decision rests on ministerial discretion.

When the US dollar shortage will ease cannot be predicted. It depends on new gas supply, much of it from fields not yet producing.

The fiscal 2027 budget, which may change fees, taxes or fuel prices, had no confirmed date as of 27 September 2026.

More: Caribbean news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need a visa to move to Trinidad and Tobago?

Not to arrive. Citizens of the US, UK and most CARICOM states can visit visa-free, usually for up to 90 days. Living or working there needs a separate permit, and every traveller must file a free online arrival card at travel.gov.tt before travel.

How much does a Trinidad and Tobago work permit cost?

The employer pays a TT$1,200 processing fee (about US$177) and then TT$900 a month (about US$133) for the approved period. The minimum duration fee is TT$2,700 (about US$399). The ministry asks for applications at least six weeks before the start date.

Can I get permanent residence in Trinidad and Tobago?

Yes, through five years of continuous residence, marriage to a citizen or resident, or family sponsorship. CSME-based permits are another route, and approval is always discretionary. No official processing time is published.

How much is rent in Port of Spain?

Numbeo data from September 2026 put a central one-bedroom flat at about TT$6,883 a month (about US$1,017). Outside the centre the average was about TT$3,524 (about US$521). Gated homes in western suburbs cost more.

Is Trinidad and Tobago still under a state of emergency?

No. The state of emergency ended on 17 September 2026 after 199 days. A Special Operations Bill allowing local ‘closed areas’ passed the Senate on 24 September 2026.

World.title: Taxes in Venezuela for Expats: What Foreigners Pay During the Transformation
World.content:
GUIDES · VENEZUELA

Key Facts — The country Venezuela, an oil state of about 28.5 million people, has been run since January 2026 by acting president Delcy Rodríguez under close US oversight.

— Who collects SENIAT, the national tax and customs service, collects income tax, value-added tax and the tax on foreign-currency payments. Town halls collect property and business taxes.

— The key test More than 183 days in Venezuela in a year makes you a tax resident, taxed on worldwide income.

— The rates Income tax runs from 6% to 34%. Value-added tax (IVA) is 16%, and many payments in dollars carry an extra 3% levy.

— What changed in 2026 An oil-sector tax overhaul, published on 29 January 2026. As of September 2026, no reform of personal income tax, IVA or the dollar levy had been published.

— The catch Tax brackets are set in a unit worth Bs 43 (about US$0.05), so most foreign earners land in the top 34% band.

Taxes in Venezuela look modest on paper. A frozen tax unit and a falling bolívar mean most foreigners who stay long enough pay close to the top rate.

Free daily brief — no card needed Get every Analysis story in one morning email We build you a personalized brief around the topics you follow — free for 7 days. Love it? Your first month after that is US$1. Start my free brief Yes, email me my free daily brief — I can unsubscribe any time.

Taxes in Venezuela matter again because foreigners are coming back. Flights to Caracas resumed in September 2026, and oil companies are returning under US licences. This guide explains what a foreign resident, remote worker or investor actually owes, as of September 2026.

Who collects taxes in Venezuela

The main tax authority is SENIAT, the Servicio Nacional Integrado de Administración Aduanera y Tributaria. It runs income tax, IVA, customs and the levy on large financial transactions. You deal with it through its online portal and a tax number called the RIF.

The RIF (Registro de Información Fiscal) works like a taxpayer ID. You need one to file a return and for most formal dealings with SENIAT, and foreign residents can register too.

Municipalities levy their own taxes. These include an urban property tax and a tax on business turnover, with rates set by each town hall. There is no local income tax on individuals.

All tax amounts are calculated in bolívars (Bs). This guide uses the Central Bank of Venezuela (BCV) official rate of Bs 857.01 per US dollar. The BCV published it on 25 September 2026 for use from 28 September. Market data put the rate at about Bs 855.93 per dollar on 25 September.

The Central Bank of Venezuela, whose official rate converts bolívar tax amounts into dollars (Photo: JoseGre12, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

One-stop reference Company Intelligence Every listed company in Latin America — financials, ownership and structure for 1,450+ companies across 26 exchanges, in one place. Browse the directory →

Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

That rate matters for every figure below. It stood at Bs 301.37 per dollar at the start of 2026. A bolívar amount now buys roughly a third of what it did in January.

Are you a tax resident? The 183-day test

You are a Venezuelan tax resident if you spend more than 183 days in the country in a calendar year. You are also resident if you spent more than 183 days there in the preceding year. A 184th day is enough.

Residents pay income tax on their worldwide income, not only on money earned in Venezuela. That includes salary from a foreign employer paid into a foreign account while you live in Caracas.

Setting up a home in Venezuela can also make you resident under the tax code. The exception is proof, from another country’s tax authority, that you are resident there after more than 183 days abroad. Venezuelan citizens are presumed resident unless they prove otherwise.

Non-residents pay only on income whose source is in Venezuela. A short-term consultant, a rotating oil worker or a landlord living abroad usually falls into this group. The day count does not mean a visa or residence permit; those are separate immigration questions.

Income tax (ISLR): rates for residents and non-residents

The income tax is called ISLR, short for Impuesto sobre la Renta. Its current law dates from December 2015, published in Official Gazette No. 6,210 Extraordinary. Residents pay under a progressive scale known as Tariff No. 1.

Taxable income (tax units) In US$ a year (approx.) Rate Deduct (tax units) Up to 1,000 Up to US$50 6% 0 1,000 to 1,500 US$50 to US$75 9% 30 1,500 to 2,000 US$75 to US$100 12% 75 2,000 to 2,500 US$100 to US$125 16% 155 2,500 to 3,000 US$125 to US$151 20% 255 3,000 to 4,000 US$151 to US$201 24% 375 4,000 to 6,000 US$201 to US$301 29% 575 Over 6,000 Over US$301 34% 875

Tariff No. 1 of the 2015 income tax law. US$ values use one tax unit of Bs 43 at the BCV rate of Bs 857.01 per dollar, 28 September 2026.

Read the second column carefully. Because the tax unit is so small, the top 34% band starts at about US$301 of taxable income a year. For comparison, the United States’ top federal rate of 37% starts above US$640,600 for a single filer in 2026.

A worked example shows the effect. A resident with US$30,000 of taxable income would owe about US$10,156 before rebates, an effective rate of almost 34%. That is arithmetic from the published scale, not an official estimate.

Residents may take a single standard deduction of 774 tax units, about Bs 33,282 (about US$39), without receipts. Alternatively they can itemise local medical bills, school fees, insurance premiums and home-loan interest paid in Venezuela.

Non-residents do not use the scale. Salaries for work done in Venezuela are taxed at a flat 34%, withheld at source. Professional fees are taxed at 34% on 90% of the gross payment.

Residents must file if net income exceeds 1,000 tax units, about Bs 43,000 (about US$50), or gross income exceeds 1,500 units. The return is due by 31 March for the previous calendar year, filed online through the SENIAT portal. Late filing brings fines and interest.

The tax unit and the “highest-value currency” rule

Venezuela measures many tax thresholds in the unidad tributaria (UT), or tax unit. SENIAT raised it from Bs 9 (about US$0.01) to Bs 43 (about US$0.05) in June 2025. The change was published in Official Gazette No. 43,140 of 2 June 2025.

No further increase had been published as of September 2026. Meanwhile, the official dollar rate nearly tripled over 2026. The unit has therefore lost most of its value, which is why the tax brackets now look so low in dollars.

A one-bolívar note from 1989. Three redenominations since 2008 have removed 14 zeros from the currency (Photo: Jeremith.DP, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Fines work differently. The 2020 tax code, published in Official Gazette No. 6,507 Extraordinary of 29 January 2020, stopped using the tax unit for penalties. Fines are now set as multiples of the BCV’s official rate for the “currency of highest value”.

In practice that currency is the euro, which the BCV quoted at Bs 976.90 (about US$1.14) per euro for 28 September 2026. A fine set at 100 times that rate would therefore cost Bs 97,690 (about US$114). The rate that counts is the one on the day you pay.

This does not mean taxes are charged in euros. It means penalties keep their value while the bolívar falls, so paying a fine late costs more in bolívars, not less.

IVA at 16% and the 3% levy on dollar payments

Value-added tax, or IVA (Impuesto al Valor Agregado), is 16% on most goods and services. Some items, such as certain meats and domestic flights, carry 8%. Luxury goods, such as vehicles worth US$40,000 or more, carry a separate 15% luxury rate.

The law also allows an extra IVA rate of 5% to 25% on goods and services paid in foreign currency or crypto. As of PwC’s January 2026 summary, that rate had never been set, so it does not apply.

The levy most foreigners notice is the IGTF, the Impuesto a las Grandes Transacciones Financieras. Since a 2022 amendment, it charges 3% on payments in dollars, other foreign currencies or crypto through Venezuela’s banks.

It also charges 3% when you pay a large company designated as a “special taxpayer” in cash dollars. A US$100 supermarket bill, IVA included, paid in notes then costs US$103. The shop collects the levy and passes it to SENIAT.

Paying in bolívars by card or mobile transfer avoids the 3%. The separate 2% levy that special taxpayers paid on bolívar debits was cut to 0% from July 2024. Small shops that are not special taxpayers do not collect the IGTF on cash dollars.

Las Mercedes, a Caracas business and restaurant district (Photo: Vicente Quintero, CC BY 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Other taxes: wealth, inheritance, property and payroll

A tax on large fortunes applies only to people SENIAT has formally designated as special taxpayers. The threshold is net worth of 150 million tax units, about Bs 6.45 billion (about US$7.5 million). The rate is 0.25%, assessed on 30 September and filed in October and November.

Inheritance and gift tax applies to Venezuelan property, shares and rights, whatever the heir’s nationality or residence. Rates rise with distance of kinship and reach 55% at the top. Urban property tax is charged by each municipality.

Employers pay most payroll costs. Since May 2024 companies owe a 9% pension-protection contribution on total pay, including bonuses. Since May 2026 it has been calculated on at least US$240 per worker per month, the government’s dollar-indexed minimum income.

Employees pay 4% into social security, capped at five minimum wages. The monthly minimum wage has stayed at Bs 130 (about US$0.15) since March 2022, so the cap is tiny. Much of the pay in Venezuela now comes as dollar-indexed bonuses rather than formal wages.

Double-tax treaties: which countries are covered

A double-tax treaty decides which country may tax which income, so you are not taxed twice on the same money. Venezuela has treaties in force with about 30 countries, according to PwC’s January 2026 summary.

They include the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Spain, Portugal, Italy, France, Germany, the Netherlands, Switzerland, Brazil and China. The US treaty was signed in 1999 and remains listed by the Internal Revenue Service.

A treaty with Mexico has been signed but is not in force. Neighbouring Colombia is not on the list. Without a treaty, residents can still credit foreign income tax, but only up to the Venezuelan tax on that foreign income.

US citizens remain taxed by the United States wherever they live. For them, the treaty and US foreign tax credits matter more than any Venezuelan rate.

What changed in 2026 under the Transformation, and what did not

The Rio Times calls the political transition since January 2026 “the Transformation”. It has changed oil taxation, but not the personal taxes most foreigners pay.

The main enacted change is a reform of the Organic Hydrocarbons Law, published in Official Gazette No. 6,978 Extraordinary of 29 January 2026. It sets a royalty of up to 30% and an integrated hydrocarbons tax of up to 15% of gross revenue. The government sets the rates for each project and may lower them to keep a project viable.

Nothing comparable has been published for personal income tax, IVA or the IGTF. That is based on our checks of gazette summaries to 27 September 2026. The tax unit also remains at its June 2025 value.

Several ideas remain proposals only. Tax lawyers called for an integral tax reform in May 2026. A dollarisation plan drafted with US economist Steve Hanke was blocked by the National Assembly’s leadership in August 2026. None of these is law.

The executive can still move quickly. An economic emergency decree, in force since April 2025 and last extended for 60 days in August 2026, lets it suspend taxes or exemptions by decree. Check the gazette before any large payment.

What this means for you

Count your days first. Under 184 days a year, you are usually taxed only on Venezuelan-source income. Over that, all your income counts, and a treaty or foreign tax credit becomes essential.

Expect the top rate if you earn a normal foreign salary while resident. The 6% to 34% scale sounds gentle, but a tax unit of Bs 43 (about US$0.05) means almost everything falls in the 34% band.

Pay in bolívars where you can to avoid the 3% IGTF, and keep receipts for local medical and school costs. Get a RIF early, and use a Venezuelan accountant for your first return.

Taxes in Venezuela can change by decree, so treat this guide as a map rather than advice. Confirm every figure against SENIAT and the official gazette on the day you file.

Sources: Tax rules come from Venezuelan official gazette summaries, SENIAT, the Central Bank of Venezuela and PwC’s Worldwide Tax Summaries, with treaty data from the US Internal Revenue Service.

What Is Not Known

Whether SENIAT will raise the tax unit again is not known. It went from Bs 9 to Bs 43 (about US$0.01 to US$0.05) in June 2025. Since January 2026, the bolívar has lost about two-thirds of its dollar value. No date or figure for a new adjustment has been published.

Whether the transition brings a broader tax reform is not established. Tax lawyers and business groups have called for one, and the IMF plans to open a Caracas office in 2027. No draft law for personal income tax, IVA or the IGTF had been published as of 27 September 2026.

How strictly SENIAT enforces worldwide-income rules on foreigners is not documented. Official audit statistics by nationality are not published. PwC notes that audits focus mainly on companies and designated special taxpayers.

How easy it is to claim treaty relief in practice is unclear. Treaties with the United States and European countries remain listed as in force. Cooperation between tax administrations after years of sanctions has not been publicly assessed.

Whether the July 2025 suspension of IVA exemptions on imported food and medicines still applies is not confirmed. PwC reported the suspension from 5 July 2025. We found no official statement on its status in September 2026.

More: Venezuela news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do foreigners pay income tax in Venezuela?

Yes. Anyone who spends more than 183 days in Venezuela in a year becomes a tax resident and pays on worldwide income at 6% to 34%. Non-residents pay only on Venezuelan-source income, usually a flat 34% withheld at source. Because the tax unit is worth Bs 43, about US$0.05, most resident foreign earners fall in the top 34% band.

What is the IGTF and when do I pay it?

The IGTF is a 3% levy on payments in dollars, other foreign currencies or crypto made through Venezuelan banks. It also applies when you pay a large company designated as a special taxpayer in cash dollars. Paying in bolívars by card or mobile transfer avoids it.

How much is IVA in Venezuela?

The general IVA rate is 16%. A reduced 8% rate applies to a short list of items such as certain meats and domestic flights. Luxury goods such as vehicles worth US$40,000 or more carry a separate 15% luxury rate.

When is the Venezuelan income tax return due?

Individuals file by 31 March for the previous calendar year, online through the SENIAT portal. Residents must file if net income exceeds 1,000 tax units, about Bs 43,000 or US$50, or gross income exceeds 1,500 tax units. Late filing brings fines and interest.

Does Venezuela have a tax treaty with the United States?

Yes. The US–Venezuela income tax treaty was signed in 1999 and is listed as in force. Venezuela also has treaties with Canada, the United Kingdom, Spain, Portugal, Germany and about two dozen other countries. There is no treaty in force with Mexico or Colombia.

Did taxes change after Maduro’s capture in 2026?

Only for oil. A hydrocarbons law reform published on 29 January 2026 set royalties of up to 30% and an oil tax of up to 15% of gross revenue. As of September 2026, no reform of personal income tax, IVA or the IGTF had been published, and a dollarisation plan was blocked by the National Assembly’s leadership in August.

World.title: Is Barbados Safe for Expats in 2026? Crime by Area, Scams and Daily Reality
World.content:
GUIDES · BARBADOS

Key Facts — The country Barbados is a stable Caribbean republic of 269,090 people at the 2021 census, living largely from tourism.

— The official view The US State Department rates Barbados Level 1, its lowest warning, in an advisory dated 10 April 2026.

— The problem Gun crime has risen. Barbados recorded 49 murders in 2024, its highest total on record.

— Who is at risk Most violence involves rival groups in parts of St Michael, not visitors. Petty theft is the main risk for foreigners.

— The other risks Roads, strong sea currents and the June-to-November hurricane season deserve as much attention as crime.

Barbados is safe for most expats who take ordinary city precautions. The honest answer also includes a sharp rise in gun crime, fast minibuses and a real hurricane risk.

Free daily brief — no card needed Get every Analysis story in one morning email We build you a personalized brief around the topics you follow — free for 7 days. Love it? Your first month after that is US$1. Start my free brief Yes, email me my free daily brief — I can unsubscribe any time.

Is Barbados safe? For a foreigner living on the west or south coast, the answer is mostly yes. Serious violence is concentrated, and the risks you meet daily are theft, traffic and the sea.

This guide covers police figures, foreign advisories and where crime clusters. It also explains how to handle scams, roads and storms. Figures are as of September 2026 unless dated otherwise.

What the crime figures show

The Barbados Police Service publishes annual crime totals. It was called the Royal Barbados Police Force until the island became a republic in 2021. They show falling overall crime but a sharp rise in gun violence.

Barbados recorded 49 murders in 2024, plus one manslaughter case, for 50 homicides. That was the highest number ever documented in a single year, and roughly one killing a week.

OSAC, the US government’s security advisory council for American organisations abroad, put the 2024 rate at 17.7 killings per 100,000 people. It still describes Barbados as having lower violent crime than many regional neighbours.

In 2025 the picture split. Richard Boyce, then Commissioner of Police, reported in February 2026 that total offences fell 4%, from 6,301 to 6,063, and murders fell 2%. Sonia Boyce succeeded him in July 2026 as the first woman to lead the service.

Residential burglaries fell 7% and thefts from cars fell 26%. Police seized 84 firearms in 2025, up from 71 the year before.

Gun crime moved the other way. The government’s Criminal Justice Research and Planning Unit counted 638 firearm-related crimes in 2025, up 60% from 400. Armed robberies rose from 62 to 157.

As of 2 September 2026, the homicide toll for the year stood at 36, according to Barbados Today, the latest published tally. That is a little above the average pace of the 2024 record year.

St Lawrence Gap in Christ Church, the south coast’s restaurant and nightlife strip (Photo: Mtaylor848, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

What foreign governments advise

The US State Department keeps Barbados at Level 1, “exercise normal precautions”, in its advisory of 10 April 2026. It calls the island generally safe but says petty crime is common in tourist areas.

It also notes that violent crime, including murder, sexual assault, robbery and shootings, occasionally occurs. It advises vigilance on party cruises, in downtown areas at night and at ATMs.

The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) is blunter. Its advice, last updated on 23 January 2026, reports an increase in gang-related gun murders, some in public areas.

The FCDO also lists armed robbery, sexual assault and carjackings. Neither government advises against travel, and neither says foreigners are targeted as a group.

OSAC’s May 2025 report adds one practical warning for residents. Police response times vary, and it is “not uncommon to wait an hour or more”, especially in rural areas.

Crime by area

Barbados is divided into eleven parishes, local districts that serve as its basic map. Crime is not spread evenly across them.

Area What the record shows Bridgetown and wider St Michael About 61% of firearm murders in 2025 happened in this parish. Police name it, with Christ Church and St Philip, among the parishes with higher crime levels. West coast: St James and St Peter Villas, hotels and many expat homes. Police do not list these parishes among the higher-crime areas; theft and break-ins are the usual concerns. South coast: Christ Church Hastings, Worthing, St Lawrence Gap and Oistins. Police list Christ Church among the higher-crime parishes, and nightlife brings pickpocketing and late-night robbery risk. East coast and rural parishes Official warnings focus on dangerous sea currents and slower police response, not crime clusters.

OSAC says most violent crime involves rival gang members and stays outside tourist zones. That does not mean tourist areas are crime-free. It means most shootings involve local rivals, not visitors.

By day, the main risk in Bridgetown is pickpocketing in crowds. After dark, the US advice to avoid downtown areas applies, especially if you are alone or on foot.

The government is responding with law as well as policing. A Domestic Terrorism Bill, debated in both houses of Parliament in August 2026, creates a separate offence for violent crimes in public places that show reckless disregard for public safety. Our report on the bill has the detail.

Privately run yellow minibuses in Bridgetown; together with ZR vans they carry much of the island’s public transport (Photo: Postdlf, CC BY-SA 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Scams and petty crime

Most crimes against foreigners are crimes of opportunity, such as purse snatching and pickpocketing, the State Department says. Beaches, cars and crowded events are the usual settings.

OSAC lists ATM fraud and card fraud as common. Use machines inside banks or shopping centres, cover your PIN and check statements often.

Taxis have no meters, the FCDO notes. Agree the fare and the currency before you get in.

Offers of drugs on beaches or at parties are a trap. Drug possession is illegal, and both the UK and US governments warn of severe penalties and long jail terms.

For rentals, see the property before paying a deposit, or use an agent you can verify. Pay by traceable bank transfer, never in cash to a stranger.

Crowds at Crop Over, the summer carnival, and its Kadooment Day parade need extra care. The State Department singles out these large gatherings.

Road safety

For most expats, the road deserves as much attention as crime. Barbados drives on the left, and main roads are generally sound but potholed.

Rural roads are narrow, poorly marked and full of blind curves, the State Department warns. Many have no pavement, so pedestrians walk in the road.

ZR vans, private minibuses with number plates starting with Z, “tend to travel at excessive speeds”, in the State Department’s words. Give them room when driving, and expect sudden stops.

Avoid unfamiliar rural roads at night, when lighting is poor. Wear a seat belt, never drink and drive, and slow down in rain.

Bathsheba on the east coast, where strong currents make swimming unsafe on many beaches (Photo: Postdlf, CC BY-SA 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

The sea, hurricanes and storms

Currents can be deceptively strong on popular beaches, the FCDO warns. Swimming is not recommended on many east-coast beaches, where the Atlantic surf is rough.

The hurricane season runs from June to November, with peak activity from August to October. A storm does not need to make landfall to do serious damage.

Hurricane Beryl passed about 150 kilometres off the south coast on 1 July 2024. The World Bank counted 240 fishing vessels damaged or destroyed, and damage to the port, cruise terminal and fisheries marina.

The World Bank also reported damage at 73% of hotels, apartments and guest houses. It approved US$54 million in emergency financing for the recovery.

Follow the Department of Emergency Management and the Barbados Meteorological Services during any storm. Check that your home insurance covers wind and flood, and keep water, medicines and documents ready.

Daily reality for expats

Official advice treats Barbados as a place for normal precautions, not special measures. For most foreign residents, that means the care they would take in a mid-sized city.

OSAC lists burglary and car break-ins among the most common crimes. Choose housing with good locks, lighting and, ideally, a gated compound or alarm.

The High Court struck down the laws against consensual same-sex relations between adults in December 2022, although the State Department’s country page still describes them as criminalised. The FCDO describes attitudes as mostly conservative.

Do not bring firearms or ammunition without clear government permission. Save two numbers now: police on 211 and ambulance on 511.

What this means for you

Barbados is safe enough for most expats to live a normal, relaxed life. The rise in gun crime is real, but it is concentrated and rarely touches foreigners directly.

Choose where you live with care, secure your home and avoid downtown Bridgetown alone at night. Drive defensively, respect the east-coast sea and prepare for hurricane season.

Treat the numbers here as a snapshot. Check the latest police figures and foreign advisories before you move, because gun crime trends have shifted fast since 2024.

The expat safety net that actually exists

Barbados’ real security infrastructure for foreigners is social as much as official. The island has dense, long-established expat networks — from the Welcome Stamp remote-worker community to British and Canadian retiree circles on the west coast — and they function as an early-warning system: break-in patterns, scam attempts and road problems travel through WhatsApp groups hours before any official channel moves. Joining two or three of these groups in your first week is worth more than any alarm system. Neighborhood watch schemes cover most expat districts, the police force runs a dedicated tourism unit, and response in the resort corridors is visibly faster than elsewhere on the island. None of this makes Barbados risk-free; it makes it a place where risk is known, shared and managed collectively — which, in practice, is what “safe” means anywhere in the Caribbean.

Sources: Crime figures come from the Barbados Police Service and the Criminal Justice Research and Planning Unit as reported by Barbados Today, with advisories from the US State Department, OSAC and the UK FCDO, and storm data from the World Bank.

What Is Not Known

The exact murder total for 2025 is not settled in public sources. Police reported a 2% fall, but press reports give different final counts.

No official crime table by parish or neighbourhood is published regularly. The area picture here rests on the 2025 firearm review and on official advisories, not on a full map of crime rates.

Police reported 17 road deaths in 2025, but no official figure for 2024 or 2026 so far was found, so no trend can be given here.

When the Domestic Terrorism Bill comes into force is not confirmed. Its effect on gun crime cannot be judged until it is in use.

More: Caribbean news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Barbados safe for expats in 2026?

Yes, for most expats who take ordinary precautions. The US State Department rates Barbados Level 1, its lowest warning, in an advisory dated 10 April 2026. Gun violence has risen, but it is concentrated in parts of St Michael and mostly involves rival groups, not foreigners.

Which areas of Barbados have the most crime?

Bridgetown and the wider parish of St Michael carry most serious violence, with about 61% of firearm murders in 2025. Police also list Christ Church and St Philip among the higher-crime parishes. The west coast in St James and St Peter, where many expats live, faces mainly theft and break-ins.

How many murders does Barbados have a year?

Barbados recorded 49 murders in 2024, its highest total on record, or roughly one a week. Police reported a 2% fall in 2025. As of 2 September 2026, the homicide toll for the year stood at 36.

What scams should foreigners watch for in Barbados?

OSAC lists ATM fraud and card fraud as common, so use machines inside banks and cover your PIN. Taxis have no meters, so agree the fare first. Refuse any offer of drugs, because penalties are severe.

When is hurricane season in Barbados?

The season runs from June to November, with peak activity from August to October. Hurricane Beryl passed about 150 kilometres off the south coast on 1 July 2024 and damaged or destroyed 240 fishing vessels, according to the World Bank.

World.title: Moving to Guyana: Visas, Costs, Oil-Boom Jobs and Daily Life in Georgetown
World.content:
GUIDES · GUYANA

Key Facts — The country Guyana is South America’s only English-speaking country, with about 836,000 people. Offshore oil has made it one of the world’s fastest-growing economies.

— Getting in Americans, Britons and Canadians need no visa to visit. The officer at the border sets the stay, which Washington puts at up to 90 days and London at 30. Any work needs a separate permit that the employer requests.

— The jobs The oil sector hires foreigners mainly for specialist roles. A 2021 law requires companies to give qualified Guyanese first consideration.

— What it costs Furnished flats aimed at foreigners in Greater Georgetown were listed from about US$1,500 a month in September 2026. Family houses ran US$4,000 and up.

— Why it matters now The economy grew 33.3% in the first half of 2026, and demand for skilled staff still outruns supply.

— The catch Housing is scarce and dear, crime is high by Western standards, and serious medical cases often need evacuation.

Moving to Guyana means joining an oil boom in a small English-speaking country. The jobs are real, but so are the permits, the rents and the risks.

Free daily brief — no card needed Get every Analysis story in one morning email We build you a personalized brief around the topics you follow — free for 7 days. Love it? Your first month after that is US$1. Start my free brief Yes, email me my free daily brief — I can unsubscribe any time.

Moving to Guyana has become a serious option for engineers, managers and service providers since oil began flowing offshore in December 2019. Most newcomers arrive with a job offer, because the work permit follows the employer, not the person.

This guide covers entry rules, work permits and the oil sector’s local content law. It also sets out housing and daily costs in Georgetown. It also explains safety, healthcare and everyday life, with links to our detailed guides on each.

Why people are moving to Guyana

Guyana lies on the north-east coast of South America, between Venezuela, Brazil and Suriname. It was a British colony until 1966, drives on the left and hosts the headquarters of CARICOM, the Caribbean Community.

ExxonMobil and its partners Chevron and CNOOC pumped about 900,000 barrels a day offshore in the first half of 2026. That is roughly one barrel for every resident, as our Guyana explainer sets out.

The finance ministry’s 2026 mid-year report put economic growth at 33.3% in the first half of the year, and 10.1% outside oil. Unemployment stood at 6.2%, and employers describe a shortage of skilled workers rather than of jobs.

That does not mean anyone can arrive and find work. The boom favours people with scarce skills and an employer willing to sponsor them.

St George’s Cathedral in Georgetown, one of the timber buildings of Guyana’s English-speaking capital (Photo: Spiralwidget, CC0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

Visas and how long you can stay

Citizens of the United States, the United Kingdom and Canada do not need a visa to visit. Other nationalities should check the list of visa-exempt countries kept by Guyana’s foreign ministry before booking.

The length of stay is set by the immigration officer at the airport. The US State Department says no visa is needed for stays of 90 days or less. The UK Foreign Office says visitors are normally given 30 days and can apply for one-month extensions.

Your passport should be valid for at least six months after arrival. The US government also warns that sums above US$10,000 must be declared on entry and exit.

What this does not mean: visa-free entry never allows paid work. Guyana had no dedicated visa for remote workers or retirees on the Ministry of Home Affairs’ public pages as of September 2026.

Work permits: the employer applies

Work permits are handled by Immigration Support Services, part of the Ministry of Home Affairs in Georgetown. Since October 2025 a new, fully digital system at eservices.iss.gov.gy handles visa and extension applications. The ministry’s Brickdam office still accepts them in person.

The employer usually files the request and supplies its registration, tax records and the job description. The worker supplies a passport and proof of qualifications. A work permit approval letter then lets the worker enter or stay to take up the job.

Immigration law firm Fragomen reported in 2023 that permits are endorsed only if the sponsor is up to date with its taxes. After arrival you will also need a tax number and national insurance registration.

CARICOM nationals with a skills certificate have their own, simpler route under regional free-movement rules. It does not apply to people from outside the Caribbean bloc.

Oil-boom jobs and the Local Content Act

The Local Content Act 2021, Act No. 18 of 2021, shapes who gets hired. It requires oil companies and their contractors to give first consideration to Guyanese nationals with the relevant qualifications and experience.

Its First Schedule reserves minimum shares of 40 service areas for Guyanese companies, from 5% to 100%. A “Guyanese company” must be at least 51% Guyanese-owned, with Guyanese holding 75% of senior management and 90% of other posts.

Service area (examples) Minimum local share Immigration support, work permit and visa applications, customs brokerage, local insurance, staff ground transport 100% Security services 95% Accommodation, office rental, catering, local legal and accounting services 90% Manpower and crewing 50% Medical services 25% ICT support; engineering and machining 20%; 5%

The penalties are real. Carrying out petroleum operations without the minimum local content carries a fine of GY$50 million (about US$239,000). A company that files a false local content report faces GY$10 million (about US$48,000).

The local workforce is growing fast. At a government ceremony in June 2026, ExxonMobil Guyana’s head, Alistair Routledge, said about 68% of the workforce supporting the sector was Guyanese by the end of 2025, including 1,800 people offshore. In June 2026 Natural Resources Minister Vickram Bharrat said qualified Guyanese should earn pay comparable to foreigners in the same jobs.

For a foreigner, the realistic openings are specialist, senior or hard-to-fill roles: subsea, drilling, process engineering, safety and project management. Services such as catering, security and staff transport must largely be bought from Guyanese firms, so jobs in them rarely go to foreigners.

The floating Demerara Harbour Bridge near Georgetown; river crossings and East Bank traffic shape daily commutes (Photo: FrWaters, CC BY 2.5 via Wikimedia Commons)

Where to live and what rent costs

Foreigners typically settle in Georgetown districts such as Bel Air, Prashad Nagar, Queenstown and Kingston. Many others live in gated developments in Providence and Eccles, on the East Bank of the Demerara River.

There is no official rent survey. The figures below are monthly asking rents from two agencies serving foreign tenants, viewed on 27 September 2026.

Listing Asking rent per month 1-bedroom apartment, Providence, all bills included US$1,500 2-bedroom furnished flat, Eccles US$1,500 3-bedroom apartment, Farm, East Bank US$1,600 2-bedroom apartment, gated community, Providence US$2,000 2-bedroom apartment, Subryanville, Georgetown US$2,800 4-bedroom house, Lamaha Gardens, Georgetown US$4,000 6-bedroom house, D’Aguiar Park, Georgetown US$12,000

These are furnished homes marketed to companies and foreign staff, so they sit at the top of the market. If an employer is sponsoring you, ask whether housing can be part of the package.

Before signing, ask about water pressure, drainage in heavy rain, security and who pays the power bill. Much of the coast lies below high-tide level behind sea defences, and flooding is a year-round risk.

A minibus squeezes past stalls at Stabroek Market; minibuses are Georgetown’s everyday transport (Photo: John Cray, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Money, prices and tax

The currency is the Guyana dollar, written GY$ or G$. The Bank of Guyana quoted it at GY$207.98 to buy and GY$210.45 to sell one US dollar on 25 September 2026. This guide converts at about GY$209.

Consumer prices rose 4.4% in the first half of 2026, and food prices 6.7%, according to the mid-year report. The government kept electricity tariffs stable and its excise tax on fuel at zero.

The power grid still relies heavily on imported fuel oil. A gas-to-energy plant at Wales is due to fire its first turbine around December 2026.

Income tax has two bands, 25% and 35%, above a tax-free allowance of GY$140,000 (about US$670) a month. Staying over 183 days a year can make you taxable on worldwide income, as our guide to taxes in Guyana explains.

Opening a local account usually needs a tax number, whose first certificate costs GY$1,000 (about US$4.80). Our bank account guide covers minimums and US dollar accounts.

Safety and healthcare

The US State Department rates Guyana at Level 3, “reconsider travel”, because of crime. Police recorded 130 murders in 2025, about 15.6 per 100,000 people, and 137 road deaths.

Standard advice is to avoid showing cash, limit walking at night and use trusted drivers. Our guide Is Guyana safe for expats? names the districts that official advisories single out.

Public healthcare is free, but capacity is thin. Private hospitals often want cash up front, and the UK government advises arranging evacuation for anything serious. Read our guide to healthcare in Guyana before choosing insurance.

Daily life in Georgetown

English is the official language, and most people also speak Creolese, an English-based creole. The capital mixes timber colonial buildings, canals and busy markets, and minibuses are the everyday transport.

Georgetown is small. New hotels and restaurants have opened with the boom, but choice, shopping and nightlife remain limited compared with larger Caribbean capitals. Weekends often mean the interior, from Kaieteur Falls to the Rupununi savannahs.

One political fact hangs over everything: Venezuela claims the Essequibo region, about two-thirds of Guyana’s territory. The International Court of Justice heard the case in May 2026 and has yet to rule. Daily life in Georgetown is not directly affected, but the dispute is worth following.

What this means for you

Secure the job first and let the employer start the work permit. Negotiate housing, transport and medical evacuation cover into the contract, because these are the costs that surprise newcomers.

If your skills are ones Guyanese companies can already supply, expect the local content law to work against you. Moving to Guyana makes most sense for specialists, managers and people setting up a genuinely local business.

Money and banking in a boom economy

Guyana runs on the Guyanese dollar, but the boom economy prices serious things — rent, cars, contractor quotes — in US dollars. Banking has modernized fast: the big local banks and Republic Bank offer app banking and USD accounts, and opening one as a work-permit holder is routine, though compliance paperwork mirrors the regional norm (passport, permit, proof of address, employer letter). Two quirks shape daily money life: foreign currency is periodically scarce at the official windows, so expats keep liquidity spread rather than concentrated; and card acceptance outside Georgetown’s hotels and supermarkets is patchy — cash remains load-bearing in the markets and the interior. Salary packages in the oil sector typically solve this with offshore splits; negotiate yours before arrival, not after.

Sources: Entry rules come from the US and UK governments and Guyana’s Ministry of Home Affairs, labour rules from the Local Content Act and official reports, and rents from agency listings viewed on 27 September 2026.

What Is Not Known

The standard length of a visitor’s stay is not clear. Washington cites 90 days and London 30 days, and the officer decides at the border. Guyana publishes no single table for every nationality.

The Ministry of Home Affairs pages we checked publish no current schedule of work permit fees or processing times. Figures quoted by relocation websites could not be confirmed.

What ordinary Guyanese households pay in rent is not measured. The listings in this guide show the furnished, foreign-oriented end of the market only.

Changes to the local content schedule have been discussed by officials in 2026. No amendment to the First Schedule had been published in law by late September 2026.

When the International Court of Justice will rule on Venezuela’s claim to the Essequibo is not known. No date had been set as of late September 2026.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need a visa to move to Guyana?

Americans, Britons and Canadians do not need a visa to visit. To live and work there you need a work permit, which your employer requests from the Ministry of Home Affairs. Visa-free entry never allows paid work.

How long can I stay in Guyana as a visitor?

The immigration officer sets the period on arrival. The US government says no visa is needed for stays of 90 days or less, while the UK says visitors normally get 30 days with one-month extensions available.

Can foreigners get oil jobs in Guyana?

Yes, mainly in specialist or senior roles. The Local Content Act 2021 requires companies to give qualified Guyanese first consideration, and reserves many support services for Guyanese firms. ExxonMobil Guyana says about 68% of the workforce supporting the sector was Guyanese by the end of 2025.

How much is rent in Georgetown?

Furnished flats aimed at foreigners were listed from about US$1,500 a month in September 2026, with two-bedroom apartments in good areas at US$2,000 to US$2,800. Family houses started around US$4,000. There is no official rent survey.

Is Guyana safe for foreigners?

The US rates Guyana Level 3, reconsider travel, because of crime. Police recorded 130 murders in 2025, about 15.6 per 100,000 people. Standard advice is to limit walking at night, avoid showing cash and use trusted drivers.

What currency does Guyana use?

The Guyana dollar. The Bank of Guyana quoted about GY$208 to buy and GY$210 to sell one US dollar on 25 September 2026. Rents for foreigners are usually quoted in US dollars.

World.title: Used-Car Importers Take Costa Rica’s New Vehicle Tax Formula to Court
World.content:
Costa Rica’s association of used-vehicle importers plans to challenge in court a Ministry of Finance decree that changed how import taxes on cars are calculated. The importers say the rule, in place since Sept. 1, has doubled or tripled the taxes they pay. Under the decree, customs compares the value declared on the commercial invoice, including freight and insurance, with the Ministry of Finance’s reference value for an identical vehicle.

Import taxes are then calculated on whichever figure is higher, which the importers say is usually the ministry’s value. Stanley Quepuy, president of the association, known by its Spanish acronym Aepsau, described taxing vehicles on the ministry’s reference values as an invention. The group argues that taxes should instead be based on the depreciated value of the vehicle being imported.

Quepuy acknowledged that some importers may have taken advantage of the previous system to pay less, but said the entire sector is now bearing the consequences. The association attributes those cases mainly to weak checks by customs. Quepuy said importers agree the market needs regulation to prevent distortions, provided it rests on fair taxes.

The association also argues that the rule undermines free competition, hurts families who need a vehicle and creates legal uncertainty. The Ministry of Finance had not publicly responded to the association’s announcement. The ministry has defended the change as a correction to a distortion in tax collection. It estimates that undervalued vehicle imports led to about ₡20,000 million (roughly $44 million) in evaded taxes.

Carlos Aguilar, executive director of the Association of Vehicle and Machinery Importers (Aivema), said the loophole opened in 2024, when the previous valuation decree for new and used vehicles was eliminated. The government then took two years to replace it.

During that period, Aguilar said, informal importers paid taxes based on invoice values, which led to undervaluation and underbilling with unrealistic figures. In one case reported in 2025, a BMW valued at $195,000 was declared at $7,400, and its owner paid $3,540 in taxes instead of the roughly $62,400 that would have applied at its U.S. market price.

The decree, which covers both new and used vehicles, includes other changes. If a vehicle does not appear on the official list of reference values, the importer must provide technical information so its value can be set objectively. The Directorate General of Taxation manages and updates that list.

The decree also limits individuals who are not registered as vehicle sellers to importing one vehicle per year. The association has not said when it will file its challenge or before which court. Until a court rules otherwise, customs will continue to calculate import taxes under the new formula.

World.title: Tropical Wave 47 Brings Afternoon Storms to Costa Rica This Weekend
World.content:
If you have plans outdoors today, get them done before lunch. Tropical Wave 47 is crossing Costa Rica today, and afternoon downpours with thunderstorms are expected across the Central Valley, the Pacific and the Northern Zone, according to the National Meteorological Institute (IMN).

The morning is your window so expect mostly fair to partly cloudy skies early, with only isolated showers along the Pacific and Caribbean coasts. Clouds build toward late morning, and the storms start between late morning and early afternoon. The heaviest rain is forecast along the central mountain range and across the north. That puts the mountain roads around the Central Valley and the routes into San Carlos and the Arenal area squarely in the path.

The north already got a preview yesterday as heavy afternoon rain sent water into homes, businesses and the technical high school in Aguas Zarcas, according to local reports, and covered part of the road in La Marina de La Palmera. The National Emergency Commission (CNE) said yesterday afternoon it had no official reports of damage.

The storms won’t stop at sunset. Early tonight, downpours with possible thunderstorms are forecast for the Central and South Pacific and the Northern Zone, with scattered rain in the Central Valley and the North Pacific. Patches of fog are possible in the Central Valley overnight.

Temperatures stay warm ahead of the rain. San José ranges from 18.8°C (66°F) to 28.3°C (83°F). Liberia is the hot spot at up to 36.1°C (97°F), while Quepos tops out near 31.2°C (88°F) and Ciudad Quesada near 28°C (82°F).

The unsettled weather could carry into Sunday afternoon. Once the wave moves on, the IMN expects slightly less rain on the Pacific side from early next week. The Caribbean coast and plains should see less frequent rain than the rest of Costa Rica this weekend. If you’re driving, aim to be off mountain roads by early afternoon. Rain on ground that is already wet can swell streams and loosen slopes quickly, and visibility drops fast in a heavy downpour. Don’t try to cross a flooded road or river, because water that looks shallow can still sweep a car away.

If you’re hiking, rafting or at the beach, the same timing applies. Lightning is the main danger with these afternoon storms, so head for shelter as soon as you hear thunder and get out of the water. Rivers can also rise fast after rain upstream, even where the sky above you is still dry.

Tropical waves cross Costa Rica regularly during the rainy season, and this is the 47th of the year. Keep an eye on the IMN’s afternoon updates and call 911 to report an emergency.

World.title: Guatemala denies military flight entered Belize, accuses Belize of ‘spreading misinformation’ at United Nations
World.content:
Guatemala denies military flight entered Belize, accuses Belize of ‘spreading misinformation’ at United Nations

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Guatemala has denied that one of its military aircraft violated Belizean airspace and has accused Belize of presenting a false version of events to the international community, directly challenging Belize’s claim that its radar tracked a Guatemalan surveillance aircraft inside the country for more than an hour.

The extraordinary dispute moved onto the floor of the United Nations General Assembly on Saturday after Prime Minister John Briceño informed world leaders that a Guatemalan military aircraft had entered Belize’s sovereign airspace on the night of September 24 and intentionally disabled its transponder.

Guatemala subsequently exercised its Right of Reply, rejecting Belize’s account of the incident and disputing that the alleged violation occurred.

The response effectively places the two governments in direct contradiction: Belize says it possesses primary and secondary radar records showing exactly when and where Guatemalan Air Force aircraft FAG706 entered Belizean airspace, while Guatemala says the overflight described by Belize did not happen.

Briceño told the General Assembly that the incident constituted a “serious breach of international law,” saying the aircraft violated Belize’s sovereignty and international aviation rules.

Guatemala, however, rejected Belize’s characterization in its Right of Reply, challenging the account Belize presented before the international body.

The latest denial follows a series of increasingly direct responses from Guatemala since the aircraft was first reported over Belize.

Guatemala’s first official response came from its Ministry of National Defence on September 25, hours after reports of the flight began circulating in Belize.

That initial communiqué notably did not deny that the aircraft had flown into Belize.

Instead, Guatemala said:

“All activities and operations of the Guatemalan Army are carried out in strict compliance with the national and international legal framework.”

The Ministry further said its military acts with professionalism, discipline and transparency and reiterated its respect for the law. Guatemala’s own government news agency reported that the statement provided no operational details about the aircraft or the circumstances of the reported flight.

Belize Foreign Affairs CEO Oscar Arnold later dismissed that statement as a “nothing burger,” noting that it neither confirmed nor denied what had taken place.

But Guatemala’s position became considerably more direct when Guatemalan newspaper La Hora specifically asked the Defence Ministry whether the reported overflight had occurred.

The Ministry’s communications office responded:

“No tenemos registro de ese supuesto sobrevuelo.”

Translated: “We have no record of that alleged overflight.”

The newspaper characterized Guatemala’s position as saying the reported military overflight had not occurred.

That position has now been carried into the international arena following Briceño’s address to the United Nations.

Belize, however, says its conclusion is not based simply on civilian websites such as FlightAware or FlightRadar24.

Ministry of National Defence CEO Francis Usher said Belize pulled information from both its primary and secondary radar systems, which he described as internationally recognized systems.

According to Usher, the radar data identified the aircraft specifically as Guatemalan Air Force FAG706.

Usher said the aircraft entered Belizean airspace at approximately 7:29 p.m. on September 24, approaching from the east just beyond Lighthouse Reef at an altitude of approximately 4,000 feet.

It then began circling between Lighthouse Reef and the aviation waypoint KIRAP.

“They circled in between the Lighthouse Reef and the aviation fix called KIRAP, and they began circling as if though they were looking for something,” Usher said.

At approximately 8:07 p.m., according to Usher, the aircraft disappeared from Belize’s secondary radar system — an occurrence Belizean officials say was consistent with its transponder being switched off.

But Usher said Belize continued tracking the aircraft through its primary radar, which detects the physical aircraft independently of a transponder.

“We were able to pick them up on the primary radar, and we continued following them,” Usher said.

According to Belize’s Defence Ministry, FAG706 remained within Belizean airspace until approximately 8:40 p.m., when it exited to the south beyond the Sarstoon River area.

Belize therefore says the aircraft spent approximately one hour and ten minutes inside Belizean sovereign airspace.

Usher said Belize could “categorically” state that an unauthorized entry had taken place.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs subsequently said it would provide Guatemala with the coordinates, radar information and other technical evidence collected by Belize and demand an explanation.

Adding another dimension to the dispute is the identity and history of FAG706.

The aircraft is a Pilatus PC-12/47E, an aircraft donated to Guatemala by the United States for surveillance, security, border-control and light-transport operations.

The particular aircraft has a history dating to the U.S.-supported Afghan Special Mission Wing, where PC-12 aircraft were used for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance — ISR — missions in support of special operations.

The aircraft later returned to U.S. control before being transferred to the Guatemalan Air Force.

Specialist defence reporting has said that FAG706 retained some of its original equipment, although there is no public inventory showing exactly which sensors or surveillance systems remain installed.

Belize’s Foreign Affairs Ministry has itself said it was advised that the aircraft is used for reconnaissance and surveillance purposes rather than as an attack aircraft.

That background has raised questions about why the aircraft was allegedly conducting repeated circles near Lighthouse Reef rather than simply transiting through Belizean airspace.

KIRAP is a recognized aviation waypoint and is not itself a military installation.

It is, however, located only about 10 nautical miles from Half Moon Caye, at the southern end of Lighthouse Reef.

Half Moon Caye hosts Belizean conservation and maritime enforcement activity and has been used by the Belize Coast Guard and other authorities in joint marine patrol and enforcement operations.

That leaves several questions which the Belize Government may now face pressure to answer publicly.

Among them:

Will Belize release the radar images or complete primary-radar track showing FAG706 inside Belizean airspace?

Will Belize release the coordinates provided to Guatemala as part of its diplomatic protest?

What exactly did FAG706 do between 8:07 p.m., when its transponder signal disappeared, and 8:40 p.m., when Belize says it left the country’s airspace?

Did Belize’s radar detect any other aircraft in the area?

Were Belize Coast Guard, BDF, Fisheries or other government personnel operating around Lighthouse Reef or Half Moon Caye at the time?

And has Guatemala provided records showing where FAG706 actually was between 7:29 p.m. and 8:40 p.m. on September 24?

If Guatemala maintains that the flight described by Belize did not occur, the Guatemalan Air Force should possess operational records capable of establishing the location and mission of FAG706 during the period Belize says it was circling inside the country’s airspace.

Conversely, Belize says its own radar provides physical evidence that the aircraft was there.

The issue has therefore moved beyond a disagreement over why a Guatemalan military aircraft was in Belize.

The two neighbouring countries are now publicly disputing whether it was there at all — with Belize presenting the incident as a documented violation of its sovereignty and Guatemala effectively accusing Belize of taking an inaccurate or false account of events before the United Nations.

World.title: Tourism arrivals slump over summer, Mahler admits
World.content:
Tourism arrivals slump over summer, Mahler admits

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Belize’s tourism industry hit a rough patch this summer, but the Minister of Tourism says help is on the way.

Minister Anthony Mahler confirmed that overnight arrivals declined between June and August. June alone was down 5 percent compared to the same period in 2025.

“For the first five months of the year, the numbers were up, but the past three months have been very soft, especially August, I believe,” Mahler said.

Still, he is confident the industry will bounce back.

“We are going to be okay heading into the last quarter of the year with the new flights coming in,” he said.

Six new flights are scheduled for the upcoming peak season. Among them is BermudAir, which is expected to offer nonstop service to Belize from Fort Lauderdale, Tampa, Raleigh Durham and Boston.

United Airlines is also expected to increase service from San Francisco, Chicago and Denver.

The bigger prize may be Europe. Mahler says the Government, including Prime Minister John Briceño, has been working to secure a direct flight from Europe to Belize, and his ministry looks forward to making an announcement.

The minister also sees sports tourism as a way to fill hotel rooms during the slower months.

“Tourism globally is about $12 to $13 trillion in revenues, while sports globally is around $2.5 trillion, but sports tourism is about a trillion dollars,” Mahler said.

He said Belize wants to keep improving its facilities so it can host more sporting events, bringing in visitors and boosting the economy during the low season.

Belize’s high season traditionally begins around mid November, with the busiest stretch running from December through April.

World.title: “We stand as one,” Briceño tells Panton
World.content:
“We stand as one,” Briceño tells Panton

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Prime Minister John Briceño has publicly welcomed the support of Opposition Leader Tracy Panton, declaring that the defence of Belize rises above party politics.

In a post on Saturday evening, the Prime Minister said Belize’s freedom to determine its own future, its independence and its territorial sovereignty are not partisan causes.

“They are matters of nationhood, patriotism and our shared duty to Belize,” Briceño wrote.

He thanked Panton for backing the principles he reaffirmed before the United Nations General Assembly. Those principles, he said, are Belize’s sovereignty, its territorial integrity and the right of the Belizean people to determine their own future.

“On these fundamental matters, there should be no Government and Opposition, only Belizeans,” the Prime Minister said.

Briceño said he embraces the Opposition Leader in that shared national purpose.

“When it comes to the defence of our nation, we stand as one,” he wrote.

The message follows a strong statement from Panton on Saturday morning, just before the Prime Minister’s UN address. In it, she described recent threats by Guatemalan military forces as an affront to Belize’s sovereignty and national identity. She urged the Prime Minister to demand international monitoring, a reaffirmation of Belize’s territorial integrity and concrete assurances for the protection of Belizeans.

Panton also called on the Prime Minister to rally Belize’s allies to publicly support the country.

“Belize belongs to Belizeans. Our independence is NOT negotiable,” she wrote at the time.

The exchange comes amid heightened tensions with Guatemala. Earlier this month, the Guatemalan Navy entered the Sarstoon on September 10. More recently, a Guatemalan aircraft was reported near Lighthouse Reef and Caye Caulker, prompting the UDP to demand a direct explanation from Guatemala.

On the question of sovereignty, both sides of the House now appear to be speaking with one voice.

World.title: Benque Viejo man missing since September 19
World.content:
Benque Viejo man missing since September 19

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Crime Stoppers Belize is asking the public to be on the lookout for Emil Miguel Rivera.

Rivera, 36, is a Belizean of Benque Viejo Town, Cayo District. He was reported missing and was last seen on Saturday, September 19.

He is of Hispanic descent, with a clear complexion and slim build. He stands 5 feet 2 inches tall.

Anyone with information on his whereabouts is asked to call Crime Stoppers at 922, use the P3 app, or report to the nearest police station.

World.title: Shyne celebrates 26 years of classic debut album in New York
World.content:
Shyne celebrates 26 years of classic debut album in New York

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Belizean artist and politician Shyne Barrow has marked 26 years since the release of his classic debut album, Shyne.

The celebration took place at the Brooklyn Public Library in New York City, where supporters and members of the Belizean American community gathered to honour the milestone.

Barrow shared photos from the event on September 26, exactly 26 years after the album dropped in 2000.

“Such a great way to celebrate the 26th Anniversary of the classic Shyne Album,” he wrote, thanking New York City and highlighting the many Belizean Americans who attended during Independence celebrations.

The album launched Shyne as an international recording artist. It went platinum and showcased his signature baritone and gritty lyrics.
