World.title: Construction projects in Hungary could be halted for six months over environmental violations
World.content:
Hungary has tightened its construction rules, allowing authorities to suspend permitting procedures and block new construction or facility permits for at least six months if a project breaches environmental or nature protection requirements.

Hungary’s parliament has approved amendments to the country’s construction rules that significantly strengthen the consequences of environmental violations at major development projects.

Under the new framework, if authorities establish a breach of environmental or nature protection requirements, the relevant construction permitting procedure must be suspended. In addition, new construction or facility permits may be withheld until the unlawful situation is remedied — and for a minimum period of six months, according to Kormány.hu.

Prime Minister Péter Magyar presented the measure as a response to earlier cases in which major projects continued despite environmental concerns.

“We have seen the consequences in recent years when nothing happened after environmental rules were violated during a priority investment. We are putting an end to that now,” Magyar said in a video announcing the change.

The changes also affect major housing developments linked to the Otthon Start programme, where some priority projects may face temporary permitting restrictions while the government reshapes its wider housing construction policy.

Otthon Start projects also face new restrictions

The amendment specifically covers certain large-scale housing projects connected to the government’s fixed 3% Otthon Start housing loan programme.

Under the scheme, large housing projects can receive priority investment status if they meet specific conditions.

According to the government’s Otthon Start Programme Office, qualifying developments generally need to include at least 250 homes, with at least 70% of the units meeting the programme’s eligibility criteria. Priority status can significantly speed up administrative and permitting procedures.

The latest changes, however, introduce the possibility of temporarily halting permits even for projects that have already received priority status.

The government says this is necessary because some previously planned large-scale Otthon Start developments now need to be coordinated with a broader housing construction programme that is still being prepared. The amendment allows the government to set, by decree, a period during which authorities may not issue new permits for certain already-prioritised Otthon Start developments.

If you missed it: Budapest streets could change dramatically under new pedestrian plan

This is potentially significant for developers because priority status was originally designed to speed up these projects. In practice, the new framework means that a fast-track development could still face a pause if environmental rules are breached or if the project needs to be brought into line with the government’s revised housing policy.

New rules for construction material exports

The parliamentary package also removes an earlier restriction on exports of construction materials.

Since 2021, companies planning to export certain building materials have been required to notify the Hungarian state in advance. The state also had a pre-emption right over the products concerned.

That system will now be abolished. Exporters will no longer have to file the same notification, and the state will lose its right to intervene in those transactions or purchase the materials before they are exported.

The change follows a ruling by the Court of Justice of the European Union, which found that the Hungarian mechanism restricted the free movement of goods and therefore conflicted with EU law. The European Commission subsequently launched infringement proceedings after the measure remained in force.

World.title: Cold mornings, warm afternoons: Hungary braces for huge temperature swings next week
World.content:
Hungary is heading into a mostly sunny and dry week, with afternoon temperatures climbing to around 25°C in many areas. The catch: mornings will be sharply colder.

A stretch of settled early autumn weather is expected across Hungary next week, with plenty of sunshine and little to no rain.

According to HungaroMet’s latest forecast, daytime highs will generally remain between 21 and 26°C, keeping conditions pleasantly warm for the end of September and start of October. At the same time, nights and early mornings will feel considerably colder, with minimum temperatures falling as low as 1–2°C in some areas.

The sharp contrast will be one of the defining features of the week.

Weather portal Időkép says daily temperature swings could exceed 20°C in places, particularly where clear skies and light winds allow temperatures to drop quickly overnight before sunshine drives rapid warming during the day.

In practical terms, that means a jacket or cardigan may be essential when leaving home in the morning, while a T-shirt could be enough by the afternoon.

Sunshine dominates the week

Monday is expected to bring largely uninterrupted sunshine across the country, with dry conditions and afternoon temperatures of around 22–26°C.

Tuesday is forecast to remain similarly bright and dry. Morning temperatures could fall to between 1 and 11°C, followed by highs of 22–26°C later in the day.

Wednesday will also be mostly sunny, although some high cloud may reach northern Hungary later in the day. Temperatures are expected to range from around 1–11°C at dawn to 22–25°C in the afternoon.

The dry pattern is then set to continue into Thursday and Friday, with filtered or uninterrupted sunshine and daytime highs mostly between 21 and 25°C.

Despite the warm afternoons, the colder nights mean autumn is becoming increasingly noticeable. Időkép notes that temperatures could fall close to 5°C in many places, while ground frost may still occur in some of the country’s more frost-prone locations.

If you missed it: Budapest streets could change dramatically under new pedestrian plan

Little sign of rain

HungaroMet expects mostly dry conditions throughout the working week, with sunshine dominating and only limited cloud cover at times. Winds should generally remain light or moderate, although stronger gusts may develop locally, particularly around Sopron and parts of eastern Hungary.

The result will be a classic early autumn pattern: cold starts, warm afternoons and large temperature swings throughout the day.

For anyone heading out early, layering will likely be the safest option — because what feels like jacket weather before breakfast may feel almost summery just a few hours later.

World.title: Banking costs in Hungary have surged far faster than the EU average
World.content:
The cost of financial services in Hungary has risen dramatically over the past decade and a half, far outpacing the European Union average. A new analysis suggests that inflation and a series of taxes imposed on the banking sector have both played a major role in pushing up household banking costs.

The price of financial services in Hungary is now more than two and a half times higher than it was in 2010, according to an analysis by Bankmonitor reported by 24.hu.

Data based on the EU’s harmonised consumer price index show that the cost of financial services increased by around 2.6 times in Hungary between 2010 and 2026. Across the European Union, the corresponding rise was considerably smaller, at roughly 1.5 times.

Hungary also stands out among nearby countries. Poland recorded one of the largest increases in the region after Hungary, but even there financial services became around 2.1 times more expensive over the same period.

The rise in banking costs has also exceeded Hungary’s broader increase in consumer prices. According to Bankmonitor’s calculations, overall prices rose by roughly 2.04 times between 2010 and July 2026, compared with a 2.62-fold increase in financial services.

In other words, general inflation explains only part of the difference.

Taxes also left their mark on banking fees

Bankmonitor identified several periods when major changes in banking charges coincided with new taxes or modifications to existing ones.

Hungary introduced its bank levy in 2010, while the financial transaction tax followed in January 2013. The latter was increased later the same year, and further changes to the transaction levy were introduced in the second half of 2024.

Also, Hungarian banks cannot simply change account fees whenever they choose. Their terms and conditions set out circumstances under which charges may be adjusted, and these typically include inflation, changes in taxation and amendments to the regulatory environment.

Inflation pushed costs higher as well

A noticeable increase in banking fees followed the 14.5% average inflation recorded in 2022, while another round of price increases came after inflation averaged 17.6% in 2023.

More recently, the effect was temporarily held back by a voluntary fee freeze. Banks agreed not to apply certain inflation-linked increases to retail account charges until 30 June 2026.

With the freeze now over, some financial institutions have begun adjusting prices again. The National Bank of Hungary has said that certain fees have risen since July, although the exact impact varies considerably depending on the bank, account package and how customers use their accounts.

Cheaper accounts are still available

The sharp long-term increase does not mean every bank customer in Hungary is paying high fees. In fact, the Hungarian banking market has a somewhat contradictory feature: while average financial-service prices have risen rapidly, customers can still find relatively cheap account packages if they actively compare offers.

For a typical mixed-use customer, even the 20 cheapest bank accounts can cost between HUF 8,880 and HUF 29,400 a year.

The MNB’s comparison data show substantial differences between banks and individual packages. Depending on payment habits, the difference in annual costs between two otherwise suitable accounts can amount to tens of thousands of forints.

Another measure reducing costs for households is Hungary’s statutory free cash-withdrawal scheme. From February 2026, the monthly limit was increased to HUF 300,000, subject to the relevant conditions.

If you missed it: Major change in banking in Hungary: You can now withdraw twice as much cash for free!

Hungary remains an outlier

Even with cheaper products available, the longer-term trend remains difficult to overlook. Bankmonitor’s analysis indicates that high inflation was an important factor, but changes in taxation and the regulatory environment also contributed to the difference.

For customers, however, the sharp rise in average banking costs does not necessarily mean there is nothing they can do about it. The MNB’s comparisons show that annual fees can differ by tens of thousands of forints between account packages, even for customers with similar banking habits.

That means someone who has stayed with the same account for years may be paying substantially more than necessary. Checking recent statements, reviewing the current fee schedule and comparing alternative packages — including offers from the same bank — could therefore translate into meaningful annual savings.

Read more from us: Revolut Hungary set to enter ATM market – what will change for customers?

World.title: “A manhunt will begin next week” – Fidesz faction leader predicts political retaliation
World.content:
János Bóka, leader of Fidesz’s parliamentary group, said on Sunday that recent developments in Hungary amount to political retaliation, predicting that a manhunt targeting members and leaders of his political community could begin as early as next week.

In a video published on Facebook on Sunday, Bóka argued that institutions and figures he described as the intellectual workshops of the Fidesz community had been targeted first, and that party members and senior figures could be next.

His remarks referred to a series of recent developments involving organisations and figures associated with Hungary’s political right, including the now-defunct conservative media outlet Mandiner, the House of Terror Museum and its dismissed former director Mária Schmidt, as well as the Centre for Fundamental Rights, where police carried out searches.

According to Bóka, these cases form part of a broader political process rather than isolated incidents.

“What is happening in Hungary now is political retaliation,” Bóka said in the video.

He went on to predict that a “manhunt” would begin as early as next week, with the aim, in his view, of intimidating and weakening Fidesz and silencing people who support what he described as a sovereign Hungary.

Bóka added that his political community could not be “broken, silenced or intimidated”, and urged supporters not to be afraid.

Parliament to consider immunity cases

His comments come ahead of an extraordinary parliamentary session expected on Monday, when lawmakers may vote on requests to suspend the immunity of former ministers Balázs Hankó and Miklós Seszták, as well as Prime Minister Péter Magyar.

Prosecutors are seeking to question Hankó in connection with an investigation into the National Cultural Fund. According to the prosecution, funds were allegedly distributed through a system that caused HUF 17.3 billion in financial damage to the central budget.

Investigators say more than 1,000 grants were used for purposes outside those permitted by law. Hankó has rejected the allegations and said the decisions and use of the funds were lawful.

Seszták, a former national development minister, faces a separate corruption investigation linked to Volánbusz. Prosecutors allege that more than HUF 12 billion in bribes were involved, including more than HUF 11 billion in unlawful benefits allegedly received through an intermediary between 2015 and 2018. Seszták has denied committing any crime and said he is prepared to defend himself before the authorities.

If you missed it: Prosecutors seek suspension for PM Magyar and two former Fidesz ministers

Fidesz and Tisza offer sharply different accounts

Bóka’s latest remarks echo earlier statements in which he described the proceedings against Hankó as politically motivated. Last week, he called the case a “show trial” and an example of political arbitrariness.

The phrase “manhunt” also follows similar rhetoric used by former prime minister Viktor Orbán, who recently suggested that several senior Fidesz politicians could become targets following the change of government.

The governing Tisza Party, however, presents the situation very differently. As we reported yesterday, speaking in Szolnok, Prime Minister Péter Magyar said political responsibility should fall on a relatively small number of people rather than on ordinary Fidesz voters. He stressed that “we are all Hungarians” despite political differences and argued that voters should not be treated as enemies.

Magyar’s rally was itself marked by tension. Objects, including an egg, were thrown towards the stage, prompting him to ask protesters not to target members of the crowd. Addressing the incident, he said some frustrated Fidesz voters were now confronting the fact that the leaders they had trusted had misled them.

Monday’s parliamentary session could therefore become another focal point in the confrontation between the governing Tisza Party and Fidesz, particularly as lawmakers are expected to consider requests to suspend the immunity of former ministers and Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s.

World.title: 70 years after the Hungarian Revolution: What became of the ’56ers who fled to Australia?
World.content:
It has been estimated that 200,000 Hungarians fled the country following the 1956 Hungarian Revolution and its Soviet suppression. Of those, about 14,000, roughly one in fourteen, eventually made new lives in Australia, a country about as far from Hungary as you can get.

Author: Liam Saville

Behind these numbers are thousands of different stories of escape and starting again. My mother’s is just one of them.

My mum began life as a poor peasant girl, but the childhood she remembers is one of privilege. Adopted by a wealthy Hungarian couple, both doctors, she was nine years old when the Hungarian Revolution broke out in 1956. “I was very privileged,” she told me. “We lived in Buda…it was a massive old house, and we had the top storey.” But she remembers Christmas the most. “The beautiful fresh Christmas trees that were cut down just for us, and the presents. Everything was expensive. I mean, we had oranges…not many people could afford to buy oranges, particularly at Christmas.”

While my mum had the good fortune of being taken to the zoo, given swimming lessons and regularly treated to the opera, childhood looked different for John Garamszegi, whose family struggled financially in central Buda. His father, János, was originally from Zebegény but, by 1956, had settled in Budapest with his family.

John recalls the start of the Revolution. “My mother, even though she only had a primary school education, joined the initial protest march of mostly university students,” he said.

Things changed quickly, and the family were soon hiding in their basement as Soviet troops and Hungarian revolutionaries fought on the streets outside. Later, John recalls his father watching as Stalin’s statue in Budapest was pulled down. The next day, he returned to saw off a piece of Stalin’s boot, a fragment John still has today.

The fragment of Stalin’s statue cut from the remains by John Garamszegi’s father after the monument was pulled down in Budapest during the 1956 Hungarian Revolution. John still has the fragment in Australia today.

Credit: Photo courtesy of John Garamszegi.

Leaving Hungary

By 1956, third-generation teacher Otto Huszár was no stranger to conflict. Conscripted into the Hungarian military during the Second World War, he’d served in a mortar unit and fought the Russians on the Eastern Front before returning to his profession after the war. In his own words, “by 1956 it was obvious that the Hungarians had had enough of the so-called communism and especially the Russian occupation.”

In a memoir provided by his grandson, Ben Heydon, Otto wrote: “The American ‘free radio’ constantly encouraged the reactionary forces to act. In October it happened. The Russian forces left the country, but returned through Czechoslovakia and of course everything was lost.”

With just ten minutes of thought, Otto packed a few clothes, some nappies for his daughter, photographs and documents and headed towards Austria along the Vienna-Budapest Highway.

Otto Huszár with his daughter Kathy. A former Hungarian school principal, Otto fled Hungary with his young family in 1956 and eventually returned to teaching in Australia.

Photo courtesy of Ben Heydon.

For 92-year-old Anna Prevend, the Hungarian Revolution was a very different experience. Then 23 and living in Vác with her older sister, she too remembers the broadcasts. “It’s the wireless, Free Europe,” she told me. “It just started, ‘We’re coming, we’ll help,’ and they go to bloody Suez Canal.”

“When it all started, I told my sister I was going to go…there were no cars or anything running, no buses or nothing. So, I just started to walk.” And walk she did, right into the centre of Budapest, where, as she puts it, “the fun started.”

For the next six or seven days Anna played “cat and mouse” with the Russians, throwing Molotov cocktails at the troops, darting off and returning to do it again. For Anna, the Revolution ended abruptly in Parliament Square, when she was shot in the chest by a Russian soldier.

“The rest of them, well, whoever it was, they just took me, and I don’t know how, but I woke up in Salzburg…From there, they cleaned me up, and they sent me to Switzerland.”

My mother’s escape was very different from Anna’s, yet the memories have stayed with her to this day. “We all knew. Even I knew that people were dying. People were being killed everywhere,” she said. “I was told nothing. It had to be very harsh, because as kids, we opened our mouths, didn’t we? So, I was told nothing, only when we left that we were going on a trip.”

Her escape began with a late-night train ride towards the Austrian border with her mother, as her father chose to remain behind. It almost ended in disaster four hours later, when Russian troops boarded the train as they got off.

“We packed one small suitcase, and it was a long walk after we got off the train.” It was late December, and they trekked twenty-five kilometres across frozen fields, dodging Russian patrols with the help of paid guides. “Young guys took us over the border, and apparently their payment was gold watches and money.” At the border, they had to wait until after midnight, when the Hungarian border guards replaced the Russians.

John Garamszegi with his brother Vili and sisters Ági and Kati playing in the snow in Budapest. The family fled Hungary following the 1956 Revolution and eventually settled in Australia. Photo courtesy of John Garamszegi.

During my interviews, I heard variations of the same story again and again. A woodcutter led John Garamszegi’s family through the forest with pálinka to bribe the guards. Marie Hanzlik Brown’s parents escaped at night, while Simone Brigit’s mother, Brigitta Rati, crossed on foot at Christmas. Different routes, but remarkably similar stories of escape and leaving almost everything behind.

Onwards to Australia

Many of the ‘56ers bound for Australia spent months in Austrian refugee camps. Most eventually travelled by ship from various European ports, though some, like Anna, flew to Australia.

My mum spent six months in the Austrian mountains. “It was somewhere in the mountains, but I don’t know where,” my mum told me. “It was a big chalet right up in the mountains…there were a lot of Hungarians. It was like a camp.”

Eventually, they were cleared to travel to Australia. As my mother’s uncle was already here, they were accepted as sponsored migrants rather than refugees, though they almost didn’t come at all. “The biggest thing was that Mum got an offer in America from the Mayo Clinic…yet knocked it back because at that stage my uncle was still alive.”

They arrived in Sydney on 14 June 1957 aboard the US transport ship, USNS General Harry Taylor. But in a cruel twist of fate, my mother’s uncle died before they landed. They still avoided the migrant camps and moved into her uncle’s apartment with his partner in Sydney’s Bellevue Hill.

For many Hungarian refugees, the migrant camp at Bonegilla in northern Victoria became their first Australian home. John Garamszegi’s family lived there for months, as did Otto and his family. Originally a military camp, Bonegilla was basic and, for many, not necessarily the warm welcome they might have expected.

John remembers seemingly endless meals of mutton, and his father constructing an improvised heater to make life more comfortable. Marie Hanzlik Brown recalls her mother, Katalin, describing “corrugated iron sheds and basic cooking,” while “possums used to be on the roof, and she’d feed them bananas.”

Making a new home

As the Hungarian arrivals began building new lives, learning English and finding work often determined what came next. My grandmother already spoke English, but my mum didn’t. That changed when they moved to Brisbane after my grandmother found work with the Red Cross while waiting for her medical qualifications to be recognised. Away from Sydney’s Hungarian community, my mum had to learn English. “There were no Hungarian kids at Coorparoo State Public School,” she told me.

Other Hungarians spread across the country in search of work. Anna found herself catching sheep for shearers before heading to Mount Isa, where she met her husband and began building a life in Australia.

“We are Australians now,” she told me. “We made the best of it, and we did very well.” Otto, a former school principal, found his qualifications weren’t recognised and worked in factories before eventually returning to teaching. Marie’s mother, Katalin, needed to start again, becoming a dressmaker after being unable to find mechanical work.

Seventy years on, just what Hungary means to those ‘56ers and their families varies enormously. My mum is unequivocal: she’s Australian. Anna sees it differently. “You never lose that; you’re always Hungarian.” John is different again. He spent years distancing himself from the Hungarian community, but now that he’s retired, he describes himself as a “born-again Hungarian,” though he’s clear that Australia is his home.

As for me, I’m both Australian and Hungarian and hold both passports. I grew up knowing surprisingly little about Hungary and speaking almost none of the language, yet as I’ve gotten older, my connection to the country has grown. My mum, now in her late seventies, summed it up best when she told me, “I’m Aussie. You’re more Hungarian than me.”

What is clear, though, is that the generation who lived through the Hungarian Revolution is disappearing, taking their stories with them. So, if you are lucky enough to have a ‘56er in your family, talk to them. Ask them about Hungary, about leaving, what they left behind and the lives they built afterwards. Just do it now, before it’s too late.

To learn more about the uprising that shaped the lives of Hungary’s ’56ers, read our article on the outbreak of the 1956 Revolution: 1956, October 23 – Start of the Hungarian Revolution

World.title: 90-year-old driver may have caused fatal crash in Hungary, reigniting debate over elderly drivers
World.content:
Two people died in a serious crash on the M80 expressway near Rönök on Friday afternoon. The tragedy has once again raised questions over whether Hungary’s current medical fitness checks are sufficient for elderly drivers.

Fatal crash on the M80

Two motorists lost their lives in Friday’s crash near Rönök in Vas County. According to information reported by RTL, one of the vehicles was driven by a 90-year-old man, who may have caused the accident.

Reports say the Audi, driven by the 90-year-old man and travelling towards Szentgotthárd, first made contact with a Hungarian-registered Fiat motorhome. The Audi’s front-left wheel was damaged in the collision, after which the car crossed into the opposite lane and collided head-on with a Hyundai travelling behind the motorhome.

The Hyundai eventually came to a stop against the guardrail. Both the driver of the Audi and the driver of the Hyundai suffered fatal injuries, while the occupants of the motorhome were reportedly unharmed.

“One person was trapped in each of the two vehicles. They were freed using hydraulic rescue equipment, lifted from the vehicles and handed over to paramedics by professional firefighters from Körmend and Szentgotthárd,” Hungary’s disaster management authority said.

The exact circumstances of the crash are still being investigated. The case, however, has revived a long-running debate in Hungary over how authorities should determine whether elderly motorists are still fit to drive safely.

Drivers over 70 undergo medical checks every two years

In Hungary, the required medical fitness checks become more frequent with age. Drivers over 60 must renew their medical clearance every three years, while those over 70 are required to do so every two years.

Dr Péter Torzsa, head of the Department of Family Medicine at Semmelweis University, told RTL that these examinations are not merely administrative formalities.

Doctors may check a patient’s blood pressure, eyesight and hearing, while laboratory tests and ECG examinations can also be ordered when necessary. Chronic conditions that could affect a person’s ability to drive safely are also taken into account.

Torzsa stressed that doctors carry significant responsibility from a road-safety perspective. If a patient has serious problems with their eyesight or hearing, for example, continuing to drive could pose a danger and medical clearance should not be granted.

At the same time, he argued that age alone should not automatically disqualify someone from driving. According to Torzsa, there are people in their 90s who remain healthy enough to operate a vehicle safely.

If you missed it: Asbestos crisis deepens in western Hungary as dangerous levels detected in air

Could virtual reality improve driving fitness tests?

Road-safety expert Károly Lovas, however, believes Hungary’s current system could be modernised.

He told RTL that newer technologies could provide a more objective picture of how elderly drivers react to unexpected or difficult traffic situations.

One possible method would be the use of virtual reality. Simulated traffic scenarios could test reaction times, attention and a driver’s ability to recognise and respond to potential hazards.

The Rönök crash has therefore brought renewed attention not only to the circumstances of the fatal accident itself, but also to the wider question of how elderly motorists should be assessed.

The debate does not necessarily point towards introducing a fixed upper age limit for driving. Instead, experts have focused on whether medical and cognitive assessments could be made more precise and better adapted to the abilities required for safe driving.

World.title: Bosnia Court Blocks Republika Srpska From Funding Secessionist Lobbying
World.content:
Bosnian lawmaker Denis Zvizdic, who initiated teh legal challenge. Photo: EPA/FELIPE TRUEBA.

Bosnia’s Constitutional Court on Friday declared that budgetary funds used by Bosnia’s Serb-dominated Republika Srpska entity to pay foreign consulting firms to lobby for independence violate the state’s constitutional architecture.

The ruling targets a consulting agreement signed between the Republika Srpska Representative Office in Vienna and a Montreal-based firm, Dickens & Madson Canada Inc., which listed “the independence of Republika Srpska” as a core political objective.

The legal challenge was initiated in April by a state-level lawmaker, Denis Zvizdic, who argued that using taxpayers’ funds to lobby against Bosnia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity was unconstitutional.

A 2008 ruling allowed the entity to engage foreign firms for general economic promotion. However, the court has now established that funding campaigns explicitly promoting secession represents an assault on the constitutional order.

“The Constitutional Court hereby prohibits all payments from the budget of Republika Srpska regarding the consulting services contract concluded with Dickens & Madson Canada Inc.,” the court said. “Financing lobbying services for goals that run counter to the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina is strictly incompatible with the constitutional order.”

The applicant, Zvizdic, welcomed the announcement, saying the entity had weaponised massive public funds for anti-state campaigns.

“Public money cannot be used to finance lobbying aimed against the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, its territorial integrity, sovereignty and its institutions,” Zvizdic stated.

“This binding decision establishes a clear legal standard: citizens’ money must serve development and investment, not the undermining of the state,” he added.

Under Bosnia’s state-level laws, entities possess no constitutional right to unilateral secession. Furthermore, ignoring or violating a binding order of the Constitutional Court carries severe penalties.

The court said the full text of the judicial decision will be delivered to all parties and published on its official website within the month.

World.title: Serbia Sees First TV Debate Between Ruling Party and Student List
World.content:
Serbia’s first election debate ahead of October 25 polls aired on TV on Thursday night, pitting former prime minister and current speaker Ana Brnabic – third on the government’s “Aleksandar Vucic – United Serbia” list – against Mirjana Nikolic, Rector of the University of Arts in Belgrade and a candidate on the rival “Student List – Students Win”.

The debate on the N1 TV channel was supposed to focus on education but quickly expanded into a wider confrontation over the anti-government student movement, the media, universities and the overall political situation.

Nikolic said she was initially apprehensive about debating a senior ruling-party official but welcomed the chance to present the Student List’s programme.

She said her previous meetings with Brnabic at parliament’s Education Committee had been marked by confrontation, adding that the televised debate offered a chance for both sides to present their programmes.

The appearance was notable because ruling SNS officials have largely avoided N1 during previous election campaigns and Brnabic last appeared in 2017.

“To be honest, I was not particularly happy to come to N1 this time either, given the way your television station has, over the past ten years, engaged in what I see as the dehumanisation of my President and my friend,” Brnabic said.

She accused N1 of having spread false information but said she had agreed to appear after Vucic encouraged her to give the television station “a chance”, following its change of management.

The debate quickly became heated, including an exchange over Nikolic’s alleged refusal to shake Brnabic’s hand.

The candidates also clashed over the student-led university blockades. Brnabic said students had been discriminated against “thanks to the Student List and the blockades”, while Nikolic accused her of promoting a misleading narrative about the protests and about how universities functioned.

On education, Brnabic defended the SNS record in government, pointing to higher teachers’ salaries, increased education spending and investment in science and technology infrastructure.

Nikolic challenged the figures, arguing that nominal salary increases did not necessarily mean education workers were better off, and questioned delays to university infrastructure projects.

She also criticised Brnabic’s understanding of Serbia’s education system, telling her: “As a professor, I have to tell you – Ana, you failed, you failed the exam.”

Nikolic said the Student List advocated free education, equal opportunities for students and teachers and the modernisation of the education system.

The debate was the first in a series of thematic election debates announced by N1 ahead of the October 25 parliamentary election.

World.title: Democracy Digest: Czechia Restricts Rules for Russian Diplomats Travelling
World.content:
Sikorski confronts Lavrov as tensions rise; Russian helicopter enters Polish airspace

Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski used a UN Security Council meeting on Wednesday to deliver a direct message to his Russian counterpart, Sergey Lavrov: that after more than four years of full-scale war, Russia had failed to achieve its central objectives in Ukraine, and lacked the economic weight to outlast the countries supporting Kyiv. “You have been trying to conquer Donbas for over 12 years and Kyiv for over four,” Sikorski said. Ukraine, he noted, has only one-tenth of Russia’s GDP. But Poland alone has almost half Russia’s GDP, while Europe has roughly 10 times as much and NATO 25 times as much. “You can still kill a lot of people, but you cannot win,” Sikorski said. “You can stop this imperial war of choice at any time.” He ended by addressing Lavrov personally: “Sergey, I know you’re listening. Tell your boss: enough is enough.”

Hours before Sikorski spoke in New York, a Russian Mi-8 helicopter flying from the Kaliningrad region crossed into Polish airspace north of Braniewo at 11:08 on Wednesday. According to Poland’s Operational Command, it penetrated about 300 metres into Polish territory and remained there for 42 seconds. Warsaw scrambled fighter jets and raised the readiness of its ground-based defences. The Operational Command said the flight pattern suggested Moscow was again probing Poland’s ability to respond. The pressure continued on Thursday morning, this time from attacks inside Ukraine. PM Donald Tusk said Russian strikes close to the Polish border forced authorities to evacuate the border crossings at Hrubieszow and Dorohusk. “Just as we were talking, Ukraine was attacked again near the Polish border,” Tusk said during a meeting with Bulgarian PM Rumen Radev. He warned that “autumn and winter may be critical”.

The incidents come as Warsaw is seeking stronger security guarantees from Washington and dealing with an unexpected hitch in talks over a permanent US military presence. Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz had been due to meet his US counterpart Pete Hegseth at the Pentagon on Wednesday, with a permanent US Army base in Poland among the expected topics. The visit was cancelled at Washington’s urgent request, officially because of a scheduling conflict connected with Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the US. No replacement date has been announced. The timing caused unease in Warsaw. Onet reported, citing unnamed government sources, that some Polish officials suspect Hegseth may be seeking to slow discussions on the permanent base. Subsequent reporting, however, indicated that the Pentagon initially tried merely to change the meeting’s time before cancelling it, suggesting the explanation may be less straightforward. The uncertainty comes days after Donald Trump said “significant progress” had been made towards establishing a US Army base in Poland and suggested its location could soon be announced.

World.title: Fading Away: Sicily’s Ancient Albanian Community Fears its Identity Risks Erasure
World.content:
Piana degli Albanesi sits among the fertile mountains of western Sicily, overlooking farmland and a lake whose waters have receded dramatically.

Its Arbereshe name is “Hora e Arbereshevet”, or, “Town of the Arbereshe”, the only one among the several other Italian towns to maintain a distinct name connected to the ethnic group that inhabits it.

The word “Hora”, explains Mayor Rosario Petta, as he walks through the town’s cobbled streets, is an old Albanian word for a town or homeland that is no longer commonly used in modern Albanian.

In Piana, however, the name is everywhere. It appears on street signs, public buildings and local businesses, a reminder that this is not simply a Sicilian town with an unusual history. It is the centre of one of Italy’s most important ethnolinguistic communities.

Petta says that in Albania, the Arbereshe are almost mythical figures –reminders of a version of Albania that disappeared centuries ago but still exists in these communities.

There is a strange historical relationship between the two sides.

The people of Piana look towards Albania as the ancestral land from which their communities emerged. Meanwhile, in Albania, the Arbereshe represent a living connection to an older version of Albanian language and culture that they can no longer experience in their homeland.

But the community in Piana is shrinking.

Over the past five years, according to Petta, the town has lost more than 20 per cent of its population. Its official population is now below 6,000, although the actual number of people living there is believed to be lower.

“The more people we lose, the more our ancient heritage is threatened,” Petta said.

The reasons are familiar across rural southern Italy: limited employment, young people leaving for larger cities or abroad, and the decline of traditional agriculture.

In Piana, climate change is adding another layer to the crisis.

The olive groves around Piana are increasingly exposed to drought, extreme temperatures and wildfires.

In 2023, wildfires destroyed several hectares of land around the town. The water crisis is also affecting farmers directly.

“We have felt the water crisis a lot and it is reflected in the quantity, quality and timing of our produce,” Claudio said.

Harvests have been brought forward as summers become longer and hotter. Trees are showing signs of stress that were previously unusual.

“The summer season is longer,” he added. “This year the grape harvesting season came earlier because of weather changes.”

The climate crisis, therefore, threatens more than individual farms. Agriculture has historically been one of the ways Arbereshe communities have remained rooted in their villages and integrated within Italian and Sicilian society. If farming becomes economically unsustainable, one of the remaining reasons for younger people to stay also disappears.

The Scalia siblings are trying to make agriculture part of the solution.

Their company was established in 2022, building on an olive grove planted in 1998. Their aim is to combine modern agricultural practices with the cultural heritage of Piana.

Their products are organic, with the longer-term ambition of securing territorial recognition such as the IGP designation. Alongside olive oil, they produce honey and other agricultural products, including plums.

The names of their products pay homage to their Arbereshe heritage. One of them, “Filari”, refers to the rows of olive trees while evoking “fili d’oro”, the golden threads used in traditional Arbereshe clothing.

The point is to make the connection between agriculture and culture more visible.

“Few people invest in agriculture and innovation in these historical times,” Claudio Scalia said. “Those who do struggle to live exclusively from it these days. To keep our farming culture alive, we are also taking on other jobs to financially sustain ourselves in a more stable way.”

Children no longer speak the language

World.title: Bringing the Balkans into Schengen: a Win-Win Scenario for Europe
World.content:
How would all this work? The member states would ask the Commission to prepare a roadmap of criteria: the Schengen acquis.

That means external border control, visa policy, the Schengen Information System, police cooperation and data protection – reinforced by rule-of-law conditions.

The Commission would report on progress every six months, and once a country met all the criteria, the member states would have to give their consent in the Council.

Reforms and the closer cooperation they bring can strengthen security rather than weaken it. When the Schengen area grew from 15 to 24 members in 2007, Germany’s then Interior Minister, Wolfgang Schauble, said: “We will have a gain in security, not a loss.”

The main argument against admitting Western Balkan countries has recently evaporated. For over a decade, several EU interior ministers saw the Western Balkan borders as a brake on irregular migrants and asylum seekers heading from Turkey and Greece into central Europe.

The admission of Bulgaria and Romania to the Schengen area in 2025 overturned that. Why would anyone on that route cross several tightly controlled borders when they could travel from Greece through Bulgaria and Romania to Hungary and Austria without ever leaving the Schengen area?

Reforms and eventual membership would meanwhile help to stabilise the region’s most fragile states – Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia and Kosovo, where Bosniaks, Serbs and Albanians live on both sides of the borders. As EU membership has receded into the distant future, the dangerous narratives of the late 1980s, that led to the wars of the 1990s, are returning, and with them ideas of redrawing borders along ethnic lines (floated by the presidents of Serbia and Kosovo in 2018).

The recent state funeral in Belgrade for Bosnian Serb wartime military commander Ratko Mladic, convicted of committing genocide in Srebrenica, is only the latest reminder of that.

It is precisely because these forces are gaining ground that the EU needs a stronger counter-offer. Schengen could be one. It does not move borders but makes them invisible, as they are between France and Germany, or Lithuania and Poland.

But you cannot make a border invisible before its status is settled, and the line between Serbia and Kosovo is the very thing being fought over. Settling it would become the price of a prize that’s within reach. It is a far stronger incentive than EU membership, which is at least a decade away.

Several countries already belong to Schengen but not the EU: Norway, Iceland, Switzerland and Liechtenstein. Unlike with earlier Schengen enlargements, this time no new external borders would be required. Surrounded by Schengen members, the borders of the Western Balkan countries could simply be collapsed inwards.

Offering such a roadmap would cost the EU little, and only serious reformers would ever join. Yet the process alone would hand the EU influence and win back some of its lost credibility. More importantly still, it would offer the Balkans something better than more quarrels over where lines should run. Borders would no longer matter.

Kristof Bender is Deputy Chairman of the European Stability Initiative (ESI).

A German version of this article first appeared in the Neue Zürcher Zeitung (NZZ).

The opinions expressed are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of BIRN.

World.title: Mr Who? Professor in Race Against Time to Convince Serbia’s Undecided Voters
World.content:
On one hand, Ilija Srdanovic’s greatest asset might be his lack of political baggage. On the other, his obscurity may prove a hindrance.

With the 56-year-old medical professor from Novi Sad, northern Serbia, now the figurehead of a grassroots movement to unseat Serbia’s ruling party and president, voters will give their verdict on October 25.

Largely unknown to the wider Serbian public until this month, Srdanovic has been thrust into the spotlight, his every move and utterance picked over by tabloids and pro-government broadcasters.

Srdanovic hails from the city where 16 people were crushed to death in November 2024 when a concrete canopy at a newly renovated railway station collapsed, triggering an outpouring of anger and frustration at what many Serbs say is the mismanagement, corner-cutting and corruption that has flourished during 14 years of rule by the Serbian Progressive Party, SNS, and President Aleksandar Vucic.

Chosen by the students who took up the call for change, Srdanovic finds himself effectively going head-to-head with Vucic, a seasoned politician and, his critics say, an autocrat in the mould of Viktor Orban.

World.title: Nations League: Croatia celebrate in Prague, Slaven Bilić kicks off with a win
World.content:
Croatia began their new Nations League campaign with a win, beating the Czech Republic 2-1 (0-0) in Prague in the opening round of Group 3 of the elite League A.

It was also a winning start for Slaven Bilić, who returned to the role of Croatia head coach, succeeding the trophy-laden Zlatko Dalić.

After a goalless first half, Croatia took the lead in the 47th minute when Luka Modrić scored his 30th goal for the national team.

The Czechs equalized seven minutes later, with Adam Karabec on target for 1-1. Croatia’s winning goal was scored by Marco Pašalić in the 77th minute, following a fine assist from Ivan Perišić.

Match report

Croatia’s indestructible captain Luka Modrić started the match, while Martin Baturina missed the game due to a virus. New Croatian talent Luka Vušković was also in the starting eleven, with Igor Matanović leading the attack.

The start of the match was fairly cautious on both sides, especially from the hosts. Croatia were the first to establish some authority on the pitch, and the first notable moment for the Czechs came in the 10th minute. Kovačić broke through a Czech line and set up Ivanović, whose shot was blocked. Three consecutive Croatian corners followed, but without any real chances.

The first big opportunity came in the 23rd minute, again after Kovačić launched a Croatian attack. The ball eventually reached Luka Sučić, who aimed for the far corner, but his shot flew just wide of the post.

The Czech players were largely harmless in attack, and even when they reached dangerous areas near the Croatian goal, they struggled to convert their approach play into real threats. Play remained largely in Croatia’s attacking half for the rest of the first half, with the best chance falling to Petar Sučić in the 42nd minute. A brilliant feint freed him from his marker, but his shot was saved by Czech goalkeeper Horniček, securing a 0-0 scoreline at the break.

Matanović also went close in the 45th minute with a long-range effort that passed just wide of the Czech goal.

Croatia took the lead immediately at the start of the second half. In the 46th minute, Matanović slid in to intercept a pass in the Czech defence. Modrić collected the loose ball, advanced to around 14 meters and finished into the far corner to put Croatia ahead. The Czechs created their first real chance in the 54th minute, and it paid off instantly with an equalizer. Hložek played the ball back into the Croatian box, and Karabec finished precisely to make it 1-1.

The two goals ignited the match, with the Czechs in particular looking energized and pushing forward with more purpose. Several dangerous moments followed at both ends, prompting Croatia coach Bilić to make his first substitutions, along with a change in formation — shifting to a back three, with Perišić moving further forward from a wing-back role.

In the 71st minute, the Czechs had a golden chance to turn the match around. Radosta received the ball in front of the Croatian goal but, in a one-on-one with Livaković, shot wide of the target.

Modrić was withdrawn in the 76th minute, replaced by Mišić, and just a minute later Croatia retook the lead. Perišić broke down the left and curled a superb cross into the Czech box. Marco Pašalić rose to head it home for 2-1.

This time Croatia’s lead lasted even less. Just two minutes later, with plenty of gaps in the Croatian defence, Radosta found the net to make it 2-2 — but the goal was disallowed for offside. The Czechs pushed unsuccessfully for an equalizer until the final whistle, with Croatia repelling every attack to secure all three points on the opening matchday of the Nations League.

Croatia’s best late chance fell to Budimir, who fired a shot in the 93rd minute, but Czech goalkeeper Horniček denied Croatia’s third goal.

In the next round, Croatia travel to Seville on September 29 to face reigning world champions Spain.

Two home matches follow: against England at Rujevica on October 3, and against Spain at Poljud on October 6.

World.title: Millions Still Being Spent on Tito’s Dilapidated Galeb Ship
World.content:
September the 27th, 2026 – Millions are still being spent on Tito’s dilapidated Galeb ship, with deadlines broken and no museum in sight.

The (in)famous, rusty old vessel Galeb has a history stretching from its construction back in the 1930s, through sinking during WWII to the status of Tito’s ship and a symbol of the Non-Aligned Movement. It is still waiting for its final conversion into a museum. Index reports that in more recent years, its story has been reduced to moves between different shipyards, successive deadline overruns and constantly rising costs. Around €22 million has so far been invested in the renovation and conversion, partly from EU funds.

more repairs, more deadlines

Galeb is now going to the Viktor Lenac Shipyard for the repair of damage caused in February, when a Turkish cargo ship hit it. The cost of the repair will be covered by the insurance of the Turkish ship, and at the same time the regular annual overhaul will also be carried out. President of the Management Board of the Viktor Lenac Shipyard, Luka Hrboka, confirmed the price of the works. “The amount is €860 thousand including VAT. The whole ship was built in the riveted system and that could be a bit more demanding than on some standard ship,” Hrboka stated for RTL. The ship should return to the Rijeka Port in about one month.

Project burdened by postponements

The museum on Galeb was supposed to open its doors back in 2021. The last announced deadline was February of this year. Now the opening has been postponed to the end of the year. Rijeka Mayor Iva Rinčić believes that the project was problematic from the start.

“I think there was a series of, I will dare to say, wrong decisions, from the purchase itself to, of course, the costs that exceeded the deadlines and so on. Now we are in a situation that in talks and negotiations with the Central Agency for Financing and Contracting of EU Programmes and Projects we are trying to open the ship and bring the project to an end so that we avoid as many penalties as possible,” Rinčić said.

the museum display is ready

From the Museum of the City of Rijeka they say that around 90 percent of the permanent display is ready. The exhibition will, through original objects, cover the entire history of Galeb, and not only the period related to Josip Broz Tito.

“Tito recognised it as an interesting vessel. He observed a military exercise of the Yugoslav Navy and, when he saw that the ship was very interesting, it simultaneously became both a school ship and his residential yacht for travels around the world. Of course we document all those attractive moments on the ship,” explained the spokesperson of the Museum of the City of Rijeka, Velid Đekić. That Galeb as a museum will certainly attract visitors is also believed by Rijeka resident Slavko Vanino. “Enemies will also come and will spit on it there,” he joked and added that the ship will certainly attract attention. After a series of unforeseen problems and broken deadlines, hope remains that Galeb will finally be opened to the public by the end of the year.

World.title: Patients of One Croatian Hospital Will Need to Pay While Waiting for an Examination!
World.content:
September the 27th, 2026 – Patients of one Croatian hospital will have to pay while waiting for an examination. It’s safe to say the users of Pula Hospital are far from impressed with these latest rules.

The body that came up with these new rules would do well to remember that people generally do not come to hospital because they want to, but because they have to. As of the 1st of October, parking charges will begin in the grounds of Pula Hospital: the first hour is free, and every subsequent started hour costs two euros. Poslovni reports that that sounds simple until you sit in the waiting room and realise that you don’t actually know whether you will be called in ten minutes or in two hours.

People generally aren’t rocking up at a hospital because they fancy a break. They come sick, injured, worried, devastated, waiting for test results, sitting down anxiously awaiting examinations, or as concerned companions to someone who cannot manage alone. It isn’t a walk in the park, nor is it predictable. Then, in addition to worrying about their health or the health of their loved ones, they now also apparently need to make sure they find mental room think about the clock that is ticking outside in the car park. After three hours of stay, the bill will amount to four euros, regardless of whether you spent the time at an examination or waiting for an examination.

The hospital says that by charging it wants to free up spaces for patients and that is a goal that makes sense. However, in typical Croatian style, this idea lacks logic and hasn’t been properly thought through whatsoever. It is hard to ignore that the bill will also be paid by those who are there precisely as patients with more than enough going on. Free parking is, however, provided for people on dialysis during the procedure and for oncology patients for the duration of any active therapy. While that is of course a good thing, it leaves even more room for confusion.

World.title: Yet Another Protest Announced in Zagreb
World.content:
September the 27th, 2026 – A protest has been announced in Zagreb for the 10th of October as traders, business groups and private landlords express their fury at yet more new rules.

Craftsmen, entrepreneurs and private landlords have announced a protest in Zagreb on the 10th of October over the new rules on so-called anchor prices, tax burdens and tourism reform. Index reports that they hope to shed light on just how much stress and last-minute expectations keep being put on them by a government that seems to delight in making them feel like criminals.

As of the 1st of October, traders and service providers will have to, alongside the current price, also display the one that was valid on the 10th of September. For businesses, this means additional administration, costs and changes to price lists. Fines for non-compliance with the rules on anchor prices range from €3,000 to €30,000.

Martina Tupek, owner of a hairdressing salon with over a decade of experience, says she is faced with new costs. “The price lists are in preparation and of course they aren’t cheap to sort out. Additional costs have been imposed on us. I believe that for someone who comes to me as a client, the price is not really the decisive factor. Really, whether it was a euro or two, nobody looks at the price list to see whether something was cheaper a few months ago. Whoever gets a haircut will continue to get a haircut,” Tupek told RTL.

Danijel Habijanić, who has run a craft for selling school supplies for more than 30 years now, has to change the prices on thousands of items. “In the physical shop, we have between 4,000 and 5,000 items, and on the web over 3,000. We’ll get to work and do all of that. Especially the web part, that also costs financially and takes a lot of time. Today, when online shopping is competition from the whole world for us, we have to fight with such senseless things, as if we are to blame for prices rising,” Habijanić stated.

They emphasise that the protest is not directed against taxes, supervision or an ordered system, but against constant changes to the rules, new burdens and decisions that are made without quality analyses and discussions with the sectors they concern.

all we want is predictability

UGP president Bruno Samardžić said that entrepreneurs accept risk, but not unpredictability.

“A business owner has to accept market risks, competition and responsibility for their own decisions. That is an integral part of entrepreneurship. But what we can’t accept is that the rules are constantly changed and that people who run a business never know what awaits them in a few months. You cannot plan investments, employment or development if the framework is constantly being moved. Entrepreneurship does not seek security. It seeks predictability. We aren’t asking to be exempted from obligations, nor are we asking for a privileged position. We’re asking that decisions be made with analysis, dialogue and enough time for adaptation. The state should look at people who work and create as partners, and not as the simplest source of new revenues. We are not asking for privileges. We are asking to be able to work,” he said.

“Every craftsman who wants to grow and develop has been punished by the state if they cross the tax threshold by one cent. I do not want to live in a state that punishes growth, but in one that says: Grow, create, open jobs. That is why I am telling the state to get off our backs,” said Kristina Bakula from the association.

private accommodation owners are also joining in

In addition to business owners and craftsmen, private landlords are also coming out to the protest. Their dissatisfaction was prompted by a significant increase in the lump-sum tax, the announced tourism reform and the new categorisation of apartments.

“This time, we have all gathered together – landlords, entrepreneurs and craftsmen. We want to show the state that it cannot treat us the way Franjo Tahi treated the serfs: violently and capriciously,” said Vedran Tomić, president of the association Let’s Save Small Family Landlords. He emphasised that small landlords have since 2024 become a target because of problems of housing and the real-estate market with which they are not connected.

“You cann’t solve the problems of housing, real-estate prices and the lack of long-term rental by punishing people who have for years legally invested, worked and paid taxes. Legal certainty is the foundation of every normal business and life, and it is precisely that which is today systematically being undermined. We are not rentiers, we are not the problem and we aren’t anyone’s scapegoats. We’re citizens of this state who with our work fill the budget. Thousands of landlords from all over Croatia no longer want to remain silent and endure the constant changing of the rules of the game. The state is not the owner of our lives and towards the people who finance it it cannot behave as towards serfs. Enough is enough. It is time for citizens to fight for legal certainty as the foundation of a fair relationship of the state towards its citizens,” he said.

higher costs and less satisfaction

President of the Alliance of Associations of Small Traders (SUMT) Mladen Kramar told N1: “Expect higher costs and more dissatisfaction.” Kramar considers the obligation to display anchor prices a huge administrative problem because of the shortage of labour.

“There’s simply nobody to carry it out and the rules that have been imposed are unclear. In the end, that does not solve the problem of inflation either, which the Government invokes. It is looking for someone to point a finger at and say that they raised the price. And one tiler will not raise the price if he has no additional costs because it is in his interest to be more price-acceptable. But it turns out that we are all raising prices and that we are all super-rich, and when we file our taxes we practically fall into the category of social cases.” He mentions the example of his colleague, the owner of a bookshop and stationery shop.

“She has a billion pencils on offer just as I have a billion chewing gums in the shop. For all of that the label has to be changed, and she does not even have workers to cover two shifts so she works one herself. Just that cost of writing all of that out she will have to calculate somewhere into the price and raise that price, not because she is arrogant, but because she is forced to do so. We are constantly going round in circles. Everyone sees that this is not an anti-inflation measure, but a measure that encourages inflation,” Kramar says.

the clear demand to the government

At the protest on the 10th of October, the organisers will present a series of demands. They will seek a revision and abolition of the Decision on the anchoring of prices. They will also demand that detailed analyses be carried out before the introduction of new burdens, that changes be announced in a timely manner, and that obligations and sanctions be proportionate. Finally, they will demand that representatives of entrepreneurs, craftsmen and landlords be included in the adoption of regulations that directly concern them.

World.title: Hotels or Apartments? Split Seeks Alternative Accommodation Structure
World.content:
September the 26th, 2026 – Split is seeking an alternative accommodation structure that would steer the sector away from solely hotels or apartments with very little else in the mix.

Croatian tourism has grown and blossomed for decades on the basis of apartments and family accommodation. At the very moment when Split, the largest city on the Croatian coast, is trying to balance such a structure, the mere announcement of change has provoked resistance from private landlords. Ana Roksandic reports for Poslovni that according to data from the Split Tourist Board and the eVisitor system, back in 2025, Split was home to 27,726 beds in commercial accommodation in household facilities, as much as 5.4 times more than in hotels, which had 5,111 beds.

tourist satisfaction

Household facilities accounted for 68.28 percent, and hotels 12.59 percent of total commercial accommodation capacity. The Split Destination Management Plan for the period 2026–2029 has therefore opened a discussion on whether and how much such a structure should be changed, but also who would pay the price of that change. The association Let’s Save Small Family Landlords (SMOi) submitted an official statement to the City of Split on the Plan proposal. The association claims that the document unjustifiably presents private accommodation in a negative light.

“That Plan, prepared by the Institute for Tourism, proposes an increase in the share of hotels and campsites of as much as 65 percent, while private accommodation is through the Plan, without a convincing explanation, presented exclusively negatively and its restrictions are proposed, although the data of the Plan itself show that more than 85 percent of tourists are satisfied with the quality of accommodation,” SMOi stated. The authors of the study, Snježana Boranić Živoder and Ivo Beroš, however, dispute such an interpretation. The key difference, they say, is between increasing the physical number of hotel capacities and increasing their share in the overall offer.

“It’s important to clarify that this is not a recommendation to increase the physical number of hotel and camping capacities by 65 percent, but a recommendation to increase their share in total commercial accommodation capacities from 18.2 to 30 percent,” Boranić Živoder explained.

the goal of reducing seasonality

In the scenarios, Boranić Živoder adds, the announcements of the opening of two new hotels with a total of more than 850 beds were taken into account, as well as trends of growth in investment in hotel accommodation. But the argument for changing the structure is not only the number of beds, but their occupancy.

“Taking into account the goal of reducing seasonality, it is important to emphasise that hotel occupancy is at the level of around 160 days, while in the case of household facilities it is around 80 days,” Beroš stated. That is an important piece of data for Split, a city that already has high tourist traffic, but extremely concentrated on the summer. By comparison, according to data from the Split Tourist Board (TZ), in January 2025, 38,174 overnight stays were recorded, while in July there were 678,911, almost 18 times more. The authors of the study say: “The goal is not to replace one type of accommodation with another, nor to reduce overall tourist activity in any form of commercial accommodation. The change in accommodation structure is viewed in the context of extending the season, greater occupancy of all forms of commercial accommodation and the development of a high-quality and competitive tourist offer of the destination.” However, the question of tourist accommodation in Split cannot be separated from the question of housing either. At SMOi they consider that responsibility for the pressure on housing cannot be shifted onto private landlords.

“If one wants to manage the impact of tourism on the city, then the criteria must apply equally to everyone. A tourist bed cannot be a problem when it belongs to a citizen, and desirable when it belongs to a hotel,” warned SMOi association president Vedran Tomić. From the association, they emphasise that the Plan states the potential for the construction of as many as 14,836 new apartments, while, they claim, city and state properties that could be activated for housing are not sufficiently considered. On the other hand, Ivo Beroš emphasises that the Plan does not reduce Split’s problems only to private accommodation.

the pressures to consider…

“Commercial accommodation is one of the elements of a broader system of pressures on the Split destination, and not the only pressure,” Beroš said. According to his words, the calculation of sustainability and carrying capacity also covered traffic, crowds, noise, waste, infrastructure, housing and the spatial concentration of tourism.

“Two thirds of the beds in commercial tourist accommodation in the City of Split are located in household facilities. In them around 55 percent of total overnight stays are realised, of which almost half are realised in July and August,” Beroš stated. After public consultation, the Tourist Council of the Split Tourist Board is to decide on forwarding the Plan proposal for adoption to the City Council, which as the representative body of the City of Split adopts the Plan. After adoption, the City of Split and the Tourist Board should participate in the implementation of the selected measures. To questions about how the City sees the implementation of the Plan and its possible effects we did not receive an answer by the closing of the issue

World.title: Mirjana Rakić: Vučić Calls Croatians Nazis, Yet Justifies Ratko Mladić
World.content:
September the 26th, 2026 – Mirjana Rakić has spoken out about Serbia’s Aleksandar Vučić calling Croatians Nazis, yet being open in its justification (and glorification) of convicted war criminal Ratko Mladić.

Journalist and foreign policy analyst Mirjana Rakić analysed the speech of Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić at the UN General Assembly for RTL Direct. She also commented on the reaction of Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenković and on the European Union’s current policy towards Serbia.

a performance for a domestic audience while ignoring the eyes of the world

Commenting on Vučić’s statement that Croatia is “proud of its Nazi past”, Mirjana Rakić said that nothing else could have been expected from him. “He had to season his performance with something that would sound first and foremost good to his domestic audience,” she said and recalled that elections are soon being held in Serbia. That was, she believes, a way of saying: “Here’s what I told them from a world podium.”

“It’s pretty hard to call Croatia a Nazi country. To justify in that way what they did with Ratko Mladić, to see off with state honours a man who was convicted of genocide – that is truly terrifying,” Rakić stated, adding that Vučić’s statement that Serbia cannot accept such moral categories opens the question of which moral categories he and his voters advocate.

the eu adopts a cautious stance

Prime Minister Andrej Plenković said in his speech at the UN that seeing off a war criminal with state and military honours is not in accordance with EU values at all. Rakić believes that the European Union has been extremely cautious with Serbia throughout all these years. “Bear in mind that Serbia has a visa-free regime with the EU and the Russian population that goes to Serbia can travel around Europe. They receive European Union funds for further development. They’re on the path to EU membership, and that path will last a very, very long time, if they ever manage to arrive at the end at all,” she explained. She emphasised that no one from Brussels has announced a halt to the flow of money or the abolition of the visa-free regime.

“Obviously a game is being played here. It’s a country in the Western Balkans, there’s the Russian question. On the one hand, Belgrade looks towards Brussels, and on the other hand, it looks towards Russia. That has been tolerated until now,” Rakić said. According to her words, the EU has not even now shown determination and told Serbia that it must prove itself in deeds, and not only in words, if it wants to actually ever hold membership.

World.title: Inspectors Find Almost 500 Products in Croatian Stores Too Expensive
World.content:
September the 26th, 2026 – Inspectors have discovered that almost 500 products being sold in various Croatian stores are too expensive. The question is: is anyone remotely shocked?

The aforementioned inspections covered the application of decisions setting the highest permitted prices of individual products and product categories, as well as traders’ obligations related to informing consumers. Poslovni reports that from February 2025 to the 18th of September 2026, the Market Inspection of the State Inspectorate conducted a total of 5,409 inspections related to price control measures in stores. Irregularities were established in 1,351 inspections, or 26.45 percent of cases, while in the remaining 3,757 inspections, or 73.55 percent, no violations were found.

The inspections covered the application of decisions setting the highest permitted prices of individual products and product categories, as well as traders’ obligations related to informing consumers. Inspectors, among other things, checked whether traders display the prescribed markings, whether they offer certain products at a price within the permitted limit, and whether they fulfil obligations related to posters and separate parts of sales premises, reports Večernji list.

According to data from the State Inspectorate, in the controls a total of 4,996 products were established for which traders did not display the prescribed visual identification marking. For 466 products it was established that they were sold at a price higher than the highest permitted, while in 1,078 product categories traders did not set a price up to the prescribed highest level for at least one item they have on offer.

Among the products from the group for which traders must display a price up to the permitted amount for all items, the most violations were established for syrup with sugar – 237. These are followed by UHT milk with 2.8 percent milk fat with 220 violations, yoghurt in cups and bottles of 180 to 200 grams with 215, and shower gel of 250 millilitres with 205 violations. More than 150 violations were also recorded for sanitary pads, where there were 161. For pasta in the form of spaghetti 98 violations were established, rice 128, carrots in bulk 118, lemons in bulk 111, chicken and turkey frankfurters 106, toothpaste 104, tomato purée 100, and for chicken 89.

Inspectors also specifically checked 71 product categories in which traders must have at least one item at a price up to the highest permitted. In that group the most irregularities were recorded for unpackaged wheat bread, with a total of 182 violations. These are followed by oranges in bulk with 144 violations, Kranj sausage with 137, red or yellow onion with 118, Tyrolean sausage with 102, and pancetta with 98 violations.

A problem was also established with the obligatory informing of consumers. A total of 375 violations related to the display of posters and ensuring separate parts of the sales facility were recorded. In 306 cases traders did not display the prescribed poster, in 22 cases they did not ensure a separate part of the sales space in facilities larger than 400 square metres, while in 47 cases it was established that on that separate part at least one item at a limited price from the prescribed groups was not displayed. The inspection also controlled the obligation of traders to publish valid price lists on their websites and to display an additional price alongside certain products as a measure of direct price control. In 219 sales facilities traders did not display the additional price for a total of 2,084 controlled products.

When it comes to the publication of price lists on websites, controls were carried out at traders from the categories of supermarkets, hypermarkets, discount stores and Cash&Carry type stores. It was established that 14 traders did not fulfil all the prescribed obligations related to the publication of price lists, while some inspections are still ongoing.

From the State Inspectorate they state that for the established misdemeanours they will take the prescribed misdemeanour measures. Price control measures were introduced in order to mitigate the consequences of market disruptions and protect the economic rights of consumers, and traders, alongside price restrictions, also received obligations related to more transparent informing of customers.

World.title: Mass publication of data on deceased persons makes historians' work easier
World.content:
In September, the Ministry of the Interior began publishing, as open data, the names, birth and death dates, and personal identification codes of deceased persons. For historians and name researchers, machine‑readable data makes research easier.

Enel Pungas, head of the population operations department at the Ministry of the Interior, explained that publishing the data is important, for example, for institutions with which the deceased had contracts. "All institutions need this information that a person has died," she said.

Historian and name researcher Fred Puss said that in many countries data about deceased persons has been public for decades. According to Puss, the data is also important for historians, and searching for it across different registers has been difficult — especially concerning people who died between 1944 and 1957.

A name researcher can learn from this data, for example, when a particular surname in Estonia died out — meaning when the last bearer of that name passed away.

"Unfortunately, this happens constantly. Forty‑four percent of all Estonian surnames are represented by only one bearer, and when that one bearer dies, the name disappears from Estonia. A large part of those names are not of Estonian origin, but among them are also Estonian names," Puss said.

The Data Protection Inspectorate asked the Ministry of the Interior to assess, before publishing the names, whether making them public could cause discomfort to the relatives of the deceased.

"In the Estonian Personal Data Protection Act there is even a provision that allows certain personal data of deceased persons to be processed without consent, but if such data is processed more broadly as open data, then in fact an additional impact assessment should be carried out," said Geili Keppi, a lawyer at the Data Protection Inspectorate.

Pungas said that as a result of the impact assessment, the data of the deceased will not be published immediately, but seven days after death. The Statistics Office and the Estonian Institute for Health Development have also reviewed the level of detail in death‑cause statistics to ensure that no one can be identified by cause of death.
