World.title: ‘An Sayaw nin mga Salampati’ and Bicol’s unwavering fight for human rights
World.content:
DESAPARECIDOS. Scarecrows erected in the fields of the fictional town of Sinibaan symbolize the many farmers and activists who remain missing in the Philippines.

Weaving Bicol folk dance and music, the film 'An Sayaw nin mga Salampati’ shows the enduring hope of the families of the desaparecidos

ALBAY, Philippines – Drawing inspiration from the lives of Bicol farmers, An Sayaw nin mga Salampati (Dance of the Pigeons) transforms the grief and longing of the families of desaparecidos (victims of enforced disappearances) into a sharp look at the region’s long-standing fight against systemic human rights violations.

Through the haunting cadences of “Sarung Banggi” (One Evening), playful beats of “Salampating Guminaro” (The Little Pigeon That Has Grown Tame), the melancholic rhythm of “Kudot-kudotan” (The Pinching Game), and other Bicol folk music and dances, the film not only puts the spotlight on regional traditions, but also the people’s collective courage and resistance.

“Beyond being an agricultural nation, the Philippines suffers among the highest recorded cases of disappearances and extrajudicial killings targeting farmer-activists fighting for their ancestral land rights — a reality we aim to shed light on in this film,” said multi-awarded Bicolano filmmaker Arjanmar Rebeta.

Since the 1970s, at least 2,300 desaparecidos have remained missing in the Philippines. Among the latest recorded cases in Bicol are human rights defenders James Jazmines and Felix Salaveria Jr., who were both abducted by alleged state forces in Tabaco City, Albay.

Jazmines was taken on August 23, 2024, and Salaveria suffered the same fate five days later on August 28. Two years on, their families continue to search tirelessly and demand the safe resurfacing of both activists.

Defiance movement

“In the fictional town of Sinibaan, women dress scarecrows in the last-worn clothes of the disappeared to stand across the fields as a symbol of their families’ longing for their return. The women left behind by their desaparecido husbands dance the pantomina,” shared Rebeta.

Pantomina is a traditional Bicolano courtship dance, typically performed by newlyweds during weddings to mimic the movements of doves or pigeons.

For Rebeta, the characters performing the dance serve as “a stark reminder for the government and a courtship for justice — a movement that will continue as an act of remembrance and resistance.”

PROTEST. Reimagining the pantomina as an act of defiance, the women of ‘An Sayaw nin Mga Salampati’ channel collective grief into a movement that courts justice.

In the film, Ramona Yusay portrays Maura, a folk dance instructor whose husband, Lando (played by Jhong Hilario), has been forcibly disappeared.

Maura and the women of Sinibaan — including Gunda, played by Marietta “Pokwang” Subon — danced pantomina to “express their grief into the streets and fields, turning the dance into a challenge against a system that silences their voices and leaves their loved ones unaccounted for.”

The cast is also joined by local Bicolano artists and the region’s top creative talents in music, dance, and production, including performers Mildred Estella and Kyle Adrian Paga, alongside renowned composer and arranger Ruben Federizon.

Grassroots cinema

As a full-scale musical film, the production faced significant resource hurdles, especially for Giya Studios. Seeing the challenge, the local community stepped up — everyone from thrift shop vendors and farmers to even pigeon owners donated goods and services to drive the project forward.

“During our six-day first shooting leg in Cabusao and Libmanan, Camarines Sur, the community truly adopted us and helped us in so many ways — from small gestures to large contributions,” said Khaye Medina, managing director of Giya Studios.

“They helped us save on costs and sustain this advocacy project, doing everything from building production sets to joining us as talents.”

SOLIDARITY. Jhong Hilario, local talents, and volunteers help complete the first six-day shooting leg in Cabusao and Libmanan, Camarines Sur.

Medina shared that the local community members who joined as talents did not just help on set; they even organized a “Zumba for a Cause” event to raise funds for the film’s upcoming second shooting leg.

With most of the production crew working as volunteers, Medina and Rebeta emphasized that their top priority for the upcoming second leg is providing proper meals, accommodations, and transportation allowances for the team.

As of September 17, the film’s online crowdfunding campaign has raised P130,000 in cash donations, alongside production support and meal sponsorships provided by local communities.

“Of course, we provide honoraria to our talents, but we never expected them to take the initiative to give back and help us raise funds for production,” said Medina. “That is the real beauty of making this film — it is not just about the community; it is supported and embraced by them.”

FILMMAKERS. Filming across rural villages, production volunteers bring to life the 1990s landscape of the fictional town of Sinibaan.

– Rappler.com

The production team is preparing for its next shooting schedule and continues to seek partnerships, major sponsorships, collaborations, and other forms of support.

Those interested in helping can message ‘An Sayaw nin mga Salampati’s (Dance of the Pigeons)’ official Facebook page or contribute through its crowdfunding campaign.

World.title: Kazakhstan Appoints Myrzakhmetov as Defense Minister
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has appointed Aidos Myrzakhmetov as the Minister of Defense on Sept. 27.

Myrzakhmetov was relieved of his previous position as part of his appointment as Defense Minister, Akorda reported.

He graduated from the Military Academy of the Armed Forces of Kazakhstan in 2002. Since January 2024, he has served as Commander of the Special Operations Forces of the Armed Forces of Kazakhstan. Prior to that, he headed a department of the State Security Service. In May, President Tokayev awarded Myrzakhmetov the military rank of Major General.

Dauren Kossanov was relieved of his position as Defense Minister by presidential decree.

The appointment comes days after the deaths of 14 service members during naval exercises in the Mangystau Region on Sept. 24. The General Prosecutor’s Office is conducting a pre-trial investigation into the deaths of service members during the exercises.

On Sept. 26, by presidential order, a commission has been established to conduct a comprehensive review of the state of affairs at the Defense Ministry.

World.title: From Tiny Corals to Caspian Seals: Exhibition in Astana Traces Nature’s Connections
World.content:
ASTANA – From coral reefs and the microscopic organisms that sustain them to marine mammals inhabiting the Caspian Sea, every species is part of a larger natural system. A photo exhibition that explores this interconnected world opened in Astana on Sept. 23, bringing together stories of biodiversity from Kazakhstan and around the world.

An exhibition, titled “Invisible World: A City Underwater” will run through Nov. 1.

One biodiversity story comes from a small laboratory in London, where marine biologist Jamie Craggs, a co-founder of Coral Spawning International, managed to recreate the natural conditions required for coral spawning. The work has opened new possibilities for producing young corals in controlled conditions while maintaining greater genetic diversity.

The project later expanded to the Seychelles, where Nature Seychelles established another laboratory as part of the Assisted Recovery of Coral (ARC) Programme. Unlike traditional coral gardening methods, the project uses sexual reproduction to produce genetically diverse corals. Early results recorded the settlement and growth of around 65,000 young corals.

As Maral Rakhimzhanova, corporate communications manager at Canon’s representative office in Kazakhstan, explained, the importance of coral reefs extends far beyond their colourful appearance.

“Corals are very colorful, but in fact their color is given by algae that live in symbiosis with them. It is a relationship between two living organisms,” she said.

When water temperatures rise, corals can become stressed and expel the algae living within their tissues, causing coral bleaching. If the stress continues, the corals may eventually die. Reefs also provide food and shelter for a wide range of marine species, linking corals to the wider food chain.

Rakhimzhanova noted that these connections are relevant for a landlocked country such as Kazakhstan, as changes in one part of the natural world can have consequences far beyond it.

The same idea takes a different form in Kazakhstan’s waters, where the Caspian seal is among the species facing a changing environment. The animal, which is found only in the Caspian Sea, is included in Kazakhstan’s Red Book and has been the subject of long-term research by scientist Assel Baimukanova.

“Field research shows that these animals have their own character and social interactions that we are still learning to understand. The Caspian Sea is their home, and protecting the Caspian seal has become my main goal. These animals are affected by a range of factors, including shipping, fishing, environmental pollution and climate change. As the sea changes, seals are also forced to adapt and change their usual resting sites,” Baimukanova explained.

“The health of the Caspian seal is closely connected to the health of the Caspian Sea itself. By observing how the animals are doing, we can learn a great deal about the condition of the ecosystem they depend on. Exhibitions like this help bring scientific research closer to the public, make science more accessible and encourage more people to take an interest in these issues,” Baimukanova told The Astana Times.

Her photographs are featured alongside works by Mirgaliy Baimukanov, a director of the Institute of Hydrobiology and Ecology, Dmitry Malakhov, a researcher at the Institute of Zoology of Kazakhstan, wildlife photographer Vladislav Yakushkin and birdwatcher Gennady Dyakin. Illustrations of rare fish by designers Vladimir Timokhanov and Timofei Bannikov add another perspective to the collection.

The story extends beyond photography through virtual reality technology, allowing visitors to virtually explore coral reefs and experience the underwater environment.

World.title: Murder? Ancient Burial in Southern Kazakhstan Reveals Woman With Fatal Skull Injury
World.content:
ASTANA – Archaeologists excavating ancient burial sites in southern Kazakhstan have uncovered the remains of a woman with a fatal skull injury, among findings dating to the Late Bronze Age and the Kangju period.

Researchers are now examining whether the injury was linked to violence or to a burial practice previously undocumented in the region, according to Otyrar.kz news website.

The excavation was led by Alexander Podushkin, a doctor of historical sciences and professor at the South Kazakhstan Pedagogical University named after Ozbekali Zhanibekov, with specialists from the Ordabasy state historical-cultural reserve. Podushkin has led excavations of Kangju period burial grounds in the region before, including inscribed bricks and funerary artifacts unearthed this July.

Researchers examined two objects in the zone. The first, the Tasbastau burial mound, is around 10 meters in diameter and marked by a ring of upright stones. The finds date to the 14th to 12th centuries B.C. At the center were two burials: a stone cist and a structure enclosed by masonry walls. The site had been looted in antiquity, but archaeologists recovered fragments of pottery and a stone amulet that helped date the burial.

The second research object was the third headstone at the Kyzylkol-1 burial ground, a family grave holding the remains of a man, a woman and two children, along with a rare amulet made from marten or fox bone.

The wound on the woman’s skull, in the temporal area, matches a strike from a battle axe.

“Two possibilities are currently being considered. According to one hypothesis, the woman was killed during the burial ceremony and may have been interred alongside a man. But she may also have been wounded in battle and later died from her injuries,” Podushkin said.

“Women held a relatively high social status. During wars, they were more often taken captive than killed, as men were. Still, given that the Kangju included Sarmatian tribes, it is possible that women took part in military clashes. Women are known to have fought as warriors in Sarmatian society,” he said.

Turkistan Region has been one of the country’s most active fields for archaeology this year, with Podushkin’s team alone uncovering Kangly-era burial mounds and inscribed ceramics in the region’s Ordabasy district in June.

World.title: Kazakhstan Builds Medal Haul at Asian Games as Cycling and Combat Sports Lead Strong Start
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has continued to build its medal haul at the 20th Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, with the national team adding medals across athletics, fencing, shooting and canoeing after the opening days of competition.

Kazakhstan is represented by 558 athletes competing in 35 of the 43 sports on the programme. The Games run through Oct. 4.

At the moment of writing, Kazakhstan is fourth in the medal table with 25 medals: eight gold, eight silver and nine bronze. China leads with 76 golds, ahead of Japan that has 18 medals and South Korea – 10.

Kazakhstan won six medals, four of them gold, on Sept. 20, the first full competition day, the National Olympic Committee press service reported.

Cycling sets the pace

Alexey Lutsenko won the men’s individual time trial in 41:24.05, his fifth Asian Games gold and fourth straight title in the event after 2014, 2018 and 2022.

Rinata Sultanova won the women’s time trial. Sultanova completed the course in 36:23.72, finishing 4.86 seconds ahead of China’s Zhang Hao. South Korea’s Shin Chieun took bronze.

On Sept. 23, Lutsenko won the men’s road race, his second gold of these Games and sixth of his career, a Kazakh record for the summer Asian Games.

Before the current Games, the record belonged to Kazakh canoeist Konstantin Negodyayev, who became an Asian Games champion five times. He won three gold medals at Hiroshima 1994 and two more at Bangkok 1998.

In the men’s road race, Kazakhstan’s Yevgeniy Fedorov took silver.

Karate and mixed martial arts deliver

In karate, Zholaman Bigabyl won the men’s under-55 kilogram kumite, beating Uzbekistan’s Khumoyunmirzo Khalimov 9-1 in the final. It was his first Asian Games medal.

Sofya Berultseva took the women’s over-68 kilogram title.

Assel Kanay lost the women’s under-61 kilogram final to China’s Gong Li 2-8, securing a silver medal. Bella Samasheva and Nurkanat Azhikanov later won kumite bronzes.

In MMA’s Asian Games debut, Yerkingali Burkutalin won the 77 kilogram traditional-style final over Bahrain’s Muhammad Nabiev, and Kadyrbek Shynbayev took the 71 kilogram modern-style title over Tajikistan’s Behruz Khurshedzoda, both 3-0. Sanzhar Adilov added a bronze.

Rowing gold and a busy Thursday

Vladislav Yakovlev and Ivan Chernukhin won the men’s pair in 6:25.13, ahead of China and Uzbekistan, for Kazakhstan’s eighth gold. This is Kazakhstan’s first-ever Asian Games gold medal in rowing.

On Sept. 24, four silvers followed: Abdurashid Abdullayev in wushu sanda (75 kilogram), Milad Karimi in men’s floor exercise, Kirill Prokhodov in men’s épée, and Olga Shmeleva and Tatyana Tokarnitskaya in canoe sprint in the women’s K-2 500 meters.

Sergei Yemelyanov and Timofeш Yemelyanov took canoe-double bronze in 1:44.972.

Silver and bronze depth

Kristina Morozova took silver in the half-marathon race walk in 1:35:25.

The women’s skeet team of Assem Orynbay, Zoya Piskun and Adel Sadakbayeva was second with 336 points, and Orynbay added individual bronze.

Fencer Artem Sarkisyan won bronze after beating Olympic champion Do Gyeongdon 15-14 in the quarterfinals. Arlan Zhanabay’s triathlon bronze was the team’s first medal of the Games.

Near misses

The men’s gymnastics team and the mixed medley relay swimmers both finished fourth.

In athletics, Daisy Jepkemei was fourth in the 10,000 m with a season’s best 33:03.21. Boxers Torekhan Sabyrkhan and Alua Balkibekova won their openers and reached the quarterfinals.

More medals

Kazakhstan continued to expand its medal haul on Sept. 25, collecting several bronze medals in athletics, fencing and shooting.

Alina Chistyakova took bronze in the women’s heptathlon with 5,568 points, while Polina Ivanova cleared 4.15 meters to win bronze in the women’s pole vault. Ivanova’s result marked Kazakhstan’s first Asian Games medal in the event.

Kazakhstan also secured two fencing bronzes. The women’s épée team of Irina Bakaldina, Vladislava Andreeva, Darya Samodelkina and Sofia Nikolaichuk finished third, while the men’s sabre team also reached the podium. In shooting, Islam Satpayev won bronze in the men’s 50-metre rifle three-position event.

The medal tally grew further on Sept. 26. Sergey Yemelyanov and Rufina Iskakova won bronze in the mixed canoe double 500 meters, while Dmitry Kholmogorov added another bronze in the men’s kayak single 500 meters.

Kazakhstan’s women’s 50-meter rifle three-position team also secured bronze, adding to the country’s growing collection in shooting.

With competition continuing through Oct. 4, Kazakhstan remains in contention for further medals across boxing, athletics, shooting, canoeing, and gymnastics, among other disciplines. The country’s early performance has been marked by a combination of established champions, including Lutsenko and Berultseva, and athletes winning their first Asian Games medals.

At the 19th Asian Games in Hangzhou in 2022, Kazakhstan finished 11th with 10 golds and 80 medals in total. Eight golds after five days puts the team on pace to beat that.

The 20th Asian Games opened in Japan on Sept. 19, bringing together thousands of the continent’s top athletes. More than 15,000 athletes compete for medals in 469 events across 43 sports, spanning both Olympic and non-Olympic disciplines. Several competitions will also count toward qualification for the 2028 Olympic Games, either by awarding direct quota places or points toward Olympic rankings.

World.title: Kazakhstan Warns of Global ‘Trust Deficit’ as Foreign Minister Addresses UN General Assembly
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan called for renewed diplomacy to end the wars in the region while condemning attacks on infrastructure carrying its crude oil through the Black Sea as Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi addressed the UN General Assembly on Sept. 25, warning of a deepening breakdown in international cooperation.

“We remain deeply concerned by the Ukrainian crisis, which continues to take lives, erode global trust and undermine international security. Even the most difficult conflicts must ultimately be resolved through diplomacy and negotiation,” said Tileuberdi, who heads Kazakhstan’s delegation at the UN high-level week this year.

“Beyond the tragic loss of life, Kazakhstan strongly condemns the repeated drone attacks against eight Kazakh crude oil export infrastructure, including against commercial vessels in the Black Sea basin. Such incidents endanger civilian navigation, disrupt international trade, and threaten the stability of global energy supplies,” he said.

Renewed call for diplomacy on the Middle East

Turning to the Middle East, Tileuberdi said political and diplomatic efforts remained the only viable path toward ending hostilities and reaching a sustainable settlement. He warned that continued escalation was affecting not only regional security but also economic stability, transport links and energy security.

“A just and lasting peace in the Middle East requires an independent, sovereign, and viable State of Palestine living side by side with Israel in peace and security. We support the New York Declaration as a framework for tangible, time-bound and irreversible steps towards the two-State solution,” said Tileuberdi.

“Kazakhstan calls for the full and good-faith implementation of the Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict and Security Council resolution 2803. As a member of the Board of Peace, President Tokayev has committed to contribute to the stabilization of Gaza, by supporting civilian reconstruction, ensuring food security, and providing digital government solutions,” he said.

He also said Kazakhstan had formally announced its intention to join the Abraham Accords, describing them as an additional platform that could reinforce the UN-led political process toward a two-state solution.

Afghanistan needs more than humanitarian assistance

According to the Kazakh foreign minister, Afghanistan’s stability was inseparable from Central Asian security and development. He called for gradual international engagement coordinated through the UN rather than humanitarian assistance alone.

“Humanitarian assistance remains indispensable, but it cannot by itself break the cycle of poverty, displacement and dependency. Kazakhstan supports pragmatic, coordinated and step-by-step international engagement with Afghanistan, with the UN playing the central role,” he said.

Preserve biodiversity, not nuclear weapons

Kazakhstan also offered to host renewed high-level talks among nuclear powers, linking the proposal to its experience of relinquishing the arsenal it inherited after independence.

“Our small planet is home to more than twelve thousand nuclear weapons, each one capable of untold damage and sorrow. Every year, we seem to lose more biodiversity yet gain more armaments,” he said, stressing that world military expenditures reached a record $2.9 trillion in 2025.

“For Kazakhstan, nuclear disarmament in particular is not an abstract doctrine. It is a responsibility born of national experience,” he added.

This year marks three important anniversaries: 35 years since the closure of the Semipalatinsk test site, 30 years since the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty (CTBT) opened for signature and 20 years since the Central Asian nuclear-weapon-free-zone treaty was signed.

Expressing concern over the erosion of trust between nations, Tileuberdi pointed to the expiration of New START, a nuclear arms reduction treaty between the United States and Russia, and the failure of the 2026 NPT Review Conference to produce a substantive outcome for a third consecutive cycle. He said nuclear-armed states remained bound by their responsibilities despite the lack of agreement and must continue working toward nuclear disarmament.

Erosion of trust

The international system is becoming less capable of preventing wars and humanitarian crises as trust between states erodes, said Tileuberdi.

“The erosion of trust among nations is rapidly reshaping the international order. Our collective inability to prevent conflicts, our collective indifference toward humanitarian crises, and our collective reluctance to seek common solutions to shared challenges are all becoming normalized,” said the minister.

“Trust cannot be restored when international law is applied selectively and commitments remain unfulfilled,” he added.

Kazakhstan also backed greater Security Council representation for Asia, Africa, Latin America, developing countries and middle powers, which the minister described as a “moral imperative.”

“Equitable geographical representation must apply throughout the United Nations system as a condition of legitimacy and credibility. The selection of the next Secretary-General will be one of the defining moments of this session. Kazakhstan supports a transparent, inclusive and merit-based process conducted in full accordance with the Charter,” he said.

The address reflected Kazakhstan’s broader effort to place a larger role for middle powers in international diplomacy. Tileuberdi said Kazakhstan would continue pursuing cooperation rather than confrontation, arguing that rebuilding trust would require states not only to reform international institutions but also to honor the commitments they make through them.

On the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, Tileuberdi also held a series of meetings focused on multilateral cooperation, regional connectivity and economic ties.

In talks with UN Secretary-General António Guterres, he reaffirmed Kazakhstan’s support for UN reform and discussed the role of the UN Regional Center for the Sustainable Development Goals for Central Asia and Afghanistan in Almaty, while Guterres described Kazakhstan as a “bridge-builder” in an increasingly multipolar world.

Tileuberdi also joined an informal meeting of the Organization of Turkic States foreign ministers and held bilateral talks with counterparts from Cyprus, Georgia and Romania, covering energy, investment, transport and logistics, including the development of the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route and the Middle Corridor.

Earlier, Tileuberdi also held talks with his counterparts from Hungary, Moldova, Poland, Slovenia, Ukraine and El Salvador, the ministry’s press service reported.

World.title: Last Weekend of September: What’s On in Astana and Almaty
World.content:
ASTANA – The final weekend of September features a variety of cultural events, including ballet, theater and concerts. The Astana Times editorial team has curated a lineup of events taking place this weekend.

Astana

“The Silk Road” ballet, Sept. 27

Travel back to the era of the Great Silk Road through an evening of dance, music and colourful stage imagery. The performance brings together different traditions and cultures, turning the historic route into a story told through movement.

Venue: Astana Ballet; 43 Uly Dala Avenue. Tickets are available here.

“The Nutcracker” ballet, Sept. 27

Step into a magical world with Tchaikovsky’s “The Nutcracker.” This enchanting ballet brings to life the beloved story of Clara, the Nutcracker Prince, and their journey through a fantastical land of sugar plums, snowflakes and unforgettable music.

Venue: Astana Opera; 1 Konev Street. Tickets are available here.

Kairat Nurtas concert evening, Sept. 27

Kairat Nurtas, one of Kazakhstan’s popular pop singers, will celebrate 20 years on stage with a special concert. The evening will look back at key moments of his musical career and bring fans together for a lively night of music and entertainment.

Venue: Astana Arena; 48 Turan Avenue. Tickets are available here.

Evening of Viktor Tsoy’s music, Sept. 27

Spend an evening with the music of Viktor Tsoy and revisit songs that have remained popular across generations. Live performances will bring his familiar melodies back to the stage while capturing the distinctive atmosphere of his music.

Venue: Sintez Theater; 6 Akhmet Baitursynov Street. Tickets are available here.

Almaty

Central Asia Drifting Cup, Sept. 27

Speed, roaring engines and spectacular tandem battles will take over the track as leading drivers compete for victory in an international drifting event. Motorsport fans can expect impressive manoeuvres, high-speed action and plenty of excitement throughout the competition.

Venue: STK Sokol; 76 km of the Almaty – Astana highway. Tickets are available here.

“Into the World of Theatre Through the Museum” exhibition, Sept. 26

Discover the history of theatre through archival photographs, stage costumes and other artefacts that tell stories from behind the scenes. The programme offers a closer look at the people, productions and traditions that have shaped the performing arts over the years.

Venue: Abay Opera Theater; 110 Kabanbay Batyr Street. Tickets are available here.

“Legacy” performance, Sept. 27

Based on “Memory” by Lavrenty Son and Stanislav Li, the production looks back at one of the most difficult chapters in the history of Koreans in Kazakhstan. Beginning with the 1937 deportation, the story follows people forced to leave their homes as they face hardship, loss and the challenge of building a new life.

Venue: Korean Theater of Musical Comedy; 158 Bogenbay Batyr Street. Tickets are available here.

The Golden Middle music fest, Sept. 26

Get into the festive spirit with an evening of live music, entertainment and the lively atmosphere associated with the famous Bavarian celebration. It is a chance to gather with friends, enjoy the programme and spend the evening in a relaxed festive setting.

Venue: Tirol restaurant; 98 Zhibek Zholy Avenue. Tickets are available here.

World.title: Kazakhstan Continues to Investigate Mangystau Military Tragedy, Five Officials Detained
World.content:
ASTANA – Five military officials have been detained as part of a pretrial investigation into the deaths of service members during a military exercise in the Mangystau Region, Deputy Interior Minister Sanzhar Adilov said at a Sept. 25 government commission meeting in Aktau.

The meeting reviewed the progress of the investigation and measures to support the families of the deceased service members and those affected by the tragedy. Adilov said the Military Investigative Department of the Ministry of Internal Affairs is conducting a pretrial investigation into the deaths.

“Five officials have been detained and placed in the temporary detention facility in Aktau: the chief of staff and first deputy Commander-in-Chief of the Naval Forces of the Armed Forces, two commanders of military units, the commander of a marine infantry company and the commander of the boat,” Adilov said.

He added that investigative and procedural measures are continuing, including the necessary examinations. Investigators will provide a legal assessment of the actions of all persons involved and establish the full circle of suspects.

Aid to families to be distributed transparently

Chair of the government commission Kanat Bozumbayev said the state would fully meet its obligations to support the families of the deceased service members. Legally guaranteed payments will be made without delays, while responsible specialists will be assigned to each family to provide ongoing individual support.

The commission also thanked members of the Kazakhstan Khalyk Kenesi, Kurultai deputies, political parties, entrepreneurs, and other citizens for their support. Funds raised through a special fund have reached the required level, and the fundraising campaign has been closed.

A special commission headed by Bekmurat Zhusipov, a member of the Kazakhstan Khalyk Kenesi and chair of the Mangystau Regional Public Council, has been established to ensure transparent and targeted distribution of the funds among the families and the affected service members. Law enforcement and state bodies have been instructed to ensure strict oversight of the use of the funds.

Defense Ministry pledges accountability

Defense Minister Lieutenant General of Aviation Dauren Kosanov expressed condolences to the families of the deceased service members and said those responsible would face punishment under the law.

“We remain in constant contact with the families of the deceased and provide them with all necessary assistance and support,” he said.

The government commission continues to oversee both the investigation and assistance to the affected families. All circumstances and causes of the incident are being established, with those responsible to be held accountable in accordance with the law.

World.title: Kazakhstan Plans to Raise Oil Refining Capacity to Nearly 30 Million Tonnes by 2031
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan plans to increase the combined capacity of its three existing oil refineries from 17.5 million to 28.8 million tonnes per year as the government moves to meet growing domestic demand for petroleum products and considers construction of a fourth refinery.

The plans were discussed at a Sept. 23 government meeting chaired by Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov on the implementation of President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s instructions to modernize existing refineries and assess the construction of a fourth facility.

Existing refineries to undergo expansion

KazMunayGas Chairman Askhat Khasenov reported on the status and timelines of refinery expansion projects. According to him, the capacity of the Shymkent Refinery is planned to double from 6 million to 12 million tonnes of oil per year by 2030, while the Pavlodar Petrochemical Plant is expected to increase capacity from 6 million to 9 million tonnes by 2031.

At the Atyrau Refinery, an efficiency improvement project is scheduled for completion in 2027, increasing capacity from 5.5 million to 6.1 million tonnes annually.

The Shymkent refinery expansion will also require upgrades to oil transportation infrastructure, including increasing the capacity of the Kenkiyak–Atyrau and Kenkiyak–Kumkol main oil pipelines and the Tekesu station. A Shymkent–Almaty petroleum products pipeline with capacity of up to 3.5 million tonnes per year is also planned.

Fourth refinery under consideration

Deputy Energy Minister Kairkhan Tutkyshbayev reported on work to assess the construction of a fourth refinery. According to the Energy Ministry, Kazakhstan’s long-term demand for oil refining capacity could reach around 40 million tonnes per year.

Bektenov instructed the government to complete a comprehensive assessment and make final decisions on the fourth refinery by the end of this year. The assessment is expected to determine the facility’s optimal capacity, configuration, feedstock base, location and economic model.

Officials were also instructed to closely monitor the expansion projects, prevent delays and ensure the timely commissioning of new facilities, with further attention to increasing the depth of oil processing.

Government links refining investment to fuel prices

Bektenov said the expansion of refining capacity is closely linked to the economic conditions of the domestic fuel market.

“Increasing oil refining capacity is directly linked to the attractiveness of fuel prices on the domestic market. In the current situation, when gasoline and diesel prices in Kazakhstan are twice as low as in neighboring countries, investments in oil refining are economically unfeasible. Therefore, we need to actively continue market liberalization. This is a matter of economic security,” Bektenov said.

The government said the refinery expansion projects are intended to strengthen Kazakhstan’s ability to meet domestic demand for petroleum products over the medium and long term.

World.title: “Saturday march” in Tbilisi: “Abkhazia is Georgia” and solidarity with Ukraine. Video podcast “Protests in Georgia”
World.content:
For more than a year and half – since November 2024 – continuous protests have been taking place in Georgia, with demonstrators demanding that the country return to the path of European integration. The results of the parliamentary elections held in autumn 2024 are still not recognised by part of Georgian society.

Every evening thousands, and often tens of thousands, gather in Tbilisi and several other cities. Over this time dozens of participants have been detained, many have faced criminal charges, and some have been sentenced to prison terms.

For the first time in the history of independent Georgia, the country has up to 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the popular outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti.

In 2025 she was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer. Protesters demand the release of all political prisoners and the repeal of all anti-democratic laws adopted over the past two years.

To suppress the protests, the ruling Georgian Dream party has increasingly tightened repression against civil society and the media. However, protests in various forms continue.

World.title: Baku outraged by Georgian Patriarchate’s “unacceptable” remarks over church in Azerbaijan’s Gakh district
World.content:
Kurmukh Church, Azerbaijan-Georgia

Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry has protested against a statement by the Georgian Patriarchate regarding the restoration of a church in Azerbaijan’s Gakh district.

The Patriarchate said the Church of St George, known as the Kurmukh Church, is an important monument of Georgia’s spiritual and cultural heritage. It expressed outrage that restoration work was being carried out without coordination with Tbilisi and without official information from Baku.

The Patriarchate also said the church is located in the “historical [Georgian region of] Hereti”.

Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry said the Patriarchate’s statement regarding the church, known in Azerbaijan as Kurmuk, amounted to a territorial claim against Azerbaijan.

What happened

In a statement published on 24 September, the Georgian Patriarchate expressed concern over ongoing work at the Kurmukh Church and the surrounding area, noting that although the church is currently located in Azerbaijan, it is an important monument of Georgia’s historical and spiritual heritage and of the Georgian Orthodox Church.

“Any interventions carried out both in the church itself, in historic Hereti, and in the surrounding area are of particular concern to the Georgian Orthodox Church. Many questions arise due to both the unclear purpose of the work and the restoration of a monument of Georgian cultural heritage without the consent of the Georgian side,” the statement said.

According to the Patriarchate, it has not received any official information from the relevant Azerbaijani state authorities about the ongoing work at the Kurmukh Church.

The church believes that the relevant Georgian state authorities should be involved in the process and determine what work is being carried out at the church, what research it is based on and who is conducting it.

The Patriarchate also called for its representatives and Georgian specialists to be included in the discussions.

“Only timely and coordinated cooperation can ensure the proper protection and preservation of this monument of Georgian spiritual and cultural heritage,” the Georgian Patriarchate said.

What Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry says

Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry said that the Georgian Patriarchate’s statement regarding the church, known in Azerbaijan as Kurmuk, amounted to a territorial claim against Azerbaijan.

“Azerbaijan has always respected the territorial integrity and sovereignty of Georgia. At the same time, the Georgian side’s demonstration of the same respect for the territorial integrity and sovereignty of Azerbaijan constitutes an important foundation of the strategic partnership relations established between the two countries. […]

In this regard, repetition of the the known approaches of the Armenian Church or following its path is not recommended. […] All historical, cultural and religious monuments located in the territory of Azerbaijan constitute an integral part of the national heritage of the Azerbaijani people and the Azerbaijani state,” the ministry said.

The statement also said it was “unacceptable to refer to geographical and historical toponyms located in the territory of Azerbaijan by other names.”

“It is important that religious institutions refrain from approaches that could undermine the historical bonds of friendship and good-neighbourhood that have developed between the peoples of Azerbaijan and Georgia over the centuries,” Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry said.
