World.title: IRGC announces seizure of US unmanned underwater vehicle
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 27. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy has seized an unmanned underwater vehicle belonging to the US military.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) announced this in a statement.

“The Remus 600 unmanned underwater vehicle belonging to the US military was seized by the IRGC Navy while it was conducting a reconnaissance operation in the Strait of Hormuz. Its data is currently being analyzed by specialists from the IRGC Navy,” the statement said.

The IRGC said that its Navy seized the vehicle as a result of a complex and coordinated operation. It noted that this is the second unmanned underwater vehicle seized by the IRGC.

“The IRGC Navy firmly declares that the Strait of Hormuz is closed. It will continue to take action against dangerous activities and attempts to transit the Strait of Hormuz via illegal routes,” the statement said.

The latest escalation in US-Iran relations began on July 8. On that day, the US Armed Forces carried out several series of strikes against Iranian territory for the first time since the memorandum signed between Washington and Tehran, claiming that the strikes were in response to an attack on a commercial vessel in the Strait of Hormuz. On the same day, US President Donald Trump announced the termination of the ceasefire with Iran. In response, Tehran began carrying out strikes against US facilities located in Bahrain, Jordan, Qatar, Kuwait, the UAE, and Oman.

World.title: Tokayev orders preparation of Kazakhstan's military reform plan
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 27. President of Kazakhstan Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has instructed the Security Council Staff and the Ministry of Defense to prepare a military reform plan within 10 days, during today's meeting with Defense Ministry leadership in Astana.

This was reported by the press service of the President of Kazakhstan.

The meeting began with a minute of silence for the 14 servicemen who died during military exercises in the Mangystau region on September 24.

Tokayev said the servicemen had not been provided with the necessary equipment during the exercises, including marine life jackets.

He instructed the government commission investigating the incident to assess the actions of all officials responsible for preparing and conducting the exercises, supplying the servicemen and ensuring compliance with safety measures.

A comprehensive review of the Defense Ministry has also begun. The review will cover the organization of service, the state of supplies, and the material and financial provision of the Armed Forces.

The commission, headed by Deputy Chair of the Security Council Aida Balayeva, is expected to identify violations and determine those responsible. Tokayev stressed that military ranks and positions cannot serve as grounds for exemption from responsibility.

“It's time for a fundamental military reform. This is an urgent task,” Tokayev said, adding that Myrzakhmetov would have to address “extremely complex tasks” as the new defense minister.

The president said the reform should involve a comprehensive transformation of the military command system in line with international practices and the introduction of digital technologies.

“Our army is stuck in the last century,” Tokayev said. “At the same time, the command system needs to be completely restructured in line with advanced international experience.”

He said the goal of the reform was to create a new-model army, while calling for technology to replace human involvement wherever possible.

Tokayev also instructed the new defense minister to improve the efficiency of budget spending, ensure that military reforms take into account modern threats, and introduce transparent criteria for the selection and assessment of personnel.

He said appointments to command positions should be based on experience and competence rather than personal loyalty.

The president also called for stronger educational and ideological work among servicemen based on the values of the Constitution, military history, and achievements of Kazakh and world culture.

Tokayev stressed that the safety and lives of servicemen must be an unconditional priority.

He further instructed officials to prepare a clear, specific and phased reform plan rather than broad concepts or road maps. The plan is expected to be considered at a meeting of the Security Council in the second half of October.

The president assigned the Security Council Staff to coordinate the military reform process.

World.title: Erdogan reaffirms Karabakh as Azerbaijani territory on Remembrance Day (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 27. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has reaffirmed that Karabakh is Azerbaijani territory in a message marking Remembrance Day in Azerbaijan.

“On the occasion of Remembrance Day in friendly and brotherly Azerbaijan, I commemorate with mercy our heroic martyrs who fought to liberate Karabakh from occupation and restore its freedom, and pay tribute to our veterans with respect.

Karabakh is Azerbaijani land and will remain so forever,” Erdogan said in a post on X.

World.title: Pope urges church to admit failings and heal 'deep wounds'
World.content:
Pope Leo has urged the Catholic Church to admit its own failings and heal "deep wounds" inflicted within its ranks, hours before meeting with victims of child abuse by priests in France.

Addressing crowds of more than 150,000 in Lourdes, the Pope said the Church must have the courage to face its past, but did not directly reference abuse scandals in France that sparked nationwide shock.

"In order to heal the deep wounds, infidelities and painful errors that have occurred within [the Church], we must humbly place ourselves under the Lord's purifying gaze." he said.

Arriving in Paris on Friday, the Pope went to Lourdes on Saturday and will visit Metz in the north-east on Monday.

During the trip, he has again urged the world to reconsider the development of artificial intelligence and drew 800,000 people for an outdoor Mass on the Champs-Élysées in Paris.

More than 800,000 people arrived for Mass with the Pope in Paris. (Reuters: Stephanie Mahe)

Local leaders are hoping he will help repair the Church's standing after a 2021 report found that some 330,000 French children had been abused by Catholic clergy and lay leaders over seven decades.

The Vatican provided a statement of what Pope Leo had mentioned in an earlier, closed-door meeting with French bishops on Sunday.

" The painful scourge of abuse committed against minors by members of the clergy, "

The Pope thanked the bishops for the "courageous measures" they had taken to confront the revelation,.

Pope Leo urged the bishops to bolster their safeguarding efforts and "continue on the path undertaken, maintaining the greatest vigilance".

Victims sceptical meeting will bring action

The Pope is due to have a closed-door meeting with seven French victims of abuse by clergy later on Sunday.

Some survivors said they were doubtful the encounter would result in quick changes by the Church.

The Pope's visit to France will include Paris, Lourdes and Metz. (Reuters: Remo Casilli)

"I am quite sceptical that the pope will solve the issue, at least not immediately," said Michèle Le Reun-Gaigné, co-president of an association for survivors in western France.

" Things are moving very slowly. It isn't going to happen overnight. "

Bishop Pierre-Antoine Bozo, the spokesperson for French bishops, said the Pope's desire to have the meeting "shows that we cannot ignore this issue and that it must always remain among our concerns".

Pope Leo has previously apologised directly for abuse scandals that have damaged the Church's credibility across the world.

On a trip to Spain in June, he told local bishops they must listen to survivors and offer them reparations.

Lourdes connected to Vatican scandal

The Pope's itinerary in France includes six events in Lourdes, a town in the foothills of the Pyrenees mountains.

It attracts some 3 million pilgrims a year for visits to a shrine to the Virgin Mary and purported healing spring waters.

The site is also connected to a ⁠scandal that has ​dogged the Vatican in recent years.

The shrine's facade has a series of mosaics by Reverend Marko Rupnik, ​a prominent religious artist with Vatican ties, who has been accused of sexual abuse.

Mr Rupnik, accused by more than 20 women, is not known to have commented publicly on the accusations.

The Pope has urged the church to acknowledge its mistakes and heal the wounds of survivors. (Reuters: Stephanie Mahe)

Five of his alleged victims wrote an open letter to the pope last week, sharply criticising an ongoing Vatican trial of the cleric.

The storeys-tall mosaics have been covered for the Pope's visit with large tarps.

During his time in Paris and Lourdes, the Pope twice reiterated Catholic opposition to assisted dying initiatives, which comes two ‌months after France created a legal right to die for those with incurable illness.

He said the shrine welcomes sick pilgrims hoping to find a miracle in its waters, and stood opposed to "current trends that seek to redefine the value of human life in illness".

Reuters

World.title: Matty Johns breaks down in tears after Knights end NRL grand final drought
World.content:
Former Knights star Matty Johns has broken down in tears as he heaped praise on the Newcastle team and its fans after a gripping and gritty NRL preliminary final win over Penrith.

The Knights played more than half the game with 12 men on the field after Phoenix Crossland was sent off for a hip drop that graphically broke Nathan Cleary's leg.

Penrith scored shortly after to take a 14-6 lead into half-time, but Justin Holbrook's Knights defended resolutely against a scrappy Panthers side and managed to score three second-half tries to progress to the grand final against the Roosters.

Knights stun Panthers to reach GF The Newcastle Knights reach their first NRL grand final since 2001, defeating the Penrith Panthers 22-14 after Nathan Cleary suffered a catastrophic leg injury in the first half.

The women's team won back-to-back NRLW premierships in 2022 and 2023, but Newcastle has not played in a men's grand final since Andrew Johns led the Knights to victory over the Eels in the 2001 grand final.

A quarter of a century and five wooden spoons later, the team will return to the final day of the season next week after a similarly remarkable upset win over the most dominant team in NRL history.

So it is hardly surprising that Hunter native and former Knights star Matty Johns was incredibly emotional straight after full-time.

"To be honest, I don't know what to say," he said on Fox Sports.

"It was unbelievable. Incredible effort in that second half. I just feel so happy for all the fans."

Players past and present, as well as coach Justin Holbrook, hailed the fans who travelled to the game. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

It became increasingly hard to find the words as tears started to flow and emotion took over.

"They've had to put up with a lot of shit for a lot of years to get back to where they are now," Johns said.

Even getting to the game on Sunday was tough as an issue with a freight train caused delays and cancellations on the Central Coast and Newcastle train line, forcing fans to find alternate routes and replacement services to get down to Sydney, which led to traffic jams on the M1 motorway on a sodden afternoon.

"But it just didn't stop them in the wet," Johns said of the crowd at Homebush, which was hugely in favour of the visiting Novocastrians.

The Stadium Australia crowd was heavily favouring the away team. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"When you run onto a field like that and you look up and you see all those Newcastle fans, you don't leave the field defeated.

"If not for the fans they don't win today."

Holbrook sprinted around the field to pay tribute to the fans who turned up, and who have continued to turn up even when the team was struggling, including last year when they finished last for the fifth time in 21 seasons.

NRL final swings on Cleary's horror injury Penrith and Newcastle were going hammer and tongs when Nathan Cleary's horror ankle injury turned the NRL preliminary final on its head.

"We want to make our community proud, our Hunter region, and for the boys to deliver that performance, it was so good to see them all hang around," he said.

"We went down to 12 [when Crossland was sent off] and then 30,000 make you feel like you've got 14 out there."

Captain Kalyn Ponga agreed the supporters helped the team get over the line.

"They're a big reason why we won today," he said.

"They're loud, they're passionate, they're vocal and we're gonna need them next week."

World.title: Scaffolding at Sydney building site falls onto cars month after wall collapse
World.content:
Scaffolding at a Sydney building site has partially collapsed onto parked cars, the second safety incident within weeks at the development.

SafeWork NSW said no-one was injured when a large section of scaffolding fell onto vehicles on Wattle Street in the inner-city suburb of Ultimo on Saturday just before 6:45pm.

CCTV footage shows the scaffolding giving way due to strong winds and narrowly missing drivers on the street.

The regulator said inspectors attended the site, and that it had issued regulatory notices, including a prohibition notice to the site managers.

There were no injuries when a large section of scaffolding fell onto vehicles on Wattle Street. (Supplied)

Lisa, who lives a few doors down from the site, said she heard a loud bang and initially thought a sheet of metal was being dragged across the street.

"There was a bit of wind, and there was a loud sound of metal on the road," she said.

She only realised what happened after reviewing her security video.

"I think the structure they had on the front of the building wasn't secure," she said.

"The scaffolding and the additional panels that they placed to prevent any bricks from going over it when they demolished subsequently was … not secured, and then fell on the road."

Macroview Projects, which is managing the development, has been contacted for comment.

Residents raise safety concerns

A wall and roof collapsed at the same Ultimo building site onto a nearby petrol station last month, seriously injuring two men, one in his 60s and the other in his 30s.

The two men were pulled from rubble and taken to St Vincent's Hospital and Royal Prince Alfred Hospital with serious injuries.

Five other people were assessed by paramedics at the time, but did not need hospital treatment.

Two injured in Sydney building collapse A man in his 60s and a man in his 30s were removed from the rubble and taken to hospital in a serious condition.

Lisa said work had only recently resumed at the site after being halted for weeks.

"It raises concerns over what is happening at that building site, and the safety precautions that are going into what should be the demolition," she said.

"It is a concern that this has happened twice in two months on the same place."

Lisa said she was relieved no-one had been hurt this time, but that the collapse had come at a cost to others.

"There are costs to other people, such as the cars that were affected last time … Coles Express, where its forecourt was closed for eight weeks, so it couldn't sell any petrol for eight weeks, and now cars in front of the building are being damaged."

SafeWork NSW are investigating

The building was previously home to a rehearsal studio, but had since been approved for demolition to make way for a multi-storey mixed-use development.

After last month's incident, Fire and Rescue NSW said the situation had been extremely dangerous given the weight of falling brickwork.

The site was subsequently handed to SafeWork NSW for investigation.

World.title: Freo finds joy in AFLW win, Pies finally off the mark
World.content:
Fremantle's women have lifted their club as they surged into the AFLW top eight, while Collingwood broke through for its first win of the season.

The fast-starting Dockers outscored Adelaide 28-0 in the first quarter and led by as much as 45 on their way to a comfortable 9.6 (60) to 5.5 (35) victory over Adelaide at Unley Oval.

Adelaide (3-4) kicked three straight goals either side of three-quarter time, but never got the deficit below 25, as Fremantle (4-3) defended its advantage, unlike its male counterparts in Saturday's AFL grand final.

It was the Dockers' first win in their past seven AFLW encounters with Adelaide, who had a 9-1 record in the fixture before Sunday.

In the other early game on Sunday, Collingwood (1-6) outlasted GWS 4.10 (34) to 3.7 (25) in a low-scoring arm wrestle at Victoria Park.

The Giants (1-6) led by margins of one, four and seven at the end of the first three quarters respectively, but Collingwood dominated the final term.

They finished with 18 more inside 50s and 16 more contested possessions.

In Sydney, the Lions fell short of a stirring comeback of their own in a 5.7 (37) to 3.5 (23) defeat to the Swans.

The victory held Sydney's position in the top four and saw Brisbane's record fall to a disappointing 2-5.

The Lions were second best for most of the afternoon but managed to stay in touch through three quarters, and were only a point behind at the final term.

But after Cynthia Hamilton goaled inside the first minute of the last quarter, the Swans didn't look back, running out comfortable 12-point winners.

In the final game of round seven, Gold Coast took St Kilda another step closer to the wooden spoon by running out 10.9 (69) to 6.3 (39) winners.

The Saints led by 15 points at half-time but were gunned down by the home side after the break, conceding eight goals to one as the Suns moved to sixth place on the AFLW ladder.

ABC/AAP

World.title: Dynasties and destinies swing on Cleary's horror ankle injury
World.content:
Mark the 35th minute of Sunday's NRL preliminary final as the hinge on which a storied dynasty and a potential premiership destiny swung.

Penrith and Newcastle had fought a first-half that made both look like worthy foes for the Roosters in next week's grand final.

The Knights faithful turned Stadium Australia into a little piece of the Hunter, proving yet again they would follow their team into hell itself if Sid Fogg's would charter a bus there.

Francis Manuleleua's long-range try, the latest scorching adventure of the screaming Knights, gave the beast inside the 55,000-strong crowd a smell of blood and it turned the Panthers into strangers in their own country.

The Penrith half of the crowd rose for Blaize Talagi's score off a clever Jack Cogger kick, but never has Nathan Cleary, benched before kick-off, copped such treatment on his home turf as he did before he entered the game in the 20th minute.

Just 10 minutes later came the tackle that ended his season as he suffered an graphic fracture to his ankle, also ending Phoenix Crossland's afternoon after he was sent off, and putting this game on the raggedy edge.

In the end, it was the Knights who pushed the Panthers over the side to write their names in history, with a 22-14 win that sends Newcastle to their first grand final in 25 years.

Cleary suffered a compound fracture after a tackle from Newcastle hooker Phoenix Crossland. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

The two sides provided a fascinating contrast from the start as they left the field following the warm-up.

Penrith, the ultimate professionals and avatars of pure ruthlessness, had eyes of steel, a picture of focus.

Newcastle, by contrast, waved to friends and family, faces beaming that they were here together on the verge of a dream.

Rage and joy proved to be equally potent fuels, with rare courage on both sides amid the furious desperation you only see when the stakes are highest.

The Knights finished with 12 on the field after Crossland's dismissal but, somehow, rarely looked shorthanded.

Newcastle through to grand final after Cleary's horrific leg break The Newcastle Knights are through to their first NRL Grand Final since 2001, defeating the Penrith Panthers 22-14 after Nathan Cleary suffered a catastrophic leg injury in the first half.

There is a temptation to call that a miracle, but Newcastle didn't need divine intervention to flat-out-play the Panthers in a second half.

They bent occasionally but never broke as Penrith fought hard, denied only by a series of last-gasp efforts from the Knights.

Kalyn Ponga pulled off a tackle on Moses Leota that any footy hit man would have been proud of. Mat Croker dived on loose balls like they were live grenades.

Dane Gagai played like his Newcastle life depended on it, and given he has earned one last day as a Knight, it kind of did.

They were able to take advantage of the Panthers not quite being their razor-sharp selves, as best typified by Smith's first try off a quick tap that caught Penrith on the hop.

The Panthers missed Cleary, their edges blunted, but Casey McLean came agonisingly close to scoring.

It is a mark of the steel in the Panthers that they weren't out of it until Sandon Smith's late intercept try, even with injuries mounting.

Aside from Cleary — already carrying a broken foot into the game — Blaize Talagi did his Achilles, Dylan Edwards hurt his PCL and Isaah Yeo defied belief to play through a torn pec.

They regrouped well in the moments after Cleary's injury, scoring through Lindsay Smith while the game was still in something of a punch-drunk stupor.

But they did not trouble the scorers again as Newcastle ran in three tries in the second half, all of which began from their own side of halfway.

Newcastle have a chance to create a special piece of history. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

That ability to strike fast and from anywhere on the field is the Knights' greatest gift — it has happened too many times to call this a charmed run or a triumph of abstract, random brilliance.

It has taken them through a high-octane South Sydney, to the heart of Auckland and back and now, a man down and all, through the greatest dynasty many will ever know.

That dynasty is not at its end, but preliminary final losses in each of the past two years show how thin the margins have become.

Penrith are still one of the heavyweights, but the world is changing and Newcastle, with their speed and hunger and endless belief, are the first of the new powers to rise.

Those Knights will be underdogs again next Sunday against the Roosters, with all their glory and splendour, and they must overcome the weight of history.

Of the 117 premiers in the history of Australian rugby league, 115 have finished in the top four. For Newcastle to prevail, it is beyond once in a lifetime and closer to once in the lifetime of the sport.

But after what the Knights have been through and what they have done to get here, the odds seem to matter little.

At this point it feels like there is nothing Newcastle cannot do, no challenge they cannot rise to and no foe they could fear.

World.title: Manhunt for gunmen who killed 27 in two shootings in South Africa
World.content:
South African police have launched a manhunt after gunmen killed at least 27 people in two mass shootings in Cape Town and Johannesburg.

The first incident occurred about 9:30pm local time on Saturday when eight gunmen armed with assault rifles stormed a bar west of Johannesburg, killing 17 people and wounding 15 others.

Police said the suspects opened fire on customers drinking outside before moving inside where they continued to shoot.

The victims included 13 males and four females, police said.

In a statement posted by South African police on social media, the shooters "allegedly searched some patrons and took their cellphones before fleeing the scene in two unidentified motor vehicles".

South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa said Police has photos of the suspects, and were working to track the down.

"This cannot go on like this" Mr Ramaphosa said.

Illegal mining motive

Authorities were still working to establish the motives for the shootings near Johannesburg and Cape Town, but initial investigations suggested one could be a turf war between illegal miners and the other a business rivalry.

Residents said illegal miners, known locally as zama zamas from an isiZulu expression for "taking a chance", live in the area where powerful gangs control the illicit gold mining trade.

The province's police commissioner Tommy Mthombeni told reporters that one line of inquiry was that the shooting was a "turf war in terms of illegal mining".

Saturday's shooting could be retaliation for another at the same tavern about a month ago, he added.

They said the suspects also torched two vehicles after fleeing.

Business rivalry

Early on Sunday during a separate shooting at dining venue just outside Cape Town, gunmen killed 10 people and wounded 11 more.

Police said the shooters entered the venue near the town of Lwandle at 1:46am local time, and "shot at patrons".

Five of the victims were declared dead at the scene while the others succumbed to their injuries while being taken to hospital.

"Suspects were reportedly armed with AK-47 rifles and pistols," South African police said in a statement posted on social media on Sunday.

No suspect has been arrested in either case, police said, and detectives are working to find the gunmen.

An eyewitness video from the venue shows people dancing and singing in a crowded outdoor area when a burst of shots rings out and screams are heard.

A police official said "a business jealousy might have been the issue," following reports people had been buying alcohol in cheaper shops and going to the venue to drink.

A third attack on Tuesday night killed 11 people including a pregnant woman, after multiple gunmen opened fire at a house party in KwaMakhutha township south of Durban.

Police have not reported any arrests.

Ongoing violence

The attacks come as the country grapples with illegal firearms, gun violence and gang rivalries.

The country of about 62 million people records roughly 60 murders a day, among the highest rates globally.

In March, soldiers moved into violence hotspots in Johannesburg to support police efforts to tackle rampant crime.

President Cyril Ramaphosa described ongoing violence and crime as one of the biggest threats facing the country.

Cyril Ramaphosa says crime is one of the biggest threats facing the nation. (AP: Jerome Delay)

Despite ongoing military intervention to keep crime at bay, gun violence still remains a persistent problem.

In Johannesburg, 10 women have been killed in a single municipality in two months, the latest was found on Saturday partially unclothed and stoned to death.

A suspect has been taken into custody, police said.

The nine other victims were mostly in their 20s and 30s, with some found stripped of their clothes and showing signs of sexual assault.

Police have offered a 400,000 rand ($25,000) reward for information leading to the arrest of the killer or killers, while the Democratic Alliance, South Africa's second-largest political party, has put up a further $31,000.

Wires/ABC

World.title: UK police arrest five over alleged attack attempt on air base used by US
World.content:
Five men have been arrested on on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act after a security scare at a British air base used by the US Air Force in south-west England.

A major incident was declared, and homes were evacuated in a village near RAF Fairford, with residents moved to a nearby leisure centre on Sunday.

The five men were also charged with allegedly committing offences under the Explosives Act.

Counter-terrorism police are now leading the investigation into the incident, which authorities say has now been contained.

Gloucestershire police said army bomb disposal experts were "currently examining a number of vehicles".

The security scare comes after the British government gave authorisation to the US to use RAF Fairford to carry out strikes on Iranian missile sites that are attacking ships in the Strait of Hormuz.

An eyewitness said armed police were blocking access to the main gate of the base.

A B‑1B Lancer bomber at Fairford air base, from where the US has targeted Iranian locations. (Reuters: Toby Shepheard)

About 30 emergency vehicles, including police cars, ambulances and fire engines, were stationed in the village of Fairford.

"A number of properties are currently being evacuated following the declaration of a major incident," Gloucestershire police said in a statement.

" It follows the arrest of several men on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act. "

Police said the men were taken into custody on Sunday morning.

The area has been blocked off to traffic and residents have been evacuated. (Reuters: Toby Shepheard)

"We are working closely with our partners and are enacting the well-rehearsed plans we have in place," Gloucestershire police said.

The base has been used to deploy US bombers since the conflict in Iran began on February 28.

Iran war has spread beyond one strait The Middle East conflict isn't just widening, it's highlighting more vulnerabilities in the region.

A spokesperson for the US Air Force declined to discuss specific force protection measures.

"The 501st Combat Support Wing and our fellow UK-based Wings remain vigilant and will take appropriate actions to ensure the safety and security of our US service members, civilians, contractors, and their families," the spokesperson said.

"We constantly assess a variety of factors that determine what measures we institute or modify to protect our installations, our people and their families."

On Saturday, US President Donald Trump rejected an Iranian plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days, while threatening the possibility of further bombing.

Wires/ABC

World.title: Wallabies reduced to 11 men in chaotic upset win over world champ Boks
World.content:
The Wallabies have desperately held on to defeat the world champion Springboks 42-38 in Perth after being reduced to 11 players during the final five minutes.

In one of the most chaotic finishes in Test rugby history, the Wallabies were shown four yellow cards late in the match after comfortably leading 42-17.

Captain Harry Wilson, Ryan Lonergan, Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii and Hunter Paisami were each sent to the sin-bin by referee Andrea Piardi.

Wilson was shown a yellow card for a high shot on Malcolm Marx in the 69th minute, before the Springboks were awarded a penalty try due to an infringement from Lonergan.

As Lonergan received his marching orders, the Wallabies' lead was cut to 42-24.

They subsequently lost Suaalii for the remainder of the match after he committed an offside play.

The Springboks capitalised on their numerical advantage to score a converted try through Morné van den Berg.

Wallabies captain Harry Wilson (left) attempts to speak with referee Andrea Piardi. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

The Wallabies appeared to seal victory in the 76th minute when Tom Wright intercepted a pass from Springboks captain André Esterhuizen.

Wright raced away to cross the goal line, but the try was denied as Paisami was ruled to have made contact with Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu's head in an earlier tackle.

Paisami was given his yellow card, leaving the Wallabies with 11 players.

The Springboks got within striking distance of the Wallabies on the scoreboard after Ox Nché scored a converted try in the 78th minute.

The Wallabies' lead had been slashed to four points, but they managed to hold on and record a famous victory in front of a boisterous crowd of 54,678.

Adding to the bizarre scenes during the final 10 minutes, Piardi was forced to speak with his fellow match officials via a mobile phone following a malfunction with their communications system.

"It was a crazy last 10 minutes," Wilson told the Nine Network after the match.

"But that first 70 minutes … the way we played, we implemented our game plan. We did exactly what we wanted.

"We stepped up in the physical battle and I'm so proud of the boys."

The Wallabies survived an extraordinary finish in Perth. (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre)

Wilson was right to highlight the Wallabies' dominance until the flurry of late yellow cards.

They led 24-17 at half-time and extended their advantage in the second term with tries to Wilson and Max Jorgensen.

Lonergan helped build scoreboard pressure with two conversions and as many penalty goals.

Len Ikitau, playing in his preferred outside centre position, impressed in the first half with two tries.

His move back to the number 13 jersey meant Suaalii played on the wing, with the former NRL star handling the role superbly.

The Springboks arrived in Australia following their recent victory in the four-Test series against the All Blacks.

The physical and emotional impact of their win in the series, billed as Rugby's Greatest Rugby Rivalry, will be open to debate.

They made 13 changes to the starting line-up that defeated the All Blacks 43-28 in Baltimore earlier this month.

The triumph saw the Wallabies awarded the Mandela Challenge Plate for the first time since 2022, which was also the last occasion they beat the Springboks on Australian soil.

They face the All Blacks in the first of two Bledisloe Cup Tests in Auckland on October 10.

The return clash will be played in Sydney on October 17.

Look back at how the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: Five men arrested near British air base used by the US on suspicion of terror plot
World.content:
Updated WorldEuropeEmergency services Five men arrested near British air base used by the US on suspicion of terror plot David Crowe Updated September 28, 2026 — 4:26am ,first published 7:39pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: British police have stopped a suspected terror plot at a Royal Air Force base used by American aircraft to strike Iran, triggering an evacuation due to fears of a potential bombing. Police arrested five men at the Fairford air base, in south-west England, during a pre-dawn emergency after residents saw men in black balaclavas running toward the secure area. Authorities were called in to check three white vans for explosives. A bomb disposal robot was used to check the suspects’ vans, which were painted to look like commercial vehicles carrying fuel and were driven to the airfield in the night. Local residents shared this image online of the arrests of the five men. Armed police maintain road blocks and security checks around RAF Fairford. Getty Images



US President Donald Trump hailed the work by the British authorities and said the suspects had been under surveillance for a “long time” and were attempting to do “big damage” to the base. Editor's pick Opinion

UK As three countries move to quit UK, a Brexit reversal might be its only hope George Brandis Former high commissioner to the UK and federal attorney-general At least 85 households were evacuated, with residents taken to a community centre in the nearby town of Cirencester because of the concern about the scale of a potential explosion. The suspected plot marks a major escalation in the security threats to British bases due to the war in the Middle East, as American forces rely on Fairford to refuel and maintain the B-1 bombers that have struck Iran since the war began on February 28. One local farmer told London’s Telegraph that she saw the men and the vans on a road at about 1.30am on Sunday (10.30am Sunday AEST ). She drove away quickly to alert the police.



“I saw a group of Middle Eastern-looking young guys running off through the trees,” she told The Telegraph. “Some of them had masks or balaclavas on, and they all scattered ahead of us as we drove back past. “Some of them ran into the fields, and some of them turned to run towards the air base. We realised this was something pretty serious. We knew the air base had a credible threat of a terrorist attack before last night. So as soon as I saw them I was worried. Police at a road block near the RAF Fairford as the incident unfolded. Alamy Stock Photo “I mean, you don’t see masked men running around at half one in the morning in the countryside near a secure air base and not have concerns.”



British media outlets including the BBC published photographs of the vans and five suspects sitting on the ground near the airfield. The BBC said the image was said to come from a WhatsApp group of local residents. The national broadcaster’s Verify team geolocated the image to a place near where the white vans were parked. RAF Fairford is located west of Oxford and has been shared by RAF and US Air Force personnel for decades, making it a target for protesters in the past. Police made no comment on the possible motive for the suspected plot and did not say whether they believed the alleged perpetrators were protesters, Islamists or agents of a foreign state. Gloucestershire Police said they received a call at around 12.45am on Sunday about three suspicious vehicles travelling towards RAF Fairford.



“Armed officers responded and subsequently arrested five men in the Whelford area on suspicion of committing offences under the Explosives Act,” the police said. “The men were taken into custody where they remain. Counterterrorism police are now leading the investigation.” A 400-metre cordon was set up around the white vans while the British Army’s Explosive Ordinance Disposal unit examined them. “Work to establish the full nature of this incident is ongoing and we are in constant communication with our partners locally and nationally,” the police said. Speaking to reporters in the US, Trump praised the UK authorities for the arrests and said the suspects had been under investigation.



“They were looking to do big damage to our fort,” he said, referring to the air force base. “And working with the British worked out great. “We had them under view for a long time and we got them.”

World.title: 150,000 words, zero guarantees: Bullock’s high-stakes interest rate revolution
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalRBA 150,000 words, zero guarantees: Bullock’s high-stakes interest rate revolution Shane Wright September 28, 2026 — 4:25am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Across 22 press conferences and 150,000 words, Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock has headed a revolution in how interest rates are set in this nation. The person who is most central to Australians’ day-to-day economic fortunes stood up on February 6, 2024, to face her first press outing in charge of the central bank. Michele Bullock was all smiles at her first press conference as RBA governor in February 2024. Louise Kennerley Since then, she has answered almost 600 questions while speaking directly to millions of borrowers, investors, business operators and people with savings. At that press conference, the first by an RBA governor outside the turmoil of the COVID pandemic, she spent an hour warning that the bank was “not ruling in or out anything”, explained the damage caused by inflation and reflected on how her children had saved to pay for tickets to Taylor Swift’s Eras Tour of Australia.



While Bullock’s predecessor, Philip Lowe, had done a handful of press conferences during the pandemic, the event on February 6, 2024, marked a critical turning point in how the Reserve Bank would explain interest rates, the economy and even the inflationary impact of major touring artists. By most measures, Bullock – and the bank – affects the daily economic lives of Australians in more direct ways than Treasurer Jim Chalmers or his state counterparts. Each decision to cut, hike or hold rates has billions of dollars riding on it, the most visible being the potential change in millions of monthly mortgage payments. But until the press conferences began, the bank’s communication could only be described as cryptic. For instance, there were decades when the RBA did not even tell the public if official interest rates had been changed. Former Reserve Bank governor Phil Lowe at a rare pandemic-era press conference after the bank’s July board meeting in 2021. James Brickwood That had improved dramatically under a succession of governors, beginning with Bernie Fraser and then the significant steps taken by both Glenn Stevens and Lowe. But the independent review of the bank released in 2023 urged the RBA to take the next step – have the governor face a gaggle of journalists.



In less than three years, she has arguably answered more questions from the media than the past five governors put together. Ahead of another critical press conference at which she is likely to confirm another interest rate rise for the nation’s borrowers, an analysis of every word uttered by Bullock across her 22 press appearances shows just how her communication with the public has changed, albeit with one constant. Uncertainty. The hold phase (2024) Bullock chaired her first meeting as RBA governor in October 2023. A month later, the bank pushed the official cash rate to 4.35 per cent. It would not change until early 2025. This was the start of the RBA’s “hold phase”.



Her first press conference marked not only the bank’s new way to communicate with the public but a year-long period in which economists and the media tried to understand Bullock and her view of inflation and the economy. Philip Lowe had talked often about the “narrow path” the bank was trying to negotiate through, and out of, the pandemic. It was one of his defining analogies. But Bullock revealed her own key catchphrase early in that February press conference. “We are not ruling out what we might have to do next. We’re not ruling in or out anything.” (February 6, 2024)



Bullock held eight press conferences during 2024. She used the term “not ruling in or out” 11 times in seven of those press grillings. That first occasion facing a room full of journalists also marked the initial utterance of an even more common refrain – that inflation is not good. Bullock has used a variation of the “inflation is bad” term on at least 21 occasions, or effectively every time she has conducted a press conference. Usually “high inflation is bad for everyone” or “inflation hurts all Australians”. While serious in her discussion about the economy, Bullock has proven to have a sense of mischief. At that very first press conference, she was asked about services inflation.



Describing the concept of services as something “that you can’t drop on your foot”, she then went on to discuss whether Taylor Swift’s high-priced Eras Tour tickets were a sign of latent inflationary pressures. “Clearly, for a lot of people, Taylor Swift is very important,” she said. Loading It was in August 2024 that she suggested those who knew exactly what the RBA should do might be showing overconfidence. “I’ve read commentators with absolute certainty that we must lower interest rates … I’ve also heard commentators with absolute certainty that we must raise interest rates now. I wish I had their certainty.” (August 6, 2024)



The rate cut phase (2025) At her first press conference in 2025, Bullock confirmed news welcomed by home borrowers, business owners and Anthony Albanese – official interest rates would be cut. The quarter percentage-point reduction was, the governor said, recognition that inflation pressures had eased and wages growth was moderating. But it came with a large caveat. “The board judges it’s time to reduce a little bit of that restrictiveness, but we cannot declare victory on inflation just yet.” (February 18, 2025)



War, particularly Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, had been a key factor in the oil price surge that contributed to the interest rate rises of 2022 and 2023. But another type of war was about to upend everything. On April 2, Donald Trump held court outside the White House where he announced his “liberation day tariffs”. From Brazilian soybean farmers to the penguins and seals of Australia’s Heard and McDonald Islands, no one was spared from the Trump tariff onslaught. Related Article Trade wars The tiny Australian islands no one expected to draw Trump’s fury The turmoil roiled financial markets, economies and the thinking of every central banker. The Reserve Bank briefly discussed a half percentage point cut to offset the expected fallout. “Since our last meeting, global economic and policy uncertainty has increased substantially following tariff announcements by the US administration … It’s been a complete rollercoaster, I’d have to say.” (May 20, 2025)



Business operators, consumers and investors all prefer stability when it comes to the economy. But Trump, the leader of the world’s largest economy, was deliberately adding instability. At half of the governor’s press conferences, the Reserve also releases its quarterly outlook on the economy. These “statements on monetary policy” contain key forecasts on everything from inflation to household spending. Through the hold phase, these outlooks had contained the word uncertainty on 104 separate occasions. In the May report alone, released as the governor discussed the Trump rollercoaster, uncertainty got used 132 times. In Bullock’s own words, it was even worse than that. “The key point about the situation we’re in is it’s not just uncertain, it’s actually unpredictable.” (May 20, 2025)



So common were Bullock’s references to uncertainty becoming that we created a measure of it. While Trump abandoned his liberation day tariffs (only to revisit them a year later), the Reserve Bank’s own faith in its fight against inflation started to weaken as the year progressed. At the last meeting of the year, Bullock noted that inflation had picked up, but it wasn’t yet clear whether it was a permanent lift or a passing phase. It was also the first time that she faced a question about data centres. The explosion in private sector spending on these was only just starting to be noticed. It would be an issue of much more importance as the bank entered the third distinct phase of Bullock’s tenure.



The rate hike phase (2026) Bullock opened her first press conference of this year by confirming an increase in the cash rate – the first of three straight rate rises. “The recent run of data gives the board a clear enough view that the underlying pulse of inflation is too strong.” (February 3, 2026) The move was not unexpected. Inflation had clearly increased through the previous two months with little sign it would ease without tighter monetary policy.



But this was on February 3. The uncertainty that had dominated her first two years facing press conferences was to climb again three weeks later when US and Israeli forces launched Operation Epic Fury against Iran. At the bank’s mid-March meeting, where the cash rate was lifted again, the impact of the Iran war was still being digested. “If the Middle East conflicts get worse or are not resolved soon, higher fuel costs will push inflation here even higher. There’s also a risk that global growth slows, which could flow on to lower growth here.” (March 17, 2026) While Donald Trump had said he expected the war to be over in four to five weeks, most outside observers were far more sceptical of a short conflict. Some of that scepticism was evident in the bank’s March decision. It was a 5-4 vote to hike.



For a central bank, pushing up interest rates to deal with inflation that may be fuelled by an event beyond its control – such as a war in the Middle East – is the worst of all worlds. It was Bullock who first raised the prospect of an economic downturn. Related Article Opinion

US politics Alarms flashing red as Trump takes US debt to level almost beyond comprehension Shane Wright Senior economics correspondent “We don’t want to see a recession or a large rise in unemployment if we can avoid it.” (March 17, 2026) The war caused havoc with the bank’s own key forecasts. In early February, the bank expected headline inflation would be 4.2 per cent by June, with underlying at 3.7 per cent. By May, with the war still going, it forecast inflation to hit 4.8 per cent in June (with underlying at 3.8 per cent). But in August, inflation was actually at 3.9 per cent with underlying at 3.6 per cent.



At the May meeting, where the scary forecasts for an inflation spike were digested, the bank pushed up the cash rate for a third time this year. But, like her entire term so far in charge of the bank, the decision was grounded in events from overseas. “It’s quite possible that we wouldn’t have had to increase interest rates a third time if the shock hadn’t occurred, but the fact is the [oil] shock did occur.” (May 5, 2026) Now, financial markets are convinced the Reserve will drive up the cash rate to 4.6 per cent by year’s end – perhaps as soon as later this month. That would take the cash rate to its highest rate since 2011. The federal government and borrowers are bracing for the hit that will come as the bank struggles to get inflation within its 2-3 per cent target, something it has achieved in just 20 of the past 138 months going back to 2014. All of this analysis is up to Bullock’s last press conference in August. Since then, interest rates on government debt have soared, oil prices have pushed beyond $US100 a barrel, and Donald Trump has promised $US5000 cheques to voters and banned Canadian yoghurt (among other goods) for American consumers.



When Bullock faces her next press conference on Tuesday, the only certainty is that the governor will talk again about the uncertainty facing her and the Reserve Bank. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘A lonely hearts club’: The Sunday market where people shop by torchlight
World.content:
NationalWAPlaces of Perth ‘A lonely hearts club’: The Sunday market where people shop by torchlight Indigo Lemay-Conway September 28, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

While most people are still tucked in bed on a Sunday morning, bargain hunters and sellers south of Perth have already begun their day. For more than 40 years the Melville Markets have been an institution for people to sell their second hand goods and for buyers to find an epic score. Looking for something to do on a Sunday morning? Well, the Melville Markets might be the answer. Indigo Lemay Conway But getting a spot in the Melville Plaza Shopping Centre carpark is no easy feat, and requires some serious dedication. For Valerie and Stephen Brennan, setting up their stalls is a 12-hour process.



While the markets officially open at 6am, the duo – among a number of other stallholders – will arrive at the car park at 6pm the previous night to drop off their car to reserve a spot. Shoppers arrive to the Melville Markets by 4.30am to look for a bargain while traders set up their stalls. Indigo Lemay Conway “We usually get here at 6pm, put one car and some witches hats out and go home and sleep. Then we leave home at 1.30am and come back,” Valerie said. “We will sit in the car for about an hour, and then we set up.” The couple sets up across six car bays, which costs them $120 or $20 per car bay. They sell second-hand clothing, shoes and accessories.



“If it’s raining, we’ll go to Karrinyup SwapMart because it’s undercover, but here there are better sales. We get much, much more money,” Valerie said. On a good day, the duo will make more than $1000 in sales. But they’re not alone with setting up early, as Stephen points out many people will sleep in their cars overnight to reserve a spot as the markets are a first-come-first-serve basis. “They’ve always known that Melville is the place to get a good bargain,” he said. Stalls across the market will vary from second-hand items like clothing and accessories to art, books, tools, bikes and plants.



Friends Anna Ott and Lucia Zanini arrived at 4.30am and said people were already looking through their bags with torches on their heads. “We come here just to declutter a little bit and instead of giving it all to the op shop, maybe we can make a little bit of money,” Ott said. Friends Anna ott and Lucia zanini arrived at 4.30 to sell their second hand goods. Indigo Lemay Conway “I think most of these items have a second life.” Zanini said the markets are a good way to socialise as well.



“I think it’s a good idea as well to share it with a friend, it’s kind of a fun thing to do, and something that is really easy to access for people to do,” she said. Paula Garcia at her stall at the Melville Markets. Indigo Lemay Conway One thing that sets the Melville Markets apart from others in Perth are the prices. Paula Garcia said while some sellers can make great money, it really is a buyers’ market. “If you are the buyer, it’s amazing. But if you want to sell these things to make a lot of money, it’s harder,” she said.



“A guy was telling me that I should sell my things more expensive, but this is not the place.” Items are typically priced anywhere between $2 and $30, with more niche pieces selling for a higher price tag. Garcia uses the markets to declutter some of her wardrobe, and sell her handmade pottery. “I’ve been making pottery for a couple of years really just for fun, and just gave it to my friends, just because it was just a way of practicing,” she said. “So at least selling at the markets, I can make a little bit of money to just buy more clay and make more pieces.”



Dani Hansen has been both a buyer and a seller at the markets for around 15 years, but these days she’s more of a peruser. Dani Hansen, right, with her children Isabella and Jarvis shopping at the markets. Indigo Lemay Conway “Sometimes you just get absolute gems. I think now as women, we consume so much, and we don’t know where else to sell stuff as well,” she said. “So it’s great to see what’s down here. I think when you do a big wardrobe clean out, then this is a great place to come.” Run by the Melville Rotary Club, the markets first began in 1984 in the same location they’re in today.



In one morning the market raises around $4500 and in a good year more than $80,000 for local charities. Market manager Kareena Ballard says there are strict rules on what people can and can’t sell. “It’s got to be second-hand, and we’re allowed to sell plants,” she said. “Because we’re not allowed to also be in competition with the shopping centre. The shopping centre gives us the license to use their grounds, and we have to be out by 10am.” Ballard describes the traders and items sold as “eclectic”



“It’s a great meeting place for people who once a week get together. It’s a bit of a lonely hearts club,” she said. Rotary captain Trevor ridgwell, Ross Ballard and Melville Market manager Kareena Ballard. Indigo Lemay Conway The markets run from 6am to 10am every Sunday except for Christmas and New Year’s Day and while winter attracts slightly fewer traders, summer is a different ball game. “For sellers, some of them have sold everything by 6am because people come down here, especially in the summer, with torches on their heads ready to buy,” Ballard said. World.title: Wow. Just wow. Reduced to 11 men, the Wallabies pulled off a victory of pure grit and resilience
World.content:
SportRugby UnionWallabies Opinion Wow. Just wow. Reduced to 11 men, the Wallabies pulled off a victory of pure grit and resilience Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author September 28, 2026 — 2:58am

September 28, 2026 — 2:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The hell with the match report, let’s just go straight to the exultation. Wow! Just WOW! This, friends, was a Test match for the ages, one for the Wallabies to put in a bottle and place on the very top shelf - one for us all to take down when the days grow cold and we grow old, to take out the cork and say: this, this was how good Australian rugby could be at its very best! Loading And it wasn’t just the extraordinary result, a spanking 42-38 victory in Perth over the incumbent back-to-back world champion Springboks, the No.1 ranked team in the world for no less than 52 of the last 53 weeks. It was the manner in which they did it, the chutzpah, verve and swerve they showed for the first 68 minutes of the match to completely dominate in all aspects of play. And then what took the breath away was how they managed to overcome the unprecedented challenges thrown at them in the last 10 minutes to win anyway, the resilience they displayed to triumph against all odds, just when they had every reason to lose.



Let’s go back. Going into this match, we of rugby could legitimately ask ourselves: on this extraordinary footballing weekend in Australia, just what could the Code-of-XV, deliver in the way of drama that could compare to what we had just seen in the other codes? It was not going to be easy. Len Ikitau makes a break to score a try against the Springboks. Getty Images After all, the Socceroos had just had a fabulous 1-1 draw with Brazil in Townsville – including a stupendous goal from Nestory Irankunda – and were unlucky not to get an outright victory over the perennial world champions, thwarted only by a Brazilian goal in the 95th minute.



In the AFL, you had the Fremantle Dockers on the edge of their first-ever grand final victory - three goals up with four minutes to go, only for the Brisbane Lions to reel off four goals for a staggeringly dramatic result. In the NRL preliminary final on Sunday, we saw the team of their generation, Penrith, beaten in a wonderfully open match by the working-class heroes of Newcastle, who were no less than wooden spooners last year! Yup, the hard-as-steel men of the hard-as-steel city, came from nowhere, to pass Makybe Diva at the post! So, seriously, what could rugby do against all that? Well, how ’bout this? How ’bout the Wallabies take on the best team in the world, and then completely dominate them in all facets of play? How ’bout against the most feared pack in the world, our blokes more than hold their own to shove them about in the scrum, steal balls from their lineouts, and knock them over like-nine-pins in our own fearsome forward rushes, led by Fraser McReight and skipper Harry Wilson, with Jeremy Williams and Angus Bell riding shotgun. Huh? HUH? Not bad, yes?



How ’bout in the backs - led by the masterful halfback Ryan Lonergan and the imperially imperious Len Ikitau in the centres – the smaller blokes in gold jerseys unleash havoc of their own, starting with two tries to the man they call “Flick-itau” in the first half. Related Article Australian rugby ‘Nothing could have prepared us for that’: Incredible scenes as 11-man Wallabies upset the world champion Boks On the back of that performance, the Wallabies led 24-17 at the break, before a singularly strange thing happened in the second half. We all knew that the much vaunted Bok bench – the “bomb squad” of brilliant players they’d kept in reserve - was going to come on and blow things up. The expectation was that they would restore order and dominate. Instead, they were blown up! The Wallabies continued to dominate all the same, in no small part due to the heroics of Max Jorgensen on one wing, and Joseph Aukuso Suaalii on the other. Suaalii demonstrated once more just how good he can be in the air, while getting through a mountain of work. Jorgensen, too, constantly plucked the ball from the skies to cause the South Africans endless problems, including one runaway intercept try. On the strength of Lonergan kicking all but one conversion, the Wallabies were so dominant overall they had a 25-point lead, 42-17 with 12 minutes to go against – did I mention? - far and away the best team in the world! That would have been enough to write home to mother about.



But we had seen nothing yet. For after Harry Wilson, Ryan Lonergan, Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii and Hunter Paisami were sin-binned in quick succession, it meant that for the better part of the final 12 minutes, the Wallabies were down to just 11 players. In unprecedented scenes, they had to try to hold back a green tide of 15 rampaging Boks that kept crashing on our shores with ever greater ferocity. Of course, with those mathematics the visitors couldn’t be completely stopped and the Boks did indeed score three tries in that period to make it 42-38. But that last one? Yeah, nah.



The Wallabies had come too far, played too well and overcome too many challenges to succumb and refused to cede. Instead they clung on like cats to a curtain, tackled themselves red-raw, and when granted a blessed penalty kick at the death, it was over to Jorgensen to forget the goal attempt and just kick into the grand-stand instead, to finish the game. Ben Donaldson was too quick for the Springboks. Getty Images 42-38, to the goodies! As I say, a truly great victory. Most wonderfully it was a super lead-in to both the Bledisloe which begins in a fortnight in Auckland – dare we hope? – and next year’s home Rugby World Cup. I have said for yonks that this generation of Wallabies have greatness in them if they can just put it together. Tonight, in Perth, we saw it. The fact they have not been defeated in their last six Test matches proves the point.



In one of the most dramatic football weekends in Australian history, the Wallabies more than held their own. Congratulations to them. And bring on the All Blacks!

World.title: AFLW round seven: Magpies finally record a win, frustration continues for St Kilda
World.content:
St Kilda’s frustrating season continued on Sunday as they remained winless despite taking a 15-point lead into half-time against Gold Coast Suns at People First Stadium.

The Saints came out hot as Jesse Tawhiao-Wardlaw kicked four of her career best five goals in the first half but the Suns powered back into the match kicking four goals in the third term to regain the lead eventually winning by 30 points.

Dekota Baron of the Suns handballs under pressure from the Saints. Getty Images

Suns star Charlie Rowbottom posted a game-high 38 disposals as her side kicked eight goals to one after half-time including a gut-busting running goal from Dekota Baron in the closing stages of the match.

“I’m so rapt with the girls and their fightback,” Rowbottom told Kayo.

“The Saints came out really hot and I’m so happy we won the arm wrestle.

“We just came back to basics, came back to working for each other.”

The Suns sit in fifth place at the end of round seven with a 5-2 record while the pressure grows on the Saints who remain on the bottom of the ladder at 0-7 with the least points scored and the most points conceded.

Serene Watson led the Saints with 25 possessions and Georgia Patrikios had 22 possessions.

The Suns lost Annabel Kievit to a suspected knee injury in the second half.

World.title: We get the funniest looks
World.content:
The following celebrity encounter (C8) from Jeff Wall of Thirroul is a little bit up in the air: “On a Pan Am jumbo flight out of Heathrow to New York in the summer of ’78, at the small ovular bar at the back of the lower deck (when flying was a joy), I was having a yarn with a Texan oil man over a beer, when George Best descended the stairs from first class. Five minutes later, the diminutive Davy Jones from the Monkees joined the shout.”

Eric Scott of Bondi Junction was “inspired by Seppo Ranki (C8), and had my first dabble in AI to find that my contributions to C8 are ‘witty submissions, sharp observations and humorous anecdotes’ while my letters are ‘concise and often witty’. What is rather worrying is finding that AI provides career entries for two positions I have held in the last twenty years, describing me in the second as ‘a separate Eric Scott’. That could be useful if ever called before ICAC. Instead of saying ‘I don’t recall’ I have AI to prove that it was not I.”

The expert systems concluded that Don Bain of Port Macquarie’s greatest C8 achievement is the Mal, Jono and Vic scoop: “I consulted AI but found only opprobrium against my name. ‘Responsible for the spurious notion that the venerated George Manojlovic was no more than a pseudonym for a trio of talented Herald writers, a preposterous theory, quickly disproved but lingering in the minds of some’.”

Judy Klein of Double Bay minds her language (C8): “Anyone needing ‘Romani oppidum oppugnobant’? It’s all that remains after years of Latin lessons. You never know when ‘The Romans are attacking the town’ may come in handy.”

“Visiting the Wollombi Sculpture Festival over the weekend, my wife and I came across a Bunya pine in the yard of the local gallery,” writes Malcolm McEwen of North Turramurra. “There was a sign on it with writing so small I had to stand close to read it, right under the branches. It warned that the tree’s massive (up to 10 kilogram) nuts could fall without warning, and advised not to stand close.”

World.title: Five men arrested near British air base used by the US on suspicion of terror plot
World.content:
Updated WorldEuropeEmergency services Five men arrested near British air base used by the US on suspicion of terror plot David Crowe Updated September 28, 2026 — 4:26am ,first published 7:39pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: British police have stopped a suspected terror plot at a Royal Air Force base used by American aircraft to strike Iran, triggering an evacuation due to fears of a potential bombing. Police arrested five men at the Fairford air base, in south-west England, during a pre-dawn emergency after residents saw men in black balaclavas running toward the secure area. Authorities were called in to check three white vans for explosives. A bomb disposal robot was used to check the suspects’ vans, which were painted to look like commercial vehicles carrying fuel and were driven to the airfield in the night. Local residents shared this image online of the arrests of the five men. Armed police maintain road blocks and security checks around RAF Fairford. Getty Images



US President Donald Trump hailed the work by the British authorities and said the suspects had been under surveillance for a “long time” and were attempting to do “big damage” to the base. Editor's pick Opinion

UK As three countries move to quit UK, a Brexit reversal might be its only hope George Brandis Former high commissioner to the UK and federal attorney-general At least 85 households were evacuated, with residents taken to a community centre in the nearby town of Cirencester because of the concern about the scale of a potential explosion. The suspected plot marks a major escalation in the security threats to British bases due to the war in the Middle East, as American forces rely on Fairford to refuel and maintain the B-1 bombers that have struck Iran since the war began on February 28. One local farmer told London’s Telegraph that she saw the men and the vans on a road at about 1.30am on Sunday (10.30am Sunday AEST ). She drove away quickly to alert the police.



“I saw a group of Middle Eastern-looking young guys running off through the trees,” she told The Telegraph. “Some of them had masks or balaclavas on, and they all scattered ahead of us as we drove back past. “Some of them ran into the fields, and some of them turned to run towards the air base. We realised this was something pretty serious. We knew the air base had a credible threat of a terrorist attack before last night. So as soon as I saw them I was worried. Police at a road block near the RAF Fairford as the incident unfolded. Alamy Stock Photo “I mean, you don’t see masked men running around at half one in the morning in the countryside near a secure air base and not have concerns.”



British media outlets including the BBC published photographs of the vans and five suspects sitting on the ground near the airfield. The BBC said the image was said to come from a WhatsApp group of local residents. The national broadcaster’s Verify team geolocated the image to a place near where the white vans were parked. RAF Fairford is located west of Oxford and has been shared by RAF and US Air Force personnel for decades, making it a target for protesters in the past. Police made no comment on the possible motive for the suspected plot and did not say whether they believed the alleged perpetrators were protesters, Islamists or agents of a foreign state. Gloucestershire Police said they received a call at around 12.45am on Sunday about three suspicious vehicles travelling towards RAF Fairford.



“Armed officers responded and subsequently arrested five men in the Whelford area on suspicion of committing offences under the Explosives Act,” the police said. “The men were taken into custody where they remain. Counterterrorism police are now leading the investigation.” A 400-metre cordon was set up around the white vans while the British Army’s Explosive Ordinance Disposal unit examined them. “Work to establish the full nature of this incident is ongoing and we are in constant communication with our partners locally and nationally,” the police said. Speaking to reporters in the US, Trump praised the UK authorities for the arrests and said the suspects had been under investigation.



“They were looking to do big damage to our fort,” he said, referring to the air force base. “And working with the British worked out great. “We had them under view for a long time and we got them.”
