World.title: 150,000 words, zero guarantees: Bullock’s high-stakes interest rate revolution
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalRBA 150,000 words, zero guarantees: Bullock’s high-stakes interest rate revolution Shane Wright September 28, 2026 — 4:25am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Across 22 press conferences and 150,000 words, Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock has headed a revolution in how interest rates are set in this nation. The person who is most central to Australians’ day-to-day economic fortunes stood up on February 6, 2024, to face her first press outing in charge of the central bank. Michele Bullock was all smiles at her first press conference as RBA governor in February 2024. Louise Kennerley Since then, she has answered almost 600 questions while speaking directly to millions of borrowers, investors, business operators and people with savings. At that press conference, the first by an RBA governor outside the turmoil of the COVID pandemic, she spent an hour warning that the bank was “not ruling in or out anything”, explained the damage caused by inflation and reflected on how her children had saved to pay for tickets to Taylor Swift’s Eras Tour of Australia.



While Bullock’s predecessor, Philip Lowe, had done a handful of press conferences during the pandemic, the event on February 6, 2024, marked a critical turning point in how the Reserve Bank would explain interest rates, the economy and even the inflationary impact of major touring artists. By most measures, Bullock – and the bank – affects the daily economic lives of Australians in more direct ways than Treasurer Jim Chalmers or his state counterparts. Each decision to cut, hike or hold rates has billions of dollars riding on it, the most visible being the potential change in millions of monthly mortgage payments. But until the press conferences began, the bank’s communication could only be described as cryptic. For instance, there were decades when the RBA did not even tell the public if official interest rates had been changed. Former Reserve Bank governor Phil Lowe at a rare pandemic-era press conference after the bank’s July board meeting in 2021. James Brickwood That had improved dramatically under a succession of governors, beginning with Bernie Fraser and then the significant steps taken by both Glenn Stevens and Lowe. But the independent review of the bank released in 2023 urged the RBA to take the next step – have the governor face a gaggle of journalists.



In less than three years, she has arguably answered more questions from the media than the past five governors put together. Ahead of another critical press conference at which she is likely to confirm another interest rate rise for the nation’s borrowers, an analysis of every word uttered by Bullock across her 22 press appearances shows just how her communication with the public has changed, albeit with one constant. Uncertainty. The hold phase (2024) Bullock chaired her first meeting as RBA governor in October 2023. A month later, the bank pushed the official cash rate to 4.35 per cent. It would not change until early 2025. This was the start of the RBA’s “hold phase”.



Her first press conference marked not only the bank’s new way to communicate with the public but a year-long period in which economists and the media tried to understand Bullock and her view of inflation and the economy. Philip Lowe had talked often about the “narrow path” the bank was trying to negotiate through, and out of, the pandemic. It was one of his defining analogies. But Bullock revealed her own key catchphrase early in that February press conference. “We are not ruling out what we might have to do next. We’re not ruling in or out anything.” (February 6, 2024)



Bullock held eight press conferences during 2024. She used the term “not ruling in or out” 11 times in seven of those press grillings. That first occasion facing a room full of journalists also marked the initial utterance of an even more common refrain – that inflation is not good. Bullock has used a variation of the “inflation is bad” term on at least 21 occasions, or effectively every time she has conducted a press conference. Usually “high inflation is bad for everyone” or “inflation hurts all Australians”. While serious in her discussion about the economy, Bullock has proven to have a sense of mischief. At that very first press conference, she was asked about services inflation.



Describing the concept of services as something “that you can’t drop on your foot”, she then went on to discuss whether Taylor Swift’s high-priced Eras Tour tickets were a sign of latent inflationary pressures. “Clearly, for a lot of people, Taylor Swift is very important,” she said. Loading It was in August 2024 that she suggested those who knew exactly what the RBA should do might be showing overconfidence. “I’ve read commentators with absolute certainty that we must lower interest rates … I’ve also heard commentators with absolute certainty that we must raise interest rates now. I wish I had their certainty.” (August 6, 2024)



The rate cut phase (2025) At her first press conference in 2025, Bullock confirmed news welcomed by home borrowers, business owners and Anthony Albanese – official interest rates would be cut. The quarter percentage-point reduction was, the governor said, recognition that inflation pressures had eased and wages growth was moderating. But it came with a large caveat. “The board judges it’s time to reduce a little bit of that restrictiveness, but we cannot declare victory on inflation just yet.” (February 18, 2025)



War, particularly Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, had been a key factor in the oil price surge that contributed to the interest rate rises of 2022 and 2023. But another type of war was about to upend everything. On April 2, Donald Trump held court outside the White House where he announced his “liberation day tariffs”. From Brazilian soybean farmers to the penguins and seals of Australia’s Heard and McDonald Islands, no one was spared from the Trump tariff onslaught. Related Article Trade wars The tiny Australian islands no one expected to draw Trump’s fury The turmoil roiled financial markets, economies and the thinking of every central banker. The Reserve Bank briefly discussed a half percentage point cut to offset the expected fallout. “Since our last meeting, global economic and policy uncertainty has increased substantially following tariff announcements by the US administration … It’s been a complete rollercoaster, I’d have to say.” (May 20, 2025)



Business operators, consumers and investors all prefer stability when it comes to the economy. But Trump, the leader of the world’s largest economy, was deliberately adding instability. At half of the governor’s press conferences, the Reserve also releases its quarterly outlook on the economy. These “statements on monetary policy” contain key forecasts on everything from inflation to household spending. Through the hold phase, these outlooks had contained the word uncertainty on 104 separate occasions. In the May report alone, released as the governor discussed the Trump rollercoaster, uncertainty got used 132 times. In Bullock’s own words, it was even worse than that. “The key point about the situation we’re in is it’s not just uncertain, it’s actually unpredictable.” (May 20, 2025)



So common were Bullock’s references to uncertainty becoming that we created a measure of it. While Trump abandoned his liberation day tariffs (only to revisit them a year later), the Reserve Bank’s own faith in its fight against inflation started to weaken as the year progressed. At the last meeting of the year, Bullock noted that inflation had picked up, but it wasn’t yet clear whether it was a permanent lift or a passing phase. It was also the first time that she faced a question about data centres. The explosion in private sector spending on these was only just starting to be noticed. It would be an issue of much more importance as the bank entered the third distinct phase of Bullock’s tenure.



The rate hike phase (2026) Bullock opened her first press conference of this year by confirming an increase in the cash rate – the first of three straight rate rises. “The recent run of data gives the board a clear enough view that the underlying pulse of inflation is too strong.” (February 3, 2026) The move was not unexpected. Inflation had clearly increased through the previous two months with little sign it would ease without tighter monetary policy.



But this was on February 3. The uncertainty that had dominated her first two years facing press conferences was to climb again three weeks later when US and Israeli forces launched Operation Epic Fury against Iran. At the bank’s mid-March meeting, where the cash rate was lifted again, the impact of the Iran war was still being digested. “If the Middle East conflicts get worse or are not resolved soon, higher fuel costs will push inflation here even higher. There’s also a risk that global growth slows, which could flow on to lower growth here.” (March 17, 2026) While Donald Trump had said he expected the war to be over in four to five weeks, most outside observers were far more sceptical of a short conflict. Some of that scepticism was evident in the bank’s March decision. It was a 5-4 vote to hike.



For a central bank, pushing up interest rates to deal with inflation that may be fuelled by an event beyond its control – such as a war in the Middle East – is the worst of all worlds. It was Bullock who first raised the prospect of an economic downturn. Related Article Opinion

US politics Alarms flashing red as Trump takes US debt to level almost beyond comprehension Shane Wright Senior economics correspondent “We don’t want to see a recession or a large rise in unemployment if we can avoid it.” (March 17, 2026) The war caused havoc with the bank’s own key forecasts. In early February, the bank expected headline inflation would be 4.2 per cent by June, with underlying at 3.7 per cent. By May, with the war still going, it forecast inflation to hit 4.8 per cent in June (with underlying at 3.8 per cent). But in August, inflation was actually at 3.9 per cent with underlying at 3.6 per cent.



At the May meeting, where the scary forecasts for an inflation spike were digested, the bank pushed up the cash rate for a third time this year. But, like her entire term so far in charge of the bank, the decision was grounded in events from overseas. “It’s quite possible that we wouldn’t have had to increase interest rates a third time if the shock hadn’t occurred, but the fact is the [oil] shock did occur.” (May 5, 2026) Now, financial markets are convinced the Reserve will drive up the cash rate to 4.6 per cent by year’s end – perhaps as soon as later this month. That would take the cash rate to its highest rate since 2011. The federal government and borrowers are bracing for the hit that will come as the bank struggles to get inflation within its 2-3 per cent target, something it has achieved in just 20 of the past 138 months going back to 2014. All of this analysis is up to Bullock’s last press conference in August. Since then, interest rates on government debt have soared, oil prices have pushed beyond $US100 a barrel, and Donald Trump has promised $US5000 cheques to voters and banned Canadian yoghurt (among other goods) for American consumers.



When Bullock faces her next press conference on Tuesday, the only certainty is that the governor will talk again about the uncertainty facing her and the Reserve Bank. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

“If it’s raining, we’ll go to Karrinyup SwapMart because it’s undercover, but here there are better sales. We get much, much more money,” Valerie said. On a good day, the duo will make more than $1000 in sales. But they’re not alone with setting up early, as Stephen points out many people will sleep in their cars overnight to reserve a spot as the markets are a first-come-first-serve basis. “They’ve always known that Melville is the place to get a good bargain,” he said. Stalls across the market will vary from second-hand items like clothing and accessories to art, books, tools, bikes and plants.



Friends Anna Ott and Lucia Zanini arrived at 4.30am and said people were already looking through their bags with torches on their heads. “We come here just to declutter a little bit and instead of giving it all to the op shop, maybe we can make a little bit of money,” Ott said. Friends Anna ott and Lucia zanini arrived at 4.30 to sell their second hand goods. Indigo Lemay Conway “I think most of these items have a second life.” Zanini said the markets are a good way to socialise as well.



“I think it’s a good idea as well to share it with a friend, it’s kind of a fun thing to do, and something that is really easy to access for people to do,” she said. Paula Garcia at her stall at the Melville Markets. Indigo Lemay Conway One thing that sets the Melville Markets apart from others in Perth are the prices. Paula Garcia said while some sellers can make great money, it really is a buyers’ market. “If you are the buyer, it’s amazing. But if you want to sell these things to make a lot of money, it’s harder,” she said.



“A guy was telling me that I should sell my things more expensive, but this is not the place.” Items are typically priced anywhere between $2 and $30, with more niche pieces selling for a higher price tag. Garcia uses the markets to declutter some of her wardrobe, and sell her handmade pottery. “I’ve been making pottery for a couple of years really just for fun, and just gave it to my friends, just because it was just a way of practicing,” she said. “So at least selling at the markets, I can make a little bit of money to just buy more clay and make more pieces.”



Dani Hansen has been both a buyer and a seller at the markets for around 15 years, but these days she’s more of a peruser. Dani Hansen, right, with her children Isabella and Jarvis shopping at the markets. Indigo Lemay Conway “Sometimes you just get absolute gems. I think now as women, we consume so much, and we don’t know where else to sell stuff as well,” she said. “So it’s great to see what’s down here. I think when you do a big wardrobe clean out, then this is a great place to come.” Run by the Melville Rotary Club, the markets first began in 1984 in the same location they’re in today.



In one morning the market raises around $4500 and in a good year more than $80,000 for local charities. Market manager Kareena Ballard says there are strict rules on what people can and can’t sell. “It’s got to be second-hand, and we’re allowed to sell plants,” she said. “Because we’re not allowed to also be in competition with the shopping centre. The shopping centre gives us the license to use their grounds, and we have to be out by 10am.” Ballard describes the traders and items sold as “eclectic”



“It’s a great meeting place for people who once a week get together. It’s a bit of a lonely hearts club,” she said. Rotary captain Trevor ridgwell, Ross Ballard and Melville Market manager Kareena Ballard. Indigo Lemay Conway The markets run from 6am to 10am every Sunday except for Christmas and New Year’s Day and while winter attracts slightly fewer traders, summer is a different ball game. “For sellers, some of them have sold everything by 6am because people come down here, especially in the summer, with torches on their heads ready to buy,” Ballard said. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Wow. Just wow. Reduced to 11 men, the Wallabies pulled off a victory of pure grit and resilience
World.content:
SportRugby UnionWallabies Opinion Wow. Just wow. Reduced to 11 men, the Wallabies pulled off a victory of pure grit and resilience Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author September 28, 2026 — 2:58am

September 28, 2026 — 2:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The hell with the match report, let’s just go straight to the exultation. Wow! Just WOW! This, friends, was a Test match for the ages, one for the Wallabies to put in a bottle and place on the very top shelf - one for us all to take down when the days grow cold and we grow old, to take out the cork and say: this, this was how good Australian rugby could be at its very best! Loading And it wasn’t just the extraordinary result, a spanking 42-38 victory in Perth over the incumbent back-to-back world champion Springboks, the No.1 ranked team in the world for no less than 52 of the last 53 weeks. It was the manner in which they did it, the chutzpah, verve and swerve they showed for the first 68 minutes of the match to completely dominate in all aspects of play. And then what took the breath away was how they managed to overcome the unprecedented challenges thrown at them in the last 10 minutes to win anyway, the resilience they displayed to triumph against all odds, just when they had every reason to lose.



Let’s go back. Going into this match, we of rugby could legitimately ask ourselves: on this extraordinary footballing weekend in Australia, just what could the Code-of-XV, deliver in the way of drama that could compare to what we had just seen in the other codes? It was not going to be easy. Len Ikitau makes a break to score a try against the Springboks. Getty Images After all, the Socceroos had just had a fabulous 1-1 draw with Brazil in Townsville – including a stupendous goal from Nestory Irankunda – and were unlucky not to get an outright victory over the perennial world champions, thwarted only by a Brazilian goal in the 95th minute.



In the AFL, you had the Fremantle Dockers on the edge of their first-ever grand final victory - three goals up with four minutes to go, only for the Brisbane Lions to reel off four goals for a staggeringly dramatic result. In the NRL preliminary final on Sunday, we saw the team of their generation, Penrith, beaten in a wonderfully open match by the working-class heroes of Newcastle, who were no less than wooden spooners last year! Yup, the hard-as-steel men of the hard-as-steel city, came from nowhere, to pass Makybe Diva at the post! So, seriously, what could rugby do against all that? Well, how ’bout this? How ’bout the Wallabies take on the best team in the world, and then completely dominate them in all facets of play? How ’bout against the most feared pack in the world, our blokes more than hold their own to shove them about in the scrum, steal balls from their lineouts, and knock them over like-nine-pins in our own fearsome forward rushes, led by Fraser McReight and skipper Harry Wilson, with Jeremy Williams and Angus Bell riding shotgun. Huh? HUH? Not bad, yes?



How ’bout in the backs - led by the masterful halfback Ryan Lonergan and the imperially imperious Len Ikitau in the centres – the smaller blokes in gold jerseys unleash havoc of their own, starting with two tries to the man they call “Flick-itau” in the first half. Related Article Australian rugby ‘Nothing could have prepared us for that’: Incredible scenes as 11-man Wallabies upset the world champion Boks On the back of that performance, the Wallabies led 24-17 at the break, before a singularly strange thing happened in the second half. We all knew that the much vaunted Bok bench – the “bomb squad” of brilliant players they’d kept in reserve - was going to come on and blow things up. The expectation was that they would restore order and dominate. Instead, they were blown up! The Wallabies continued to dominate all the same, in no small part due to the heroics of Max Jorgensen on one wing, and Joseph Aukuso Suaalii on the other. Suaalii demonstrated once more just how good he can be in the air, while getting through a mountain of work. Jorgensen, too, constantly plucked the ball from the skies to cause the South Africans endless problems, including one runaway intercept try. On the strength of Lonergan kicking all but one conversion, the Wallabies were so dominant overall they had a 25-point lead, 42-17 with 12 minutes to go against – did I mention? - far and away the best team in the world! That would have been enough to write home to mother about.



But we had seen nothing yet. For after Harry Wilson, Ryan Lonergan, Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii and Hunter Paisami were sin-binned in quick succession, it meant that for the better part of the final 12 minutes, the Wallabies were down to just 11 players. In unprecedented scenes, they had to try to hold back a green tide of 15 rampaging Boks that kept crashing on our shores with ever greater ferocity. Of course, with those mathematics the visitors couldn’t be completely stopped and the Boks did indeed score three tries in that period to make it 42-38. But that last one? Yeah, nah.



The Wallabies had come too far, played too well and overcome too many challenges to succumb and refused to cede. Instead they clung on like cats to a curtain, tackled themselves red-raw, and when granted a blessed penalty kick at the death, it was over to Jorgensen to forget the goal attempt and just kick into the grand-stand instead, to finish the game. Ben Donaldson was too quick for the Springboks. Getty Images 42-38, to the goodies! As I say, a truly great victory. Most wonderfully it was a super lead-in to both the Bledisloe which begins in a fortnight in Auckland – dare we hope? – and next year’s home Rugby World Cup. I have said for yonks that this generation of Wallabies have greatness in them if they can just put it together. Tonight, in Perth, we saw it. The fact they have not been defeated in their last six Test matches proves the point.



In one of the most dramatic football weekends in Australian history, the Wallabies more than held their own. Congratulations to them. And bring on the All Blacks!
